story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Glowed
story.subtitle: A LEGO bedtime adventure through Billund, Denmark

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping LEGO bricks into a shark.

Juno sat next to him, lining up her dinosaurs in a stomping row.

"Rawr," said Juno, bashing two dinosaurs together.

Milo dug through the LEGO bin, looking for a fin piece. His hand bumped something small and warm. He pulled out one plain brick. It was glowing gold.

"Juno," he whispered. "Look at this."

The brick gave a soft CLICK. Then — POOF! — a tiny man made of LEGO hopped out, waving a tiny hard hat.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Click. I live inside every brick ever made."

"Every brick?" Milo asked.

"Even this old one," said Click. "Bricks did not always look like this. Want to see where they started?"

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. Milo grabbed the glowing brick.

WHOOOOSH! The bedroom spun like a tornado made of bricks.

They landed with a soft THUMP in a small wooden workshop. Sawdust floated in the air like snow.

A man with kind, tired eyes was carving a little wooden duck.

"That's Ole Kirk," Click whispered. "He's a carpenter — that means he builds things out of wood. In **1932**, in a town called **Billund, Denmark**, he started making wooden toys to sell."

Milo picked up the little wooden duck. "No bricks yet?"

"Not yet," said Click. "But just wait."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
Ole Kirk stood outside, painting letters on a wooden sign. He kept crossing words out.

"What word means 'play well'?" he muttered.

Juno popped up on her tiptoes. "PLAY GOOD!" she shouted, stomping her dinosaur feet.

Ole Kirk laughed. "Close! In Danish, we say 'leg godt.'"

He wrote two words on the sign, then squished them together: **LEGO**.

"In **1934**," said Click, "that became the name of his whole company."

Milo grinned. "Lee-go. I like it."

"Here's a funny thing," Click added. "In a totally different old language, far away, the word 'lego' also means 'I put together.' That is probably just a happy accident. But it fits perfectly, doesn't it?"

Juno tried to say the old language's name and it came out all wobbly, which made Milo laugh so hard he snorted.

The sign went up, fresh and shiny: LEGO.

"Play well," Milo read slowly. "I like that rule already."

Juno pressed her sticky dinosaur right under the letters. "Dino plays well too," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hissing Machine
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Time spun again. They landed beside a big clanking machine, full of pipes and a chugging motor.

HISSSSS, it went. Juno jumped, then giggled at her own jump.

"In **1947**," said Click, "Ole Kirk got one of the very first machines like this in Denmark. It could squirt hot, melted plastic into molds to make toy shapes. That's called an injection-molding machine — a machine that pushes soft, melted plastic into a shape, like squeezing toothpaste into a mold, then lets it cool hard."

Milo peered into a bucket of little plastic shapes. "Are these bricks?"

"Almost," said Click. "Watch."

The machine chugged, then — PLOP! — out dropped a small hollow brick with bumps on top.

Milo held it up to the light. "It's shiny. Not like wood at all."

"Plastic doesn't splinter," said Click, "and it never gets soggy in the rain."

Juno sniffed the brick. "Smells like... nothing."

"Exactly," laughed Click. "Good toy plastic shouldn't smell like much at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Wobbly Tower
chapters.text:
On a long table sat rows of hollow plastic bricks with bumps on top.

"In **1949**," said Click, "these were called **Automatic Binding Bricks**. They were the great-great-grandparents of your LEGO bricks at home."

Milo stacked three bricks into a little tower. He gave it a gentle push.

The tower wobbled. CLACK — it fell apart.

"They don't hold very tight," Milo said, picking up the fallen pieces.

"Good eye," said Click. "That's the one thing missing. Somebody still needs to fix it."

Juno stomped her dinosaur right next to the fallen tower. "ROAR! Dino knocked it down!"

"Dino had help," Milo laughed. "It was already wobbly."

Milo studied the wobbly tower for a long moment, tapping his chin like a true inventor.

"Hang on to that wobble," said Click, smiling a secret smile. "Someone is about to solve it. Someone pretty soon."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Tiny Tubes, Big Click
chapters.text:
A young man named Godtfred sat frowning at a loose brick in his hands.

"It needs something underneath," he mumbled, "to grab onto the bumps below."

Milo flipped a brick over and peeked at the hollow space inside. "What if there were little tube things in here? Like tiny hugging arms?"

Godtfred's eyes went wide. He grabbed a pencil and drew round tubes inside the bottom of the brick.

A new brick popped out of the machine. Milo snapped two together.

CLICK!

He pulled. It held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo yelled.

"In **1958**," said Click, "Godtfred got a special paper called a patent, which means grown-ups all agreed it was really his new idea. The date on that paper was **January 28th**."

Juno pulled two bricks apart with a POP, then clicked them back together, giggling every single time.

"Here's the best part," said Click. "A brick made back then still clicks perfectly with a brick made today. Not one single bump has changed."

Milo looked at the brick in his hand like it was magic.

Maybe it was.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Gates in Billund
chapters.text:
Tall gates swung open with a CREAK, taller than Milo's whole house.

Behind them stood tiny towns, bridges, and animals, every single piece built from LEGO bricks.

"Welcome to **LEGOLAND**," said Click. "It opened in **1968**, right next to Ole Kirk's very first factory — a factory is just a big building where lots of the same thing gets made. It's here in **Billund**, too."

Juno stomped through a tiny model town like a giant dinosaur. "STOMP STOMP! I'm bigger than the whole town!"

Milo counted little brick windows on a tiny church. "Twenty-two!" he shouted, though nobody had asked him to count.

"Close enough," Click laughed.

A small brick dinosaur stood near the path, taller than Juno. She reached out and patted it gently, careful not to knock off a single bump.

"Good hands," said Click. "Even brick dinosaurs like gentle visitors."

Milo found a brick shark half-hidden in a tiny pond and gave it a happy little wave instead of touching it. Milo wondered how many bricks the whole park used, but Click just winked and said, "More than any shark could count."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bricks for Small Hands
chapters.text:
A bin of giant bricks sat in the corner, twice the size of normal ones.

Juno grabbed two and clicked them together. CLUNK!

"These fit my hands best!" she said, holding them up proudly.

"In **1969**," said Click, "LEGO made special big bricks called **DUPLO**, sized just right for little toddler hands. Toddler means a kid who's still pretty small, like you, Juno."

Milo tried to squeeze his tiny shark pieces onto a DUPLO brick. To his surprise, they clicked right on.

"They still fit together!" Milo gasped.

"Big or small," said Click, "every LEGO brick ever made is still friends with every other one."

Juno built a tall DUPLO tower, higher than her own head, and gave it one proud pat.

"Dino tower!" she announced.

It did not wobble one single bit.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Little Yellow People
chapters.text:
A box tipped over, and tiny yellow-headed people spilled out across the floor.

Milo picked one up. Its little arms swung side to side. He popped off its hat and tried a different one instead.

"In **1978**," said Click, straightening his own tiny hard hat, "LEGO made the very first minifigures. Little people with arms that move, and hats and heads you can swap around."

"Wait," Milo said slowly. "Are you a minifigure?"

Click grinned his widest grin yet. "Took you long enough."

Juno clapped both hands. "Click is a LEGO guy!"

The golden brick in Milo's hand began to glow brighter and brighter.

"Time to go home," said Click softly. "Play well, you two."

WHOOOOSH! The bedroom spun back into place around them.

Milo and Juno landed softly on their own carpet, right where they started. The half-built shark still sat there. The dinosaurs still stood in their stomping row.

Between them, on the carpet, sat one plain, ordinary-looking brick.

Milo picked it up and held it to his ear.

It gave one tiny, warm CLICK.

"Goodnight, brick," Milo whispered, and tucked it safely into the bin for next time.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Before LEGO bricks, Ole Kirk Christiansen built wooden toys in a workshop in **Billund, Denmark**, starting in **1932**.
In **1934**, Ole Kirk named his company **LEGO**, short for Danish words meaning **"play well."**
In a different old language, the word "lego" also happens to mean "I put together" — a fun coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
In **1947**, LEGO got one of the first machines in Denmark that could squirt melted plastic into toy-shaped molds.
In **1949**, LEGO made hollow plastic bricks with bumps on top, called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — early cousins of today's bricks.
In **1958**, Godtfred added little tubes inside the bottom of each brick so they could click and hold tight, and that idea got its own special paper on **January 28th**.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly with a brick made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right beside the very first factory.
In **1969**, LEGO made bigger bricks called **DUPLO**, sized just right for little toddler hands.
In **1978**, LEGO made its very first tiny people, called **minifigures**, with arms that move and hats you can swap.

new_recurring.name: Click
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing LEGO minifigure who hops out of a golden brick to guide the children through real history or science adventures, and always says 'Play well' when it's time to go home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno landed back on their own carpet where the glowing brick settled into an ordinary one, gave a last warm click, and got tucked safely into the bin.

story.title: Theo and the Pixel Who Started It All
story.subtitle: One glitchy screen, nine stops, and fifty years of games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Line That Bounced Back (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was lying on his bedroom floor at 11:47 p.m., Roblox Studio glowing on his laptop screen.

He was supposed to be asleep an hour ago. Instead he was fixing a soccer game, trying to make a ball bounce off a wall at the right angle. It kept going in one boring straight line.

"Come on," he muttered, tapping the keyboard. "Bounce like a real ball."

The screen flickered. Black, then green. A single glowing line appeared, bouncing back and forth like a tiny tennis match with no players.

"FINALLY," said a voice. "Someone who cares about a good bounce."

A blocky green pixel popped out of the screen and landed on Theo's pillow. It had two dot eyes and a mouth like a comma.

"I'm Pip," it said. "I'm the oldest pixel in every game you've ever played. Want to see where I started?"

Theo blinked at it twice, which seemed like the correct response to a pixel talking on his pillow. "Sure," he said. "Why not."

The green line stretched into a doorway. Theo stepped through — and landed in a room full of humming machines the size of refrigerators.

"**Brookhaven National Laboratory**," Pip announced. "**1958**. This whole room is one computer."

A scientist in a white coat, **William Higinbotham**, was hunched over a round screen called an **oscilloscope** — a scientist's screen for drawing lines of light.

"Visitors' day," Higinbotham explained. "I needed something more fun than graphs." He handed Theo a metal box with a dial and a button.

On the round screen, a dot bounced over a line, like a net. Theo turned the dial. The dot's angle changed.

"It's **Tennis for Two**," Pip whispered. "The first video game anybody played just for fun."

Theo grinned and turned the dial hard. The dot rocketed over the net at a sharp angle, and Higinbotham laughed out loud.

"That's exactly the bounce my Roblox ball needs," Theo said. "An angle, not just a straight line."

"PRESS START," said Pip, who apparently said that a lot. "There's more where that came from."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Two Spaceships (1962)
chapters.text:
The doorway reopened onto a cluttered college room stacked with reels of tape.

"**MIT**, **1962**," said Pip. "Smell that? That's electricity and leftover pizza."

A fridge-sized computer called a **PDP-1** blinked lights across one wall. A student named **Steve Russell** sat in front of a round screen, chewing a pencil.

"We're stuck," Russell admitted. "Two spaceships are supposed to shoot each other. Mine keeps missing."

On the screen, two tiny ships drifted through black space, a star blinking in the middle.

"Gravity," Theo said, squinting. "Is the star pulling your ship off course?"

Russell's eyebrows shot up. "...Yes. Exactly that."

"So steer *around* the star, not straight at it," Theo said. "Like a corner kick curving around a wall of defenders."

Russell tried it. His ship swung wide, looped past the star, and clipped the enemy ship dead center. A tiny burst of pixels lit the screen.

"**WHOOOSH**," said Pip, unnecessarily, since the computer made no sound at all.

Russell went for a high five, missed, and hit his own pencil instead. Theo laughed so hard he nearly fell out of the game entirely.

"It's called **Spacewar!**," Pip said. "Two college friends and a computer that filled a whole room. Nobody even sold it. They just wanted to play."

"That's basically every Roblox game I've ever started," Theo said. "Built because somebody wanted to play it first, before anyone else even knew it existed."

Pip's comma-mouth curled into something like a smile. "Now you're getting it. Next stop smells like static and ambition."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Brown Box in the Basement (1972)
chapters.text:
The doorway dropped them into a cramped home workshop wired with cables like spaghetti.

"**Ralph Baer**," Pip said. "Some people call him the father of video games. He thinks that's a bit much."

"I do think that's a bit much," said a man soldering a circuit board, without looking up.

The TV in the corner showed two white rectangles, paddles, and a square ball bouncing between them.

"It's on a regular television," Theo said, surprised. "Not some lab machine."

"That's the whole idea," Baer said. "Everybody already owns one of these." He handed Theo a second controller. "Try it."

Theo moved his paddle. The square ball bounced his way. He missed it on purpose once, just to watch it reset, then actually tried.

"You need a box kids can plug in at home," Theo said. "Not something that fills a whole room like Pip's last stop."

Baer tapped the circuit board. "That's what I keep telling the company."

Pip fast-forwarded the doorway's glow. "**1972**," it said. "Baer's basement invention got a new name and a real box."

A sign hung above a store shelf: **Magnavox Odyssey**. Rows of the little console sat boxed and ready, the very first game console anyone could buy for their own living room.

Theo picked up a box, turning it over like a trading card. "It actually got made. It's actually real, sitting on a shelf."

"Because somebody kept tinkering in a basement," Pip said, "until a TV could play games too."

Theo set the box down carefully, like it mattered. "I want to see the game that made everyone line up with quarters."

Pip's eyes lit up. "Oh, I was hoping you'd ask that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine Full of Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
They landed in a noisy arcade, coins clinking, a crowd three people deep around one machine.

"**Atari**," Pip said. "Founded in **1972** by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**."

A wooden cabinet buzzed with a screen showing two paddles and a bouncing square, simple like Baer's TV game, but built for a crowd instead of a living room.

"It's called **Pong**," Pip said. "Put a quarter in, play until you lose."

Theo fed a coin into the slot. BEEP. The ball launched. He missed the first return completely, the paddle moved slower than he expected, then got the hang of the timing and started a rally that drew a small cheer from the strangers behind him.

"Legend has it," Pip said, lowering its voice like it was telling a ghost story, "that one of these machines got so popular it actually jammed, stuffed completely full of quarters."

"Jammed? Like, broke?" Theo asked.

"Might be a slight exaggeration," Pip admitted. "But it tells you how fast people fell for this thing. A box that bounces a square was suddenly the most popular machine in the building."

Theo watched the line forming behind him, people patting their pockets for change.

"It's basically a game that went viral before the internet existed," Theo said.

"Precisely," said Pip. "Except instead of likes, it was quarters. A *lot* of quarters."

Theo stepped aside to let the next kid play, and the machine let out a happy little BEEP as a new game began.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Cartridges, Invaders, and a Pizza (1977–1980)
chapters.text:
The arcade blurred into a toy-store aisle, shelves stacked with flat plastic rectangles.

"**1977**," Pip said. "The **Atari 2600**. Pong's cousin, except now you can swap games."

Theo picked up a rectangle with a rocket on the cover. "What's this thing?"

"A **cartridge**," Pip said. "Pop it in the slot, and the console plays a whole different game. No more machine stuck doing just one thing forever."

"That's like installing a new game instead of buying a whole new console," Theo said. "Finally, somebody with sense."

The aisle shifted into rows of arcade cabinets, one surrounded by the biggest crowd yet, white alien shapes marching down its screen.

"**1978**," Pip said. "**Space Invaders**, by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It kicked off an arcade craze nobody saw coming."

Theo grabbed the joystick and fired. The aliens marched faster the fewer of them were left, a detail that made his palms sweat a little, in a fun way, not a scary way.

"They speed up on purpose," Pip said. "To keep you nervous."

One more flicker, and a yellow circle chomped dots across a glowing maze.

"**1980**," Pip said. "**Pac-Man**, made by **Toru Iwatani**. The story goes he got the idea staring at a pizza with one slice missing."

"That checks out," Theo said, guiding Pac-Man around a corner. "I get my best ideas staring at pizza too."

"It might just be a good story," Pip said. "But everybody loves this one anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Crash and the Buried Treasure (1983–2014)
chapters.text:
The maze faded into a warehouse full of unsold boxes, dust thick on every shelf.

"**1983**," Pip said, voice a little quieter. "Stores got flooded with rushed, sloppy games. People stopped trusting the shelf. The whole games market in North America shrank, hard."

Theo picked up a dusty box. "That's rough. What happened to all this leftover stuff?"

"Funny you should ask," Pip said, grinning again. "Legend says a truck full of unsold Atari games, including one based on a movie called **E.T.**, got dumped into a landfill in New Mexico. A landfill's just a giant dump for trash, buried under dirt."

"Buried? Like, actually buried-buried?"

"For decades, people thought it was just a story," Pip said. "Then in **2014**, a crew of diggers went looking, and they actually found the cartridges. Real boxes, real dirt, right where the legend said."

Theo laughed. "So the legend was just... true the whole time?"

"Mostly," Pip said. "Which is the best kind of legend."

Pip tossed Theo a flashlight that hadn't been there a second ago, and the warehouse floor cracked open into a shallow, dusty pit. Theo knelt and brushed dirt off a half-buried cartridge, its label faded but readable.

"Found one," he said, holding it up like a trophy.

"Proof that even a bad year in games isn't the end of the story," Pip said. "Something always comes along to fix it."

"Something like what?" Theo asked, dusting off his hands.

Pip's eyes glowed. "Oh, you're going to like this part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
They climbed out of the pit into a toy store glowing with a brand-new red-and-white box.

"**1985**," Pip said. "The **Nintendo Entertainment System**, the **NES** for short, showed up and basically rescued the whole industry."

The box came bundled with a cartridge showing a mustached man in overalls jumping over a turtle.

"Meet **Mario**," Pip said. "Designed in **1985** by **Shigeru Miyamoto**. A plumber who jumps on things. Simple as that."

Theo grabbed a controller and pressed the jump button at exactly the wrong moment, landing Mario straight into a turtle shell. He tried again, timed it better, and cleared the gap clean.

"Jump a beat earlier," he muttered to himself, already thinking like a level designer. "Same thing I had to fix in my obstacle course last week."

"Funny you say that," Pip said, "because our next stop is a game that's basically nothing *but* timing."

The store shifted into a small computer room in Moscow, falling shapes tumbling down a screen.

"**1984**," Pip said. "**Tetris**, invented by **Alexey Pajitnov**, right here at a computer center."

Theo watched a long block fall and rotated it with a tap, sliding it into a gap at the last second. A full row vanished with a satisfying flash of light.

"It's just shapes," Theo said, "and somehow I cannot stop playing."

"That," said Pip, "is exactly why it's one of the most-played puzzle games on the whole planet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Blue Blur and the Disc (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
Mario's world spun into a loop of green hills, and a blue blur shot past so fast Theo felt the wind.

"**1991**," Pip said. "**Sonic the Hedgehog**, from Sega. Built fast on purpose, to compete with Mario."

Theo tried the controller and promptly ran Sonic straight off a cliff, which Pip found hilarious.

"Speed's not the same as control," Pip said, still laughing.

"Noted," Theo said, trying again, slower this time, timing his jump off the loop. It worked. Barely.

The hills dissolved into a living room with a gray console and a shiny silver disc spinning inside it.

"**1994**," Pip said. "**Sony**'s **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** instead of cartridges, the same idea as a music CD, but packed full of a whole game, with fuller video and sound."

Theo turned the disc over, catching the light. "Smoother graphics, louder music. Makes sense."

One more flicker dropped them into a room lit by a dozen glowing monitors, cables running between them like a spiderweb.

"**1993**," Pip said. "A game called **Doom** got people wiring their computers together just to play against each other in the same room. They called it a **LAN party**, a bunch of computers linked up so everyone could play at once."

"That's just a sleepover, but for gaming," Theo said.

"Exactly," Pip said. "People have been doing that for thirty years. You're basically ancient history already."

Theo laughed and nudged a cable back into place. "Rude. But fair."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Screen (2006–Now)
chapters.text:
The cables melted into a living room with a small white console and a controller shaped like a remote.

"**2006**," Pip said. "The **Wii**. You wave this thing around instead of pressing buttons."

Theo swung the controller like a tennis racket, and on the screen, a tiny avatar swung back. He grinned. "My grandma would actually play this one."

"That," Pip said, "was the whole point. It brought in people who'd never picked up a controller before in their lives."

The living room gave way to a wide-open blocky landscape, green cubes stretching to a pixel horizon.

"**2011**," Pip said. "**Minecraft**, made by a Swedish coder named **Markus Persson**, who went by **Notch**. It went on to become the best-selling video game ever made."

Theo looked around at the cube trees, the cube sheep, the cube everything. "It's basically building with digital LEGO. No wonder it blew up."

"Funny," Pip said, "considering what you were doing before I even showed up tonight."

One last flicker, and they stood in a museum hall, cabinets of old consoles lit behind glass, a plaque reading **World Video Game Hall of Fame**.

"**2015**," Pip said. "The Strong museum, in Rochester, New York. Every game you've met tonight has a case in here somewhere."

Theo pressed his palm to the glass over the old Brown Box. "All of this, because people kept fixing one bad bounce at a time."

The glass rippled like water, and Theo dropped, gently, back onto his bedroom carpet, laptop screen glowing its normal blue.

Pip blinked once from the corner of the screen, smaller now, barely a pixel.

"Press Start again sometime," Pip said, and faded into the code.

Theo looked at his half-finished soccer game, cursor blinking, and typed a new line, an angle, not a straight line, and the ball bounced exactly right.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Theo had a boss level to build — and he already knew exactly how it should bounce.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built **Tennis for Two** at **Brookhaven** lab, drawn as a bouncing line on a lab screen.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and friends made **Spacewar!** on a computer called the **PDP-1** that filled a whole room.
**Ralph Baer** built a home TV game called the **Brown Box** before it became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first console anyone could buy for home, in **1972**.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and made the arcade hit **Pong**.
Legend says a **Pong** machine once jammed from too many quarters — probably exaggerated, but it shows how fast the game caught on.
In **1978**, **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, starting a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** — legend says a pizza missing a slice gave him the idea.
In **1983**, stores got flooded with rushed games and the games market shrank hard — a rough year for the industry.
A famous story said unsold games, including one called **E.T.**, were buried in a dump in New Mexico — and diggers actually found them in **2014**.
The **NES** console launched in **1985** and helped bring the games industry back to life.
In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** in Moscow.
In **1991**, Sega made **Sonic the Hedgehog**, a fast blue character built to compete with Mario.
**Minecraft**, made in **2011** by **Markus 'Notch' Persson**, became the best-selling video game ever made.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Deep Blue Shark Brick
story.subtitle: A deep-sea trip with the magic red brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet, building a tower of LEGO sharks. Last night, their tower's last brick had gone CLICK and held tight.

Tonight, a new brick on top began to glow red. It buzzed. It hummed. It blinked like a tiny heartbeat.

'It's doing the thing again!' said Juno.

Milo grinned and pressed the brick. WHOOOOSH! The carpet turned to blue water, cool and deep.

'Where are we?' asked Juno, holding tight to Milo's hand.

A voice came from the glowing brick. 'Welcome to the ocean,' it said. 'Sharks have swum here for a very, very long time. Longer than dinosaurs!'

Juno gasped. 'Longer than DINOSAURS?'

'Yes,' said the brick. 'Sharks were here more than four hundred million years ago. That's before dinosaurs. Before trees, even!'

'That's older than Grandpa!' said Milo.

Juno laughed so hard, she forgot all about the dark water around them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A huge shadow slid over them, big as a school bus.

'Is that a whale?' asked Milo.

'Nope,' said the brick. 'That's a whale SHARK. It's the biggest fish in the whole world. It can grow longer than forty feet!'

Juno counted its white spots. 'One, two, three... lots!'

'Guess what it eats,' said the brick. 'Not big bites. Tiny food, smaller than a LEGO stud. It sucks in water and strains out teeny snacks.'

Milo laughed. 'A giant shark eating baby food?'

The whale shark opened its huge mouth, and water rushed in with a SPLOOSH. Out came a cloud of bubbles, right in Juno's face.

Juno giggled. 'He sneezed bubbles on me!'

'Some whale sharks live over a hundred years,' said the brick.

Milo high-fived the water. 'That's a lot of birthdays.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
Something swam closer with a mouth full of teeth.

'Whoa,' said Milo. 'Is that a GREAT WHITE SHARK?'

'It sure is,' said the brick. 'It can grow almost twenty feet long. Its teeth have little bumpy edges, like a saw. That's why they're called serrated.'

Milo leaned in. 'One of its teeth looks loose!'

'Good eye,' said the brick. 'Sharks lose teeth all the time. But new teeth are already lined up behind, moving forward to take their place.'

'NEW TEETH ALL THE TIME!' shouted Juno.

Milo grinned. 'I wish my LEGO did that when a piece broke.'

The great white swished its tail and swam on, not in a hurry at all. It wasn't interested in two kids one bit — only its next tiny fish snack, far away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tooth on the Sand
chapters.text:
On the sandy floor lay something huge and pointy.

'Is that a rock?' asked Juno.

'That's a tooth,' said the brick. 'As long as a hand. It belonged to Megalodon, a giant shark.'

Juno pressed her little hand next to it. 'It's bigger than my whole hand!'

'Megalodon isn't around anymore,' said the brick. 'It lived a long, long time ago, and now it's extinct, which means it's all gone. But its tooth turned hard like stone over millions of years, so we can still find it.'

Milo tilted his head. 'How do we know about the rest of it, if it's all gone?'

'Mostly from teeth like this one,' said the brick. 'The rest of its body was too soft and bendy to last that long.'

Juno hugged the giant tooth like a stuffed dinosaur. 'Goodnight, big old tooth.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin
chapters.text:
Milo reached out and touched a shark gliding by. 'Whoa, it feels like sandpaper!'

'That's its skin,' said the brick. 'It's covered in teeny tiny tooth-like bumps. They help the shark zoom through water smoothly.'

Juno poked her own arm. 'Mine's not bumpy.'

'Sharks are different from us another way too,' said the brick. 'Their bones aren't hard like yours. They're bendy, like the squishy part of your ear.'

Milo folded his own ear in half. 'Boing! Like that?'

'Exactly like that,' said the brick.

Juno folded her ear too and giggled. 'My ear is a shark bone!'

The shark swam off, smooth and silent, never bumping into a single rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
A strange shape swam past — its head was flat and wide, like a hammer.

'That shark has a weird head!' said Juno.

'That's a hammerhead shark,' said the brick. 'Its eyes are far apart on each side. That lets it see almost all the way around itself.'

Milo spun in a circle. 'Like looking backward and forward at the same time!'

Then something even stranger appeared near the rocks — a small shark, walking on its fins.

'IT'S WALKING!' shouted Juno.

'That's an epaulette shark,' said the brick. 'It uses its fins like little paddles to walk across the reef. It barely needs any air to do it.'

Milo laughed. 'I'm building that shark out of LEGO the second we get home. With walking legs!'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A friendly diver swam up, waving.

'Hello!' she said. 'I'm Eugenie Clark. Some people call me the Shark Lady.'

'You study sharks?' asked Milo.

'For a long, long time,' she said. 'I learned that sharks are curious. I even taught some of them little tricks.'

Juno gasped. 'Sharks can do tricks?'

'They sure can,' said Eugenie, smiling.

Milo asked the question he'd been saving. 'Why do we even need sharks?'

'Great question,' said Eugenie. 'Sharks help keep all the other ocean animals healthy and balanced, by eating the extra ones.'

'There are more than five hundred different kinds of sharks,' added the brick, 'all doing that important job.'

Juno counted on her fingers. 'Five hundred! That's SO many!'

Eugenie laughed. 'More than you can count on your fingers, that's for sure.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
Something small and leathery drifted past, shaped like a little pouch with curly strings.

'What's that?' asked Juno.

'That's called a mermaid's purse,' said the brick. 'Some baby sharks hatch out of cases just like that one. Other sharks are born live, ready to swim right away.'

Milo scooped it up gently. 'Can we keep it?'

The brick glowed brighter. 'Time to go home.'

WHOOOOSH! The water swirled away. The ocean turned back into soft carpet under their knees.

Milo looked down. The little mermaid's purse sat right there on the rug, beside their LEGO tower.

On top of the tower, one brand-new brick glowed — a tiny red LEGO shark.

Juno yawned a huge dinosaur yawn. 'Goodnight, shark friends.'

Milo tucked the little purse beside his pillow. 'Goodnight, big ocean.'

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks swam in the ocean more than **four hundred million years ago** — before dinosaurs, and even before trees!
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the world, and it eats tiny food by straining it out of the water.
Some whale sharks might live more than **one hundred years**.
The **great white shark** can grow almost **twenty feet long**, with teeth that have bumpy, saw-like edges.
Sharks lose teeth all the time, but new teeth are always lined up, ready to **move forward**.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark from long ago. It is **extinct** now, which means it's all gone.
We mostly know about Megalodon from its giant tooth that turned hard like stone, because the rest of its body was too soft to last.
Shark skin feels like **sandpaper** because it's covered in tiny tooth-like bumps.
A shark's bones are bendy, like the squishy part of your **ear**, not hard like ours.
A **hammerhead shark** has a wide, flat head that lets it see almost all the way around.
The **epaulette shark** can actually **walk** across the reef using its fins like little paddles.
**Eugenie Clark**, the Shark Lady, studied sharks for years and even taught some of them tricks.
There are more than **five hundred** different kinds of sharks living in the ocean today.
Some baby sharks hatch from little pouches called **mermaid's purses**; others are born ready to swim.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno came home with a tiny mermaid's purse on the rug and a brand-new glowing LEGO shark brick atop their tower.

story.title: Theo and the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: A Roblox Studio buildathon through 2,000 years of soccer history.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Kick in Ancient China
chapters.text:
Theo's bedroom floor was covered in sketches: goalposts, a scoreboard, a stadium roof that opened like a clamshell. He had been building a soccer pitch in Roblox Studio for six days straight, ever since the screen had flashed **THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD.**

He placed the last corner flag and leaned back, proud of himself. His desk lamp buzzed, flickered green, then went out completely.

**BZZZT.**

A small pixel face popped up on the monitor, blocky and grinning. "Player One!" it squeaked. "Did you miss me?"

"Bit!" Theo sat up so fast his chair spun in a full circle. "Where have you been?"

"Waiting for you to finish admiring your own stadium," Bit said. "Tonight's level isn't one you built. It's one that got built a long, long time ago — the real game. Soccer. Ready?"

A golden coin dropped out of the screen and landed, warm and glowing, on his keyboard. The room folded shut like a loading screen, and —

Theo landed in a dusty market square under a blazing sun. Men in long tunics kicked a round leather ball back and forth, aiming for a narrow gap strung between two silk banners.

"Whoa. Is that soccer?" Theo asked.

"Close ancestor," said Bit, perched on his shoulder now, tiny and pixelated. "This game is called **cuju** — it means 'kick ball.' People in **China** were playing it more than **2,000 years ago**."

Theo watched a player bend his knee and chip the ball without ever touching it with his hands. The crowd cheered every clean pass like it was a championship final. "No hands. Just like soccer."

"Exactly like soccer," Bit said. "Think you can get one through the gap?"

Theo had practiced penalty kicks all season. He planted his foot, kept his eyes on the gap, and struck. The ball sailed clean through the silk banners, and the whole square erupted.

The golden coin in his pocket buzzed once, warm and happy.

"Level complete," said Bit, grinning wider than a pixel face should be able to. "One down. A whole world of soccer history to go."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Game They Had to Ban
chapters.text:
The next loading screen dropped Theo into a muddy street, and it was chaos.

Dozens of men shoved and wrestled over an inflated ball, crashing through a vegetable stall and scattering turnips everywhere. Nobody seemed to be following any rule at all.

"This is **mob football**," Bit explained, ducking a flying cabbage. "Basically the whole town kicking one ball from one end to the other. No teams. No ref. Barely any rules."

A man on horseback rode up, unrolled a scroll, and read loudly to the crowd. Theo caught a few words: *forbidden... within this city...*

"What's he saying?" Theo asked.

"**King Edward II** just banned this exact game in **London**, in **1314**," said Bit. "Too much chaos in the streets. Smashed stalls, spooked horses, officials sick of cleaning up the mess."

Theo watched the crowd groan and scatter, clutching their battered ball like it was treasure. "They really loved this game, though."

"Oh, completely," Bit said. "They just needed structure. Somebody to write it down properly, so everyone agreed on what counted. Remember that thought."

The screen flickered, and they stood in a cold stone tower instead, dust floating in a shaft of light.

"Where are we now?" Theo asked.

"**Stirling Castle**, Scotland," said Bit. "Somewhere in this room, a secret's been hiding for centuries."

Theo ran his hand along a gap behind a wooden beam and felt something soft and leathery wedged there. He tugged it free: an old, round, stitched-up ball, flat and ancient looking.

"Found it!" he said.

"That," said Bit, eyes going wide and pixel-bright, "might be the **oldest football in the world**. Hidden in this castle, maybe since the **1540s**. And inside, just so you know, it's got a **pig's bladder** — a squishy, blown-up pouch, like a balloon, that people stitched leather around."

Theo held it carefully, like it might crumble in his hands. "People have been chasing a ball around for a really long time."

"And it was about to get a lot more organized," said Bit. "Up next: the rule book."

chapters.heading: Level 3: Writing the Rule Book
chapters.text:
The next level smelled like chalk dust and old paper.

Theo stood in a university courtyard in England, where a cluster of students argued over a ball at their feet.

"Every school plays this differently," one grumbled. "My old school let you carry it. Yours doesn't."

Theo frowned. "That's a problem. You can't have one world sport if nobody agrees on the rules."

"Exactly what **Cambridge University** students thought in **1848**," said Bit. "They wrote down the **Cambridge Rules** — one of the first tries at a single rule book everybody could actually use."

The scene shifted. Now they stood in a London pub, where a serious-looking man in a tall hat scratched notes with a pen.

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit whispered. "He just helped start the **Football Association** — the FA — right here in **London**, on **26 October 1863**."

Theo watched Morley cross something out and rewrite it. "What's he deciding?"

"Go ahead. Guess," said Bit.

Theo thought about every handball call he'd ever argued about on his own team. "No carrying the ball. Feet and head only."

Morley looked up, almost like he'd heard him, and wrote exactly that.

"Nailed it," said Bit. "Morley personally wrote the first official rules of the game. No hands. That one decision split this sport from rugby forever."

Theo grinned. "So that's why it's soccer, not just football-with-hands."

"Funny you say that," said Bit. "The word **'soccer'** actually comes from schoolboys in **1880s England** shortening 'assoc' — as in **association** football. Kids turning a long word into slang. Sound familiar, gamer?"

Theo laughed. "Like how everyone just says 'Rblx.'"

"Exactly like that," said Bit, and the golden coin buzzed warm in Theo's pocket again.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The First Leaderboard
chapters.text:
Fog rolled across a green field, and a crowd roared from wooden stands.

"**FA Cup**, first ever tournament, **1871 to '72**," said Bit. "Still being played today. Oldest football competition on Earth."

Theo watched two teams battle through the mist, nobody scoring for ages. "This is intense."

"Wait till you see this next match," Bit said, and the field changed to a wider, rougher pitch somewhere colder.

"**Scotland versus England**, **Glasgow**, **1872**," Bit announced. "First official international match ever played."

Theo watched both sides defend like their lives depended on it. Ninety minutes later, the final whistle blew. The scoreboard read **0–0**.

"Nobody scored? At all?" Theo said. "That's rough."

"Everyone was still figuring out how to attack," said Bit. "But it counted. First international ever played."

Theo noticed something on a chalkboard nearby: fixtures scrawled in rows, teams and dates stacked up neatly. "Is that... a schedule?"

"Good eye," said Bit. "A man named **William McGregor** had an idea in **1888**: organize teams into a proper league, with fixed games and a table that updated every single week."

Theo's eyes lit up. "Like a leaderboard."

"Precisely like a leaderboard," said Bit. "The **Football League** — the first one anywhere in the world. McGregor basically invented standings."

Theo tapped an imaginary scoreboard in the air, grinning. "Soccer had a leaderboard before Roblox did."

"By about a hundred and thirty years," said Bit, and the coin in Theo's pocket clicked warm against the last one.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The World Joins In
chapters.text:
A map of the world unrolled across the sky, flags pinned all over it, fluttering in a wind that wasn't really there.

"Every country wanted in by now," Bit said. "So in **1904**, in **Paris**, seven countries founded **FIFA** — the group that would run soccer's rules for the whole planet."

Theo studied the flags, tracing continents with a finger. "So who's first to host a big world tournament?"

"You tell me," said Bit. "Look for the flag that's glowing."

Theo scanned the map until one flag pulsed gold, tucked into South America, small and far from everywhere else.

"That one," he said. "Uruguay?"

"**Uruguay**, **1930**," Bit confirmed. "First ever **FIFA World Cup**. The host team beat **Argentina** in the final and took the very first title."

The map dissolved into a packed stadium, flags waving, a man in a neat suit holding up a small golden statue above his head.

"That's **Jules Rimet**," said Bit. "The FIFA president who pushed hardest to make the World Cup happen in the first place. They even named the first trophy after him."

Theo watched the crowd roar as the little trophy caught the light. "It's smaller than I thought it'd be."

"Big things start small," said Bit. "Trust me — watch where this one ends up."

The golden coin in Theo's pocket grew warmer, heavier, almost like it already knew what was coming next.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Dog Who Found the Trophy
chapters.text:
The scene jumped to a gray London afternoon, a crowd murmuring nervously on a street corner.

"**1966**," Bit said. "England's hosting the World Cup — and somebody just stole the trophy right off its display stand."

Theo's jaw dropped. "Someone stole the actual World Cup?"

"Whole country panicking," said Bit. "Police searching everywhere, newspapers printing nothing else."

They walked along a hedge-lined street while officers combed through gardens and bushes. A scruffy little dog trotted ahead of them, nose down, tail wagging like this was the best day of his life.

Theo watched the dog freeze, then dig at something wrapped in newspaper, tucked under a hedge.

"Bit, look!" Theo pointed. "That dog found something!"

A man knelt and unwrapped the bundle — and there it was, golden and gleaming, completely unharmed.

"That dog's name was **Pickles**," said Bit, practically vibrating with excitement. "Found the missing World Cup trophy under a hedge, one whole week after it vanished. National hero. Got a medal and everything."

Theo grinned. "Best player nobody put on the field."

The scene shifted again to a packed stadium, English fans singing themselves hoarse, scarves waving overhead.

"Same tournament," said Bit. "**England** went on to win the whole thing. Their only World Cup title, to this day."

Theo pumped his fist along with the crowd, and a new golden coin dropped straight into his open hand.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Five Stars and a Yellow Card
chapters.text:
Sunlight blasted down on a stadium painted in yellow and green.

"Keep count," Bit said, as jerseys flashed by in the stands. "How many stars do you see stitched above that badge?"

Theo squinted at a passing jersey. "Five. Why five?"

"Because **Brazil's** won the World Cup five times," said Bit. "**1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002**. A record nobody else has touched."

A player dribbled past three defenders like they were cones in a drill, then struck a shot into the top corner.

"Who is THAT?" Theo said.

"**Pele**," said Bit. "Brazilian forward. The only player ever to win it on three different winning teams — **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Theo watched the crowd carry Pele on their shoulders, chanting his name. "He's basically the greatest ever."

"Pretty much," said Bit.

The scene shifted to a referee pulling a small rectangle from his pocket and holding it high above his head. It was bright yellow.

"What's that for?" Theo asked.

"A referee named **Ken Aston** was stuck in traffic one day," said Bit, "staring at a stoplight. Yellow means slow down, red means stop. So he invented **yellow and red cards** for soccer, debuting right here at the **1970 World Cup**."

Theo laughed. "He got the idea from a traffic light?"

"Sometimes the best ideas are the boring ones sitting right in front of you," said Bit.

The scene shifted one last time, to a quiet workshop, a brand new golden trophy gleaming on a velvet cushion.

"Brazil kept that first trophy for good, after their third win," Bit said. "So in **1974**, FIFA made a brand new one. Different trophy, same dream."

The coin in Theo's hand clicked together with the others, heavier every single time.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Every Team Plays
chapters.text:
The next field was packed tighter than any stadium Theo had seen all night — fifty thousand people, all craning for a look at one player.

"That's **Lily Parr**," said Bit. "Star forward for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**. One of the most popular teams in all of England."

Theo watched Parr blast a shot past the goalkeeper, the crowd roaring louder than for anything else today. "They're amazing. Why haven't I heard of them?"

Bit's screen flickered, and the stadium suddenly emptied, gates locked shut with a heavy clang.

"In **1921**, the people running the FA banned women's football completely," Bit said quietly. "Stopped them from playing on any official field. For **fifty years**."

Theo stared at the locked gates, fists clenched. "That's not fair. They were packing stadiums!"

"No," Bit agreed. "It really wasn't."

"Someone has to fix that," Theo said.

"Someone did," said Bit, and the gates creaked back open, sunlight pouring in again. "**1971**. The FA finally lifted the ban."

The stadium filled back in fast-forward, decades flashing past, until Theo stood in a roaring arena somewhere far away.

"**1991**," Bit said. "First ever official **Women's World Cup**. Won by the **United States**."

Theo watched the American team lift the trophy, grinning so hard his cheeks hurt. "They waited fifty years and then just went and won the whole thing."

"Some levels take longer to unlock," said Bit. "Doesn't mean people stop playing while they wait."

Theo nodded slowly, and made a decision right there on the spot. "When I build my next Roblox game, every team plays. No bans. Ever."

The last golden coin dropped into his hand, glowing brighter than all the others put together.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Trophy Complete
chapters.text:
The loading screen folded one more time, and Theo was back on his bedroom floor, golden coins scattered across the carpet like fallen stars.

"Last step," said Bit, voice a little wobblier than usual. "Watch."

The coins rose off the carpet, spinning slowly, and melted together into one shining trophy, small enough to fit in both his hands. Theo caught it before it could even fall.

"Whoa," he breathed, turning it over. "Is this..."

"A little bit of every level you played tonight," said Bit. "Cuju. The FA. The World Cup. Pickles the dog. All of it. Yours to keep."

Theo set the trophy carefully on his desk, right next to his half-built Roblox stadium. "Thanks, Bit. For all of it."

Bit's pixel eyes went a little watery, blurry at the edges the way old game graphics sometimes glitch. "Go build something great, Player One."

The monitor flickered one last time, words scrolling slowly across the screen: **LEVEL COMPLETE. SEE YOU NEXT TIME.**

Then the room went quiet, lamp glowing warm and steady, the little trophy catching the light on his desk.

Theo looked at his half-finished stadium, then at the trophy beside it, and smiled.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole new level to build — and this time, he knew exactly where to start.

true_facts.text: Long before soccer, people in **China** played a kick-the-ball game called **cuju** more than **2,000 years ago**.
A game called **mob football** got so wild that **King Edward II** banned it in **London** in **1314**.
An old ball stuffed with a **pig's bladder** was found hidden at **Stirling Castle** — maybe the **oldest football in the world**, from the **1540s**.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** helped start the **Football Association** in **London** on **26 October 1863**.
Morley personally wrote soccer's first official rule book, including the biggest one: **no hands**.
The word **'soccer'** came from schoolboys in **1880s England** shortening **'association'** football to **'assoc.'**
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is still the **oldest football competition** running today.
In **1904**, seven countries met in **Paris** to start **FIFA**, soccer's worldwide rule-keepers.
The first ever **FIFA World Cup** was played in **Uruguay** in **1930** — and Uruguay won it.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London and found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Pele** is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
**Lily Parr** and the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** once packed stadiums full of fans to watch them play.
The FA finally lifted its ban on women's soccer in **1971**, fifty years after it began.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991** and won by the **United States**.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo's nine golden coins fused into one small trophy now sitting on his desk beside his half-built Roblox stadium, while Bit's screen scrolled LEVEL COMPLETE. SEE YOU NEXT TIME.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Glowing Rock of Fire
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey into the fiery heart of the Earth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick That Glowed
chapters.text:
Milo lay on the carpet, building a LEGO volcano. He stacked gray bricks into a tall, wobbly cone.

Juno roared like a dinosaur beside him, stomping her toy triceratops up the plastic slope.

Theo sat cross-legged on the rug, tapping his tablet, building a city in Roblox.

Then one gray brick on Milo's tower began to glow. It turned warm, then bright red, like a tiny ember.

"Whoa!" said Milo. He picked it up. It was not hot. It just glowed.

The brick wobbled, then popped into a round red pebble with two blinking eyes.

"Hello!" said the pebble. "I'm Pip. I live inside real volcanoes. Want to see one?"

"A volcano is a hole in the ground," Pip said, "where hot melted rock, ash, and gas can escape."

"Is it like my LEGO tower?" Milo asked. "Does the rock pour out the top, like my gray bricks?"

"Just like that," said Pip. "Underground, we call that hot rock magma, melted rock still inside the Earth. Once it pours out on top, we call it lava instead."

Juno poked the pebble. "Does it ROAR like my dinosaur?"

"Sometimes," laughed Pip. "Hold on tight, all three of you. We're going down, down, down!"

The bedroom floor melted into swirling orange light. WHOOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
They landed on a soft, floating cloud, looking down at a giant map of the whole world.

Glowing dots circled the edge of one huge blue ocean, like beads on a necklace.

Theo leaned closer. "That looks like the border of a map in my Roblox game! A big loop, all the way around!"

"Good eye," said Pip. "That loop is called the Ring of Fire. It circles the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about three out of every four volcanoes on our whole planet."

"Why there?" asked Milo, tilting his head.

Pip explained it slowly. The ground under our feet is not one solid piece. It is made of giant pieces, like puzzle pieces, that fit together and slowly move. Where two pieces push together, or pull apart, or slide past each other, volcanoes like to pop up.

Juno pressed her finger onto one glowing dot on the map. "I found one!"

"You found Indonesia," grinned Pip. "Good job, Juno. Want to see it up close?"

"YES!" shouted all three at once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: So Many Volcanoes!
chapters.text:
The cloud swooped down toward a long chain of green islands poking out of blue water.

Juno counted bumps on the map with her small finger. "One, two, three... so many!"

"You're right," said Pip. "Indonesia has more awake volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

Theo frowned. "Awake? Like they sleep?"

"Sort of," said Pip. "An active volcano is one that can still erupt someday. Lots of Indonesia's volcanoes are wide awake right now."

Milo scanned the water for sharks and spotted a gray fin slicing through the waves. "Look! A shark, right next to a volcano island!"

"Sharks and volcanoes both like warm water," said Pip. "This ocean has plenty of both."

Juno waved at the shark from high in the sky. She did not touch it, just waved and smiled. "Swim well, shark!"

"Next stop," said Pip, "the island where I was born."

The cloud zoomed onward. SWOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Pip's Hawaiian Home
chapters.text:
They landed beside a wide, gently sloped mountain, bubbling softly near the top.

"This is Kilauea," said Pip proudly. "It is one of the busiest volcanoes on Earth. It has been bubbling and glowing, on and off, for years and years and years."

Milo studied its shape carefully. "It's not pointy like my LEGO volcano. It's wide and flat, like a shield lying on the ground!"

"Smart eyes," said Pip. "Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, shaped like a shield. Others are tall and pointy, shaped like a party hat. Both kinds work the same way underneath."

Next door stood an even bigger mountain, so tall its top almost touched a cloud.

"That one is Mauna Loa," said Pip. "It is the biggest active volcano on our whole planet, bigger than any other one anywhere."

Juno gasped and spread her arms as wide as they would go. "That BIG?"

"These Hawaiian volcanoes grew over a hotspot," said Pip, "a spot deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising up, like a candle that never blows out."

"IT NEVER STOPS!" shouted Milo, bouncing on his toes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Island That Popped Up
chapters.text:
Pip carried them north to a cold, windy island, gray rock all around.

"This is Iceland," said Pip. "It sits right where two giant puzzle pieces are pulling apart, instead of pushing together."

Theo thought of soccer practice. "Like when two kids on a team pull a net in opposite directions until it rips open in the middle!"

"Exactly," laughed Pip. "And right through that gap, hot rock can bubble up to the surface."

Suddenly the sea in front of them began to fizz and pop. Steam shot straight up. SPLOOSH!

"In 1963," said Pip, "a brand new island popped up right out of this ocean. It kept erupting underwater until it grew tall enough to breathe fresh air. They named it Surtsey."

"A whole island was BORN?" said Milo, eyes wide. "Like a LEGO build, but made by the Earth!"

"Just like that," said Pip, smiling.

Juno clapped both hands together. "The Earth builds too!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Biggest Volcano in the Sky
chapters.text:
Pip then lifted them off the ground, past soft clouds, past twinkling stars.

"Where are we going now?" asked Theo, gripping tight.

"Somewhere even a Roblox builder would love," said Pip. "Mars."

They landed on red, dusty ground, in front of a mountain so tall its top disappeared into dark sky.

Theo's jaw dropped open. "That's bigger than anything I've ever built in any game!"

"It's called Olympus Mons," said Pip. "It's the biggest volcano anyone has found in our whole solar system. It stands about thirteen miles high, nearly three times taller than the tallest mountain on Earth."

Milo tried to picture it in LEGO bricks. "I'd need SO many bricks for that one."

Juno tipped her head all the way back, looking up and up and up. "It touches the sky!"

"Good thing it's quiet now," said Pip, "and good thing it's very, very far away."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleeping Giant
chapters.text:
They floated back down to Earth, landing on a grassy field full of steaming pools.

"This ground is hiding something huge," said Pip. "This place is called Yellowstone. Underneath it lies a supervolcano, a volcano so enormous it could cover whole states in ash if it ever went off big."

Theo's eyes went wide. "Is it going to erupt? Like, tonight?"

"No, no," said Pip quickly. "Its last huge eruption was about 640,000 years ago. Scientists watch it closely, and right now there is no sign it will erupt again soon."

Milo let out a big breath. "Phew."

"How do scientists watch a sleepy volcano?" asked Theo.

"They use a seismograph," said Pip, "a machine that feels tiny wobbles in the ground, even ones too small for you to feel. They also use satellites in space to see if the ground is puffing up like a balloon."

Juno pretended to be a seismograph, wobbling her whole body side to side. "I feel the wobbles!"

Everyone laughed, and even the steamy pools seemed to giggle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Pip, "before bed."

They landed beside a farm, green and leafy, growing right next to a quiet volcano.

"Why would anyone grow carrots so close to a volcano?" asked Milo, wrinkling his nose.

"Old volcano ash breaks down into soil that is wonderful for growing plants," said Pip. "That's why farmers like living near volcanoes, even knowing the risks."

Juno patted the dark soil with her small hand. "It feels soft, like chocolate cake!"

Theo grinned. "Nature's secret ingredient."

Then the orange light swirled around them again. WHOOOOSH!

Milo landed back on his bedroom carpet, right where his LEGO tower stood waiting. The gray brick sat quietly on top, not glowing anymore, just an ordinary brick.

Juno hugged her triceratops tight. Theo set down his tablet, his Roblox city still waiting there for morning.

"Thank you, Pip," whispered Milo, tucking the little brick safely into his pocket.

Somewhere deep inside it, Pip gave one last tiny wink of red light.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Sleep tight, and dream of glowing rocks.

true_facts.text: A volcano is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gas can escape.
Underground that hot rock is called **magma**. Once it pours out on top, it's called **lava**.
The **Ring of Fire** circles the Pacific Ocean and holds about three out of every four of Earth's volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more awake volcanoes than any other country.
Hawaii's volcanoes grew over a **hotspot**, a place deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising.
**Kilauea** has been bubbling and glowing on and off for years and years.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest active volcano on the whole planet.
Some volcanoes are wide like a **shield**; others are tall and pointy like a party hat.
In **1963**, a brand new island named **Surtsey** popped right out of the ocean near Iceland.
Iceland sits where two giant puzzle pieces of ground are pulling apart.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found, about thirteen miles high.
**Yellowstone's** last huge eruption happened about **640,000 years ago**, and scientists see no sign of another one coming soon.
Scientists use a **seismograph** to feel tiny ground wobbles, and satellites to watch volcanoes from space.
Old volcano ash turns into soil that's wonderful for growing plants.

story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Bee from the Amber Bead
story.subtitle: A tiny bee teaches a dino-loving girl how honey gets made.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Amber Bead Glows
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor. It was way past bedtime.

She lined up her toy dinosaurs in a row. Her triceratops wore a tiny necklace with one gold bead.

Suddenly the bead went warm. It glowed like a tiny sun. Then it buzzed, soft and low.

CRACK! A tiny, friendly crack. Out popped a tiny bee.

"Hello!" said the bee. "I'm Bramble."

Juno's eyes went wide. "A real bee? In my dinosaur's necklace?"

"This bead is amber," said Bramble. "Amber is old tree juice, turned hard as rock. I got stuck inside it long, long ago. Dinosaurs were still stomping around!"

Juno gasped. "You know dinosaurs?"

"Bees have buzzed since before dinosaurs said goodbye," said Bramble. "Want to see how my hive makes honey?"

Juno nodded so fast her hair flopped. ZOOM! She shrank down, tiny as a bee, and off they flew.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzing Hive
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They landed by a hive, humming loud.

"This is my home," said Bramble. "Thousands of bees live here together!"

Juno tried counting. "One, two, three... too many!"

"At summer's busiest," said Bramble, "our hive can hold up to eighty thousand bees. Almost all are girls, called workers. A few boy bees too, called drones. And one queen, the hive's busy mom."

Juno spotted the queen, big and slow and calm.

"She's the boss?" asked Juno.

"Sort of," said Bramble. "She's the mom of almost everybody here."

Juno giggled. "That's a LOT of kids."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Egg-Laying Queen
chapters.text:
The queen bee waddled from tiny room to tiny room. Juno watched close.

"What's she doing?" Juno asked.

"Laying eggs," said Bramble. "She can lay up to two thousand eggs in just one day!"

Juno's mouth popped open. "Two thousand? That's more than my whole dinosaur collection!"

Bramble laughed her tiny buzzy laugh. "She's the busiest mom in the world."

Juno watched the queen dip into room after room. Tiny white eggs, smaller than sugar.

"She never stops?" asked Juno.

"Barely," said Bramble. "Want to meet the littlest helpers?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Five Eyes and Buzzy Wings
chapters.text:
A worker bee zoomed past. BZZZZ! So close, it blew Juno's hair.

"Whoa! How do you fly so fast?" Juno asked.

Bramble landed on her nose. "Look close. Count my eyes."

Juno counted slow. "One, two... FIVE! You have five eyes!"

"Two big ones for seeing," said Bramble, "and three tiny ones on top, just for feeling light."

"Five eyes is so cool," said Juno.

"And my wings flap two hundred times every single second," said Bramble. "That's what makes my buzzing sound."

Juno flapped her arms fast, trying to copy. She did not buzz one bit. She just giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Waggle Dance
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, a bee wiggled in little circles, like a tiny dancer.

"Why is she wiggling?" Juno asked.

"That's the waggle dance," said Bramble. "She found yummy flowers far away. Her dance tells the others which way to fly, and how far."

Juno watched close, then pointed. "She's pointing that way! Toward the big flower patch!"

Bramble checked the dance again. "You're right, Juno! That's exactly where the flowers are."

Juno bounced on her tiny bee feet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Honeycomb Shapes
chapters.text:
Juno peeked into a wall of tiny little rooms. Each one had six sides.

"These shapes look funny," said Juno. "Like pointy stop signs!"

"Those are hexagons," said Bramble. "Six sides each. Bees build this shape because it holds the most honey, using the least wax."

Juno touched one gently. "So smart, for such tiny bees."

"We think so too," said Bramble, buzzing proudly.

Juno drew a hexagon in the air with her finger. Six sides, just like Bramble said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Flowers Into Honey
chapters.text:
Bees zoomed out from the hive, like tiny race cars.

"Where are they going?" Juno asked.

"To flowers," said Bramble, "to sip sweet flower juice called nectar. One bee only makes a tiny drop of honey her whole life. About a twelfth of one teaspoon."

Juno frowned. "That's so little!"

"That's why it takes lots of bees," said Bramble. "Together, bees visit about two million flowers, just to make one jar of honey."

Juno's eyes went huge.

"Busy, busy bees," said Bramble, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Honey That Never Spoils
chapters.text:
Bramble showed Juno a jar of golden honey, gleaming like treasure.

"Long, long ago," said Bramble, "people in Egypt kept bees too. They even painted pictures of it on walls."

"As old as dinosaurs?" asked Juno.

"Not quite that old," laughed Bramble. "But honey hardly ever goes bad. People found honey pots in old tombs, thousands of years old, and it was still good to eat!"

Juno wrinkled her nose. "Still good? That's like magic."

"Almost," said Bramble. "Time to fly you home now."

ZOOM! Juno shrank back up and landed softly on her bedroom floor. The amber bead glowed once more, then went still and warm in her hand.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Sleep tight, little bee, and dream sweet, honey dreams.

true_facts.text: Bees buzzed around even back when **dinosaurs** were still stomping on the earth.
A bee hive has one **queen** mom bee, lots of girl **worker** bees, and a few boy bees called **drones**.
A busy hive can hold up to **eighty thousand bees** in summer.
The queen bee can lay up to **two thousand eggs** in just one day.
A bee has **five eyes** — two big ones for seeing, and three tiny ones on top for feeling light.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times every second**, and that makes the buzzing sound.
Bees do a **waggle dance**, wiggling in circles to tell other bees which way the flowers are.
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides**, called hexagons, because that shape holds the most honey with the least wax.
One bee makes only a tiny drop of honey, about **a twelfth of a teaspoon**, in her whole life.
Bees together visit about **two million flowers** just to make one jar of honey.
Honey hardly ever goes bad — people found **very old honey pots** that were still good to eat.
Long ago, people in **Egypt** painted pictures of beekeeping on their walls.
