story.title: Sam and Gus the Gecko's Sticky Night
story.subtitle: A wall-climbing bedtime adventure for Sam.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko Who Peeled Off the Wall
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor with his flashlight. A fat roly-poly bug sat in his bug jar. He had caught it in the garden that afternoon.

'Lights out, Sam!' Mom called from the hall. Sam clicked off his flashlight. The room went dark and quiet.

Then the little green gecko sticker on his wall began to glow. It glowed bright green, like a glow stick at a fair.

Sam sat up fast. The gecko wiggled one foot. Then another. Then - **PEEL!** - it peeled right off the wall. Its toes came off last, like pulling up a sticker.

'Whoa,' Sam whispered.

The gecko hopped onto Sam's pillow. 'Hiya! I'm Gus,' he said. 'Did you see my toes? That's how I walk on walls.'

Sam leaned in close. Gus's toes looked fuzzy, like they had tiny hairs all over.

'They do have tiny hairs,' Gus said. 'Millions of them. Too small to see. They let me run straight up glass. I can even walk upside down on the ceiling.'

'Upside down? Show me!' Sam said.

Gus walked right up the wall. He crossed the ceiling, toes first, cool as could be. Sam clapped so hard his hands turned pink.

'I know a trick too,' Sam said. 'My spider in the garden climbs the wall just like you. Does she have hairs too?'

Gus's eyes went wide and sparkly. 'Only one way to find out. Hop on, Sam. We're going on a sticky tour.'

Gus tapped one glowing toe to Sam's window. **FWOOMP!** The whole room seemed to grow huge around them - or maybe Sam just got tiny. Either way, Sam stood on Gus's back, smaller than a fingernail.

'Hold tight,' Gus said. 'Stick with me!'

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Gus's Sticky Secret
chapters.text:
Gus and tiny Sam zoomed up the glass window, quick as a wink. Up close, Gus's toe looked wild. Each tiny hair split into even tinier tips, smaller than a speck of dust.

'Those tiny, tiny tips are why I stick,' Gus said. 'They get so close to the glass, they just... hold on.'

'Is it glue?' Sam asked.

'Nope! No glue at all,' Gus said. 'My feet never get sticky-messy. Watch.'

Gus peeled one toe up, slow and easy, like pulling up a strip of tape. Then another toe. Then another.

Sam tried it on the glass with his own tiny finger. He pressed it down, then peeled it up nice and slow.

'It's like tape!' Sam said. 'Pull it slow and it comes off easy. Yank it fast and - '

'And you'd fall right off,' Gus laughed. 'So geckos always peel, toe by toe.'

Sam pressed his whole hand flat and peeled it off, one finger at a time, just like Gus. He grinned so wide his cheeks hurt.

'I want hairy toes,' Sam said, wiggling his fingers like he could grow fur right then and there.

'You've got the next best thing,' Gus said. 'A great big brain for noticing things. Now come on - someone outside this window wants to meet you.'

He nodded toward a small shadow in the corner of the glass. Sam's eyes went bright.

'Is that -'

'Go see,' Gus said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Fuzzy-Footed Spider
chapters.text:
A spider sat in the corner of the window, spinning silky thread. Sam grinned - spiders were his favorite.

He pulled his little magnifying glass from his pocket. He always kept one, just in case.

'Look at her feet,' Sam whispered, peering close. 'They're fuzzy! Just like your toes, Gus!'

Gus leaned in - then leaned back a little. 'Fuzzy feet, sharp fangs. Are you sure she's friendly?'

'She's just a garden spider,' Sam said. 'I watch her every day. She never bothers anybody.'

Gus relaxed. 'Well, you'd know. You do pick up every bug in the garden.'

'Spiders have tiny hairs too,' Sam said, still peering through his glass. 'That's how she climbs the glass, right?'

'Exactly right,' Gus said. 'Thousands of tiny hairs on her feet. Different from mine, but the same clever idea.'

The spider scooted straight up the window, smooth and quick, never once sliding.

'GO, SPIDER, GO!' Sam cheered, careful to stay back and just watch. He did not touch her web. Watching was plenty exciting.

Then, just like always, Sam remembered to let every bug stay exactly where she belonged.

'Good job spotting that,' Gus said. 'Most folks never notice spider feet at all.'

'I notice everything about bugs,' Sam said proudly.

'Then you're going to love where we go next,' Gus said, hopping toward the windowsill.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Ooey, Gooey Fly
chapters.text:
On the windowsill sat a fat little fly, rubbing its front legs together.

'Watch its feet,' Gus said. 'Flies don't have hairs like us. They've got something gooier.'

Sam squinted through his magnifying glass. 'Its feet look... wet. And shiny.'

He pressed his own tiny fingertip to the glass, trying to wiggle it the same wet, sticky way. It just slid right off, and Sam toppled backward onto the sill with a soft **THUMP**.

'That's sticky ooze,' Gus said, hiding a smile. 'Tiny pads on its feet squeeze out a gooey drop, like a tiny glue blob, every single step.'

'Gross,' Sam said, grinning as he sat back up. 'I love it.'

The fly walked straight up the glass, then stopped, then - **BURRRP!** - let out the tiniest fly burp Sam had ever heard.

Sam burst out laughing. 'Did it just burp?'

'Flies do that,' Gus said, shrugging. 'Climbing makes everybody hungry, I guess.'

'Beetles do the gooey-foot trick too,' Gus added. 'Ooze instead of hairs. They climb shiny leaves the very same way, step by sticky step.'

Sam watched the fly zigzag across the glass without ever once slipping.

'So geckos peel, spiders have hairs, and flies go squish-squish-ooze,' Sam counted on his fingers. 'Everybody climbs different.'

'Everybody climbs their own way,' Gus agreed. 'And we've only just started.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Ants on the Move
chapters.text:
Gus tapped the window twice, and **FWOOMP!** - they popped outside onto the back porch, right beside a line of marching ants.

'Watch the ants,' Gus said. 'They're about to cross from bumpy bark onto smooth glass.'

Sam watched closely. On the bark, each ant dug in with sharp little claws, holding tight to every bump.

Then the ants reached a smooth glass jar lid. Sam held his breath.

'They're going to fall!' Sam said. Then he caught himself. 'Wait - unless they switch tools.'

Sure enough, the ants' tiny claws folded up, and sticky pads popped out instead. They marched right across the smooth lid, no slipping at all.

'SWITCH TOOLS!' Sam shouted, jumping up and down.

'You got it,' Gus said. 'Ants and roaches use claws on rough stuff, and sticky pads on smooth stuff. Whatever the wall needs, that's the tool they use.'

Sam counted twelve ants crossing safely, not one single slip.

'Like how I use my rain boots when it's wet, and sneakers when it's dry,' Sam said.

'That's exactly it,' Gus said, delighted. 'You've got a scientist's brain, Sam. A scientist is just someone who notices things and asks why.'

Sam puffed up proud. 'Then I'm a bug scientist.'

'The best kind,' said Gus.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Goats and Squirrels on the Poster
chapters.text:
Back inside, Gus hopped up onto Sam's wall, right beside a poster of mountains and trees.

'Watch this,' Gus said, and tapped one glowing toe on the poster. The mountain goat in the picture began to move, climbing a steep, rocky cliff.

'How does he not fall?' Sam asked, pressing close to the poster.

'Look at his feet,' Gus said.

Sam studied the goat's feet. 'They're round and hard on the edges. But kind of squishy in the middle?'

'Good eye,' Gus said. 'Those are called hooves - hard and round on the outside, soft and squishy in the middle. The soft part squishes into every little bump on the rock, like a sponge.'

'Like my rain boots,' Sam said. 'Hard bottoms, but my feet feel squishy inside.'

'Exactly like that,' Gus said.

Next to the goat, a squirrel scurried straight up a tree trunk.

'Her trick has got to be different,' Sam guessed. 'She doesn't have squishy hooves.'

'Smart thinking. Watch her toes,' Gus said.

Sharp, curved claws flashed as the squirrel climbed, digging into tiny cracks in the bark, cracks too small for Sam to even see.

'A million tiny cracks, and she finds every single one,' Gus said.

Sam reached out one tiny finger and traced the bark in the poster, careful and gentle. 'I believe it.'

The squirrel reached the top and flicked her tail, like a tiny victory wave.

'Goodbye, squirrel!' Sam called, waving back with both hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Frog Pond, Snail Trail
chapters.text:
Gus flipped open Sam's favorite picture book, right to a page with a pond.

A little tree frog sat on a wet, shiny leaf. Sam leaned close.

'Her toes look flat,' Sam said. 'Like tiny stickers.'

'Flat, with a pattern like tiny honeycomb hexagons,' Gus said. 'And covered in a bit of slime. That combo grips wet leaves and wet glass, even when everything's dripping.'

The frog hopped from leaf to leaf, never once slipping into the pond.

The pond page even smelled faintly like rain, Sam thought, though that might've just been his imagination.

'What about him?' Sam asked, pointing to a snail inching up the pond's stone wall.

'No hairs, no claws, no sticky pads at all,' Gus said. 'Just slime. He glides on a slippery trail, and his squishy foot ripples along, wave after wave.'

'I saw a slug trail on our sidewalk once,' Sam said. 'It was shiny and sparkly in the sun.'

'That's the same slimy trick,' Gus said. 'Slow, but it works every time.'

Sam watched the snail reach the top of the wall, slow and steady.

'SLIP AND SLIDE!' Sam shouted, clapping for the little snail.

'Slow and steady,' Gus agreed, chuckling. 'Climbing isn't always a race.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Bats and the Woodpecker Tree
chapters.text:
Gus led Sam under the blanket fort by Sam's bed, dark and cozy like a little cave.

It was a bit dark in there. Sam's tummy did one small flip-flop.

'It's okay,' Gus said gently. 'Watch the ceiling.'

A small bat hung upside down from a fold in the blanket, fast asleep.

'He's not sticky at all,' Gus said. 'Bats use curved claws, like tiny hooks, to hang on. No peeling, no sticky pads - just a good, strong hook.'

'Like hanging your coat on a hook,' Sam said, feeling better already.

'Just like that,' Gus said, and the fort suddenly felt a lot less spooky and a lot more cozy.

Sam peeked at the bat one more time and smiled instead of worried.

They ducked back out into Sam's room, right by the window, where a woodpecker tapped on the tree outside.

'Watch his feet and his tail,' Gus said.

The woodpecker gripped the bark with two toes forward and two toes back, like a tiny four-fingered hand. His stiff tail feathers pressed against the trunk like a kickstand, holding him steady while he tapped.

'His tail is like a chair!' Sam said.

'A built-in chair,' Gus laughed. 'Every climber's got their own special trick.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again, Sticky Fingers
chapters.text:
**FWOOMP!** Sam popped back to his normal size, standing on his soft carpet. The bug jar sat right where he'd left it.

'That was the best tour ever,' Sam said, flopping onto his bed.

Gus hopped up onto the nightstand, next to a shiny little toy paddle Sam had never noticed before.

'What's that?' Sam asked.

'Scientists - people who study how things work - watched geckos for years,' Gus said. 'Then they invented, which means they made something brand new, a sticky paddle just like gecko toes. In **2014**, a person even climbed a real glass wall holding two of them.'

'A person climbed a wall? Like you?' Sam's eyes went huge.

'Just like me,' Gus said proudly. 'All because someone noticed gecko toes, the same way you noticed spider feet today.'

Sam yawned a giant yawn. 'I noticed lots of feet today.'

'You sure did,' Gus said. 'Gecko toes, spider hairs, fly ooze, ant claws, goat hooves, squirrel claws, frog pads, snail slime, bat hooks, and woodpecker tails. Ten climbers, one sleepy bug scientist.'

Sam snuggled under his blanket, already dreaming of fuzzy toes and ooey feet.

Gus hopped back to the wall and pressed his toes flat against it, slow and careful.

'Will you come back?' Sam asked, eyes already drooping.

'Always,' Gus said, peeling his last toe into place. 'Stick with me.'

He glowed one soft, green glow, then went still, just a little sticker again. But if Sam looked close, the gecko sticker seemed to wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Stick with me, and sleep tight.

true_facts.text: **Geckos** can run up glass and walk upside down on the ceiling because their toes have **millions of tiny hairs**.
Each of those tiny hairs splits into even **tinier tips**, smaller than a speck of dust, and that's the real secret to sticking.
A gecko's grip isn't glue at all - it peels its toes up **slow, like pulling tape**, so its feet never get messy.
**Spiders** have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
**Flies and some beetles** climb using **sticky ooze** that squeezes out of their feet with every step.
**Ants and roaches** use sharp claws on rough walls and switch to sticky pads on smooth ones.
**Mountain goats** climb steep rocky cliffs with **hooves** that are hard on the outside and soft and squishy in the middle.
**Squirrels** climb trees using sharp, curved claws that dig into **tiny cracks** too small for us to see.
**Tree frogs** have flat, slightly slimy toe pads with a tiny honeycomb pattern that grips wet leaves and glass.
**Snails** climb smooth walls by gliding on a trail of **slime**, rippling their squishy foot along.
**Bats** hang upside down using **curved claws**, like tiny hooks, instead of sticky feet.
**Woodpeckers** grip tree trunks with two toes forward and two toes back, and prop themselves up with **stiff tail feathers**.
In **2014**, scientists built a **sticky paddle** inspired by gecko toes, and a person used two of them to climb a real glass wall.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Buzzing Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A sweet little trip inside a bee hive.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Honey Jar
chapters.text:
Finn sat at the kitchen table. He spread honey on his toast. Nell sat next to him. She held a bunch of yellow flowers from the garden.

"I like yellow best," Nell said. She twirled a flower under her nose.

Finn took a big bite. "Mmm. Honey is the best." Golden honey dripped onto his plate.

Then the honey jar began to glow. It glowed soft and gold, like a tiny sun. Finn blinked. Nell blinked too.

BZZZZ! A tiny bee popped out of the jar. She had shiny wings and a stripy coat.

"Hello!" said the bee. "My name is Buzzby. Want to see where honey comes from?"

Finn grinned. Nell grinned too. "Yes!" they said together.

Buzzby waved a wing. POOF! The kitchen rushed away. Finn and Nell were suddenly as small as beans, standing on a giant yellow petal.

"Whoa!" said Finn, wobbling a little.

Nell patted the petal. "It's so yellow and soft! Just like my flowers at home!"

"This flower makes a sweet juice called nectar," Buzzby said. "Nectar is the sugary drink flowers make, just for bees."

A worker bee landed nearby. She had a long, curly tongue, like a bendy straw. SLURP! She sipped the nectar right up.

"Look, Nell!" Finn said. "Her tongue is a straw!"

"A flower straw!" Nell giggled, clapping her hands.

Buzzby nodded. "That's how bees drink nectar. Every bee out here is called a forager. They fly from flower to flower, sipping with their straw-tongues, all day long."

Finn pointed at another yellow flower. "Let's follow her home!"

"Good idea, Finn," said Buzzby. "Follow me!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Secret Tummy
chapters.text:
The little bee buzzed along a leafy path. Finn and Nell hopped after her, light as feathers.

"Where does the nectar go?" Finn asked. "Does she eat it?"

Buzzby landed on a twig. "Not yet! Bees have a special pouch inside, just for nectar. It's called a honey stomach. It's different from the tummy she uses for eating food."

Nell's eyes went wide. "Two tummies?"

"Two tummies," said Buzzby. "One is for food. One is just for carrying nectar home to share."

Finn patted his own tummy. "I only have one tummy. It's for honey toast."

Everyone laughed. Even the bees nearby buzzed, as if they were laughing too.

The forager bee flew past, her stripy body round and full.

"She's carrying a whole tummy of nectar," Buzzby said. "Let's follow her home to the hive."

Nell pointed ahead. A round, papery house hung from a tree branch, humming with bees going in and out.

"Is that the hive?" Nell asked, standing on her tiptoes.

"That's the hive," said Buzzby. "It's where thousands and thousands of bees live together, all busy, all buzzing."

Finn gasped. "Thousands?!"

"Come see," said Buzzby, and she flew toward the humming door, wings glinting gold.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Mouth to Mouth
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, it was warm and buzzy. Bees zoomed everywhere, busy as can be.

The forager bee landed by another bee. She opened her mouth. The other bee opened hers too.

"What is she doing?" Finn asked, leaning close.

"She's passing the nectar, mouth to mouth," said Buzzby. "It's a little like sharing a sip. The next bee gets the nectar now."

Nell scrunched her nose. "That's funny!"

"It's also clever," said Buzzby. "Every time the nectar moves mouth to mouth, a little bee magic happens. Something in their spit changes the sugar, bit by bit. It turns watery nectar into something thicker and sweeter."

Finn tilted his head. "Like a magic potion?"

"A little like that," laughed Buzzby.

Nell watched closely, bouncing on her toes. "Pass it again! Pass it again!" she cheered.

The bee passed the nectar to one more bee, then another, mouth to mouth, down a wiggly line.

"They work as a team," Buzzby said. "Just like you two, sharing your toast."

Finn grinned. "I always give Nell the crust."

"I like the crust!" said Nell, and they both laughed so hard they nearly tipped off their petal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Six-Sided House
chapters.text:
Buzzby led them deeper into the hive. Rows and rows of tiny little rooms glowed gold in the dim light.

"Whoa!" Finn said. "Look at all those little windows!"

Nell counted the sides of one shape, poking each one with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" she said. "It has six sides!"

"Good counting, Nell!" said Buzzby. "That shape is called a honeycomb cell. Bees build it from wax made by their own bodies. The wax comes out of little spots on their tummies."

Finn's mouth dropped open. "Wax comes out of their tummy?"

"It sure does," said Buzzby. "Then they shape it into these six-sided little rooms, perfect for holding nectar and honey."

A house bee flew up and spread nectar into one of the rooms, smoothing it gently with her legs.

"She's tucking it in," Nell said softly, watching with her chin on her hands.

"That's exactly right," said Buzzby. "Every single cell gets filled up, one by one, all day long."

Finn reached out and gently touched the edge of a cell. It felt smooth, like a tiny cup.

"It's so neat," Finn whispered. "Like a hundred little cups in a row."

"More like thousands," said Buzzby, smiling. "Come on. There's one more step before this nectar turns into honey."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Big Buzzy Fan
chapters.text:
Buzzby flew Finn and Nell to a row of cells, still runny with fresh nectar.

"It still looks watery," Finn said, peering close. "Not like the honey on my toast."

"That's because it needs drying out," said Buzzby. "Watch this."

A whole line of bees faced the cells. They flapped their wings, fast, fast, fast. FLUTTER FLUTTER FLUTTER! A warm little breeze rushed past Finn's face.

"Their wings flap so fast," Buzzby said, "about two hundred times every single second! That's what makes their buzzy sound."

Nell flapped her arms too, as fast as she could. "I'm helping!" she giggled.

Finn flapped his arms too, wiggling his nose like a bee. "BZZZZZZ!" he buzzed.

Buzzby laughed so hard she wobbled on her twig. "You two are great helper bees!"

Slowly, slowly, the watery nectar turned thick and golden, right before their eyes.

"It's turning into honey!" Nell cheered, hopping in a circle.

"All that fanning dries it out," said Buzzby, "until it's thick, sticky honey, just like the honey on Finn's toast."

Finn clapped his sticky hands. "HONEY!" he shouted, and the little bees buzzed happily all around.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Wax Lid
chapters.text:
Once the honey was thick and ready, a house bee came close. She patted a thin cap of wax right over the top of the cell.

"Why is she doing that?" Nell asked, tilting her head.

"She's putting on a little lid," said Buzzby. "It keeps the honey clean and safe, like a lid on a jam jar at home."

Finn peeked at rows of capped cells, each one shining gold under its own tiny wax lid.

"Why do bees make so much honey?" Finn asked. "They can't eat it all at once."

"They save it," Buzzby said. "In winter, there are no flowers. No nectar to sip. So bees eat the honey they stored, all cozy inside the warm hive."

Nell gasped. "Like a pantry!"

"Just like a pantry," said Buzzby. "And here is something amazing. If you keep honey covered and dry, it stays good for a very, very long time. It almost never goes bad."

Finn thought about his toast. "So old honey is still yummy honey?"

"Still yummy," Buzzby agreed, "even after a long, long time."

Nell tapped a capped cell gently with one finger. "Sleep tight, little honey," she whispered.

Everyone smiled at that, warm and quiet in the golden hive.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
Deep in the hive, Buzzby led them to a bigger, rounder room. A large bee moved slowly there, surrounded by helpers.

"That's our queen," Buzzby whispered. "She is the busy mom of nearly every bee in this whole hive."

Nell peeked closer, careful not to bump her. "What does she do all day?"

"She lays eggs," said Buzzby. "Sometimes over a thousand eggs in one single day!"

Finn's eyes went huge. "A thousand?! In one day?!"

"In one day," Buzzby nodded. "That is why our hive has so many bees — sometimes twenty thousand, sometimes even sixty thousand, all buzzing together in the summer."

Nell tried to count on her fingers and gave up, giggling. "That's too many to count!"

"Way too many," laughed Buzzby. "And guess what? Almost all of those bees are girl bees. They do every single job — finding flowers, making honey, cleaning the hive, and watching the door."

Finn looked around at all the busy worker bees zooming past. "They're all sisters!"

"All sisters," said Buzzby, "working together, just like a big, busy team."

Nell waved at a passing worker bee. "Hi, sister bee!"

The little bee buzzed back a happy loop, as if waving hello right back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Waggle Dance and Home
chapters.text:
Outside the hive, a bee was dancing in little circles and wiggles.

"What is she doing?" Finn asked, giggling at the silly wiggle.

"That's a scout bee," said Buzzby. "She found a wonderful patch of flowers. Her wiggly dance tells the other bees which way to fly, and how far."

Nell wiggled along with the bee, shaking her arms side to side. "Like this?"

"Just like that!" laughed Buzzby.

Finn watched bees land on flower after flower. "Do the flowers get anything back?"

"They do," said Buzzby. "Bees carry yellow flower dust from bloom to bloom on their fuzzy legs. That helps the flowers grow new fruits and new flowers too."

Nell looked at her own yellow flowers, happy. "My flowers needed bees!"

"They sure did," said Buzzby gently.

Then Buzzby smiled at them both. "Do you know how much work goes into just one spoonful of honey? It takes about twelve bees, working their whole lives, just to make one teaspoon."

Finn gasped. "For one spoon on my toast?"

"One little spoon," said Buzzby. "That's why honey is so special, and why we say thank you to the bees."

She waved a wing. POOF! The kitchen rushed back around them. Finn and Nell were home, big as before. The honey jar sat quiet and gold, not glowing anymore.

Finn looked at his toast. "Thank you, bees," he whispered.

Nell set her yellow flowers gently beside the jar. "Goodnight, bees. Goodnight, flowers."

The kitchen was warm and quiet, and it smelled just a little bit like honey.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz buzz, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: Bees sip sweet flower juice called **nectar** with a long, bendy tongue, like a tiny straw.
Bees have a special second tummy, called a **honey stomach**, just for carrying nectar home.
Bees pass nectar **mouth to mouth** to share it with other bees back at the hive.
Honey is kept in little **six-sided** rooms called honeycomb cells.
Bees make the wax for their honeycomb from little spots on their own **tummies**.
Bees **flap their wings** very fast over the nectar to dry it into thick, sticky honey.
A bee's wings flap about **two hundred times** every second, which makes the buzzing sound.
Once honey is ready, bees seal it with a thin **wax lid** to keep it safe and clean.
Bees save up honey so they have food to eat all through **winter**, when flowers are gone.
A hive can have **thousands and thousands of bees**, sometimes up to sixty thousand in summer.
The **queen bee** lays over a thousand eggs in a single day.
Almost all the bees in a hive are **girl worker bees** who do every job.
A **scout bee** does a wiggly dance to show other bees where the best flowers are.
It takes about **twelve bees**, working their whole lives, to make just one teaspoon of honey.

new_recurring.name: Buzzby the guide bee
new_recurring.rule: A small, stripy, calm and silly bee who pops out of a glowing golden honey jar to guide the children on a real science or history adventure, always says 'Buzz buzz, let's go!' before shrinking them down, and returns them home with a soft…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The honey jar stopped glowing, and Nell set her yellow flowers down beside it as she and Finn said goodnight to the bees and flowers together.

editor_notes: Fix the Wright brothers claim: replace 'light metal tubes, spoked wheels' with what really carried over, such as bicycle chains and sprockets driving the propellers and their skill at building light, strong machines. Also move Dunlop's 1888 tyre to Belfast, Ireland.

Use Omar's actual like: let him try a BMX-style bunny hop or wheelie on the Rover safety bike, or have the 1970s finale end with him riding the track, so his tricks shape a scene and he doesn't just name them.

story.title: Omar and the Bicycle That Rolled Through Time
story.subtitle: A BMX kid pedals two hundred years of wheels

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wobbly Walking Bike (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar was supposed to be asleep. Instead he sat on his bedroom floor, spinning his BMX pedal with one finger. WHIRRR.

The chain caught the moonlight and started to glow, soft green, like a firefly stuck in the links.

"Bikes don't glow," Omar whispered.

A tiny gear popped off the chain and hovered, blinking two little eyes. "Most bikes don't," it said. "I'm Sprocket. Want to see where your bike came from?"

Before Omar could answer, the glow swallowed the room. WHOOOOSH.

He landed on a muddy street in **1817**, Germany. A man wobbled past on a wooden two-wheeler, pushing it along with his feet, with no pedals at all.

"That's Karl von Drais," said Sprocket. "He calls it the running machine."

"How do you go fast with no pedals?" Omar asked.

"You don't," von Drais laughed, steering with real handlebars. "You run!"

Omar grabbed the handlebars and pushed off with both feet. The machine rolled, wobbly but working.

"It steers just like mine!" Omar shouted. "Pretty cool for the very first bike."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Pedals at Last (1866)
chapters.text:
Sprocket tugged Omar's sleeve. "Next stop!"

They landed with a BUMP outside a workshop in the **1860s**. A man named Pierre Lallement knelt by a wooden bike, bolting pedals onto the front wheel.

"Pedals!" Omar said. "Finally!"

"Watch your teeth," Lallement warned, hopping on. He rode over the cobblestones. CLACKETY-CLACK. His whole body jiggled like jelly.

"They call it a **velocipede**," Sprocket said. "A fancy word for an early pedal bike. People nicknamed it the **boneshaker**, because it shook your bones loose."

Omar tried it himself. CLACKETY-CLACK. His teeth chattered with every bump.

"In **1866**," said Sprocket, "Lallement got a **patent** — a paper saying you invented something first — for this exact design, in America."

Omar rubbed his sore seat, grinning. "Worth it. I basically invented pedals today."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
The next landing was HIGH UP. Omar blinked at a bike with a front wheel taller than his dad, and a tiny back wheel.

"Meet the **penny-farthing**," said Sprocket, "named after two old coins — one huge, one tiny, just like these wheels."

A rider rolled past, perched way up top like a bird on a fence post.

"How do you get UP there?" Omar asked.

"Carefully," the rider said, pedaling off, fast and wobbly.

Then his front wheel hit a rock. The bike jerked forward—

"He's gonna fall!" Omar gasped.

But the rider hopped off at the last second, landing on his feet, laughing. "Just a little header. Happens all the time!"

Omar let out a breath. "Scarier than any BMX jump I've tried."

"One turn of that giant wheel," said Sprocket, "sends you really far. That's why people loved it, bumps and all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bike (1885)
chapters.text:
"Somebody needed a better idea," Sprocket said.

They popped into a workshop in **1885**, England. A man named John Kemp Starley stood by a new bike. Both wheels were the same size, low to the ground.

"I call it the **Rover Safety Bicycle**," Starley said proudly. "No more giant wheel to tip off of."

Omar spotted a metal chain looping from the pedals to the back wheel, just like his own BMX. "Whoa — that's basically a real bike!"

"Low wheels, a chain to the back wheel," said Sprocket. "Way safer. This is why bikes still look like this today."

Omar pedaled a slow loop. No tipping. No header. Just smooth riding.

"Ten out of ten," Omar said. "Would ride again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Squishy Tires (1888)
chapters.text:
Omar's ride ended with a jolt. BUMP BUMP BUMP. "Ow. These tires are solid rubber. Hard as rocks."

"Someone's about to fix that," said Sprocket, zooming them to **1888**, Scotland.

A man named John Boyd Dunlop wrapped a rubber tube around his son's tricycle wheel, then pumped it full of air. PFFFT-PFFFT.

"A **pneumatic** tire," Dunlop explained. "Filled with air, like a balloon. Should ride smoother."

Omar poked it. Squishy. "Like my BMX tires!"

He rolled the tricycle across the cobblestones. No rattling, no jiggling. Just a smooth, quiet roll.

"Way better," Omar sighed happily. "And hey — your tire company is still around today!"

Dunlop beamed. "Glad somebody noticed."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everybody Rides (1890s)
chapters.text:
Sprocket zipped them to a busy street in the **1890s**, bikes everywhere, bells ringing.

"This is the **Golden Age of Bicycles**," said Sprocket. "Millions of people bought bikes, all across Europe and America."

A woman rode past wearing puffy pants instead of a long skirt.

"Those are **bloomers**," Sprocket said. "Safer for pedaling than long skirts, which could get stuck in the wheels."

An older woman named Susan B. Anthony stopped to watch the riders. "Cycling has done more to **emancipate** women than anything else in the world," she said — meaning set them free, free to go wherever they wanted, on their own.

Omar watched a dozen women pedal past, laughing, steering exactly where they wanted. "That's awesome," he said.

"IT REALLY IS," said Sprocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Flew (1890s–1903)
chapters.text:
Next stop: a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, the **1890s**. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, were fixing a bike wheel.

"We fix bikes," Orville said, "and build our own too."

Omar noticed thin metal tubes and wheels with thin spokes stacked against the wall. "Those look kind of flimsy. But light."

"That's the idea," Wilbur said. "Light and strong. We're working on something new — something that doesn't even touch the ground."

Omar's eyes went wide. "Wait. Are you building a—"

"An airplane," Sprocket finished. "In **1903**, these two bike-shop brothers build the first one that actually flies. They use bike tricks — light metal tubes, spoked wheels — to help pull it off."

Omar stared at the bike parts, amazed. "Bikes helped invent flying. Coolest thing I've ever heard."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Dirt, Jumps, and Home
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Sprocket. "Your turf."

They landed on a dusty dirt track in the **1970s**, United States. Kids raced small, tough bikes over bumps and jumps — like **motocross**, bumpy motorcycle racing, but on bikes.

"These are **BMX** bikes!" Omar yelled. "My kind of bike!"

Nearby, riders bombed down a rocky trail on bikes with thick, **knobby** tires — bumpy little nubs for extra grip.

"Mountain bikes," said Sprocket. "Built by riders in California who wanted to ride rough dirt trails without wrecking."

Omar grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "BMX and mountain bikes? Best field trip ever."

"There are over a billion bikes in the world now," Sprocket added. "More than any other ride. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars."

The glow swelled. WHOOOOSH. Omar landed back on his bedroom floor, BMX leaned against his bed, right where he'd left it.

Sprocket clicked back onto the chain, glow fading to a sparkle.

"Thanks for the ride through history," Omar whispered, smiling at his bike.

On his nightstand sat one tiny glowing gear — a keepsake from two hundred years of wheels.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride easy, dream big.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler called the running machine — you pushed it along with your feet because it had no pedals.
In the **1860s**, Pierre Lallement bolted pedals onto the front wheel, making a bumpy ride nicknamed the **boneshaker**.
In the **1870s**, the **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, so one pedal turn could send you really far.
It was named after two old coins, one big and one tiny, just like its two wheels.
Riding one was risky — if the front wheel hit something, the rider could tip forward and take a tumble called a header.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the Rover Safety Bicycle, with two same-sized wheels and a chain to the back wheel.
Its low, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, so it became the new standard everywhere.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented the pneumatic tire — a rubber tire filled with air — for a much smoother ride.
In the **1890s**, the Golden Age of Bicycles saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and America.
Susan B. Anthony said riding bikes helped set women free to go wherever they wanted on their own.
Because long skirts were dangerous near bike wheels, many women started wearing bloomers, safer puffy pants for pedaling.
In the **1890s**, brothers Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, before inventing the first airplane in **1903**.
In the **1970s**, small and sturdy BMX bikes became popular in the United States, inspired by bumpy motorcycle racing.
Around the same time, mountain bikes with thick, knobby tires were built in California for riding rough dirt trails.

story.title: Ada and Bolt the Fridge-Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the invisible pull of magnets.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Night the Magnets Woke Up
chapters.text:
Ada lay on her bedroom floor, lining up fridge magnets in one shiny row. She had a robot magnet, a rainbow magnet, and a tiny red barn. It was way past bedtime, but she wanted just one more row.

Then the red barn magnet gave a little **BZZT** and lifted off the carpet.

"Whoa!" Ada whispered.

A tiny voice popped out. "Evening, Ada! I'm Bolt, your fridge-magnet robot. Want to see how magnets really work?"

"Yes, please!" said Ada.

Bolt rolled two magnets together. They snapped — **CLICK** — and stuck tight. Then Bolt flipped one around, and they pushed apart instead.

"Every magnet has two ends, called **poles**," said Bolt. "One end is north, one is south. Opposite ends pull together. Same ends push away."

Ada flipped her own magnets to test it. North stuck to south, every time.

"They're picky friends!" Ada laughed.

"Exactly," said Bolt. "Now hop on. We've got stops to make."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Sock Drawer Mystery
chapters.text:
Bolt zoomed Ada down to the kitchen, past wooden spoons and a plastic cup.

"Why don't these stick to magnets?" Ada asked, tapping a spoon.

"Good question," said Bolt. "Everything is made of tiny bits called **atoms**, too small to ever see. In metals like iron, nickel, and cobalt, atoms can line up the same way, like a team. That makes a strong pull."

"But wood's atoms don't line up?" Ada guessed.

"Right! In wood and plastic, atoms point every which way, so no pull happens," said Bolt.

Ada tested everything nearby. Spoon — nothing. Fridge door — **CLICK**! Plastic cup — nothing.

"The fridge has a team!" Ada cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Invisible Rivers
chapters.text:
Bolt pulled out a little tray of silvery dust. "This is iron dust. Sprinkle some near a magnet, Ada."

Ada shook the tray. The dust swirled into curvy lines, looping from one end of the magnet to the other.

"Whoa, it's drawing a picture!" Ada said.

"You're seeing the **magnetic field**," said Bolt. "It's the invisible space around a magnet, where its push or pull can reach. You can't see it on its own, but the dust shows you its shape."

Ada traced one curvy line with her finger. "It looks like little rivers!"

"Rivers of pull," Bolt agreed. "Every magnet has one, even the ones too small to notice."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Started It All
chapters.text:
Next, Bolt's screen lit up with a map of faraway mountains.

"Long ago," said Bolt, "people in Greece found a special rock near a place called **Magnesia**. It pulled on metal all by itself, with no battery at all!"

"That's probably where the word 'magnet' comes from," Bolt added.

"Did they know why?" Ada asked.

"Not yet. But in China, people used that same kind of rock to make the first **compasses** — tools with an arrow that always points one way, to help travelers find their path. That was over two thousand years ago!"

Ada spun around like an arrow herself. "I'm compass Ada! I point to... the kitchen!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Earth, the Biggest Magnet
chapters.text:
Bolt beeped, and a glowing blue ball appeared — Earth!

"Guess what," said Bolt. "The whole entire planet is a giant magnet."

Ada's eyes went wide. "Our whole Earth?"

"Deep, deep down, swirling melted metal spins around and around," said Bolt. "That swirl makes Earth's own pulling power, stretching all the way out into space."

"Is that why compasses point north?" Ada asked.

"You got it," said Bolt. "A compass needle is a tiny magnet. It lines up with Earth's big pull and always points north."

Ada held her toy compass and watched the needle settle still.

"It found it!" she shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Magnets You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
Bolt led Ada past a toy crane and a doorbell button.

"Some magnets can switch on and off," said Bolt. "They're called **electromagnets**. Wrap a wire around and around into a **coil**, run electricity through it, and zap — it's a magnet! Turn off the power, and the pull disappears."

Ada pressed the doorbell. **DING-DONG!**

"Is there a magnet in there?" she asked.

"Yes! It pulls a tiny hammer to hit the bell," said Bolt. "Giant electromagnets even lift whole cars at junkyards, then drop them when the power switches off."

Ada gasped. "Switch-off magnets are basically magic!"

"Science magic," Bolt said, winking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Snap It in Half
chapters.text:
Bolt handed Ada a long bar magnet and a toy saw.

"Guess what happens if we cut this in half," said Bolt.

Ada thought hard. "Um... one half is north and one half is south?"

"Nice guess, but nope!" said Bolt, snapping it in two. "Each piece gets its own north end and south end. Cut it again, and you'd get even more tiny whole magnets."

"They never run out of poles!" Ada laughed.

"Not every shiny metal joins the fun," Bolt added. "Gold, silver, copper, and aluminum don't stick to magnets at all."

Ada tapped Bolt's shiny foot. "Lucky you're not made of those!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Floating Trains and Flying Birds
chapters.text:
Bolt's screen showed a sleek train zooming with no wheels touching the rails.

"That's a **maglev** train," said Bolt. "It floats above the tracks using strong magnets, gliding super fast with hardly any rubbing."

"No wheels at all?" Ada gasped.

"None! And in hospitals," Bolt went on, "doctors use a giant magnet machine called an **MRI** to see inside someone's body — no cutting needed, just a strong magnet doing its job."

"Even animals use magnets," Bolt said. "Birds, sea turtles, and some fish may feel Earth's pull to help them find their way on long trips."

Ada tapped her head. "Do I have a magnet feeling too?"

"Maybe just a magnet for bedtime," Bolt chuckled, scooping her up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Fridge
chapters.text:
Bolt zoomed Ada back up to her bedroom floor, right beside her sleepy fridge magnets.

"One last secret," Bolt said. "Fridge magnets like me are made of soft, bendy rubber, mixed with tiny bits of magnet powder. That's why I can bend around corners and still stick tight."

Ada squeezed Bolt gently. He bent like rubber, then snapped right back.

"You're squishy AND magnetic!" Ada giggled.

"Best of both," Bolt said, rolling back onto the fridge door with a happy **CLICK**.

Ada tucked her blanket up to her chin, her magnets lined up neatly beside the bed.

"Stick together," Bolt whispered.

"Stick together," Ada whispered back, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together, and sleep tight.

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends called **poles** — one north, one south — where its pull is strongest.
Opposite poles pull together, but two same poles push apart.
Metals like **iron, nickel, and cobalt** have atoms that line up the same way, making a strong magnet pull.
Sprinkle **iron dust** near a magnet, and it swirls into curvy lines showing the invisible pull.
Long ago, people in Greece found a magnetic rock near a place called **Magnesia** — maybe where the word 'magnet' comes from.
In China, people used magnetic rocks to make the first **compasses**, over **two thousand years ago**.
The whole planet **Earth** is a giant magnet, made by swirling melted metal deep inside.
A compass needle is a tiny magnet that always lines up and points **north**.
An **electromagnet** is made by wrapping wire into a coil and running electricity through it — and it switches off too.
Electromagnets ring **doorbells** and even help giant cranes lift whole cars at junkyards.
Cut a magnet in half, and each piece becomes its own whole magnet, with a north end and a south end.
Metals like **gold, silver, copper, and aluminum** don't stick to magnets at all.
**Maglev** trains float above their tracks using strong magnets, so they can glide super fast.
Fridge magnets are made of bendy rubber mixed with tiny bits of **magnet powder**, so they can bend and still stick.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Backyard Rainbow
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sunbeam, and the secret of every color in the sky

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Backyard Rainbow
chapters.text:
Priya sat on the porch, drawing swirly suns in her sketchbook. Dev crept up behind her with his water pistol.

SQUIRT! Cold water hit her shoulder. "DEV!" she laughed, wiping her nose.

"Gotcha," said Dev. "Water pistols never miss."

"They miss me all the time," Priya teased, flicking water right back at him.

The sun sank low behind the fence, right at their backs. Dev squirted one last big spray into the golden light — and a stripe of colors shimmered in the mist. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, glowing like a tiny bridge.

"Whoa," Dev whispered. "Did I make that?"

A cheerful voice chuckled from inside the colors. "Close! You and the sun made it together. You need the sun behind you, and water in front. I'm Roy. Want to see how it's done?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Into the Raindrop
chapters.text:
Roy stretched out like a glowing ribbon and shrank the kids down, down, down — until they stood on top of one single raindrop.

"Climb in," said Roy. "Light does."

A beam of sunlight zoomed toward them and dove into the drop. It bent sideways the second it hit the water, like a skateboarder swerving around a cone.

"Why'd it swerve?" asked Priya.

"Light slows down in water," said Roy. "Slowing down makes it bend. That bending has a name: refraction."

"Re-FRAC-tion," Dev repeated, trying it out like a magic word. "Refraction! Refraction!"

The beam bounced off the back wall of the drop like a ball off a trampoline, then bent again on its way out.

"One bend in, a bounce, one bend out," said Roy. "Every raindrop does that little dance."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Hiding in Sunlight
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, the bent beam looked different. It wasn't white anymore. It was every color at once.

"Wait," said Priya, grabbing her sketchbook. "Sunlight looks white. Where did all these colors come from?"

"They were hiding inside it the whole time," said Roy. "White sunlight is actually every color, mixed together."

Dev looked unconvinced. "Prove it."

Roy floated them back to a cozy old room with wooden shelves. A man in old-fashioned clothes sat at a table with a chunk of glass shaped like a triangle.

"That's Isaac Newton," whispered Roy. "Back in the 1660s, he shined sunlight through a glass triangle called a prism."

The sunlight hit the glass and burst out the other side as a stripe of rainbow colors on the wall.

"See?" said Newton, grinning like he'd found treasure. "The colors were in there all along."

Priya high-fived the air. "Called it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Red Always Goes First
chapters.text:
Back in the giant raindrop world, Roy handed Priya a box of chalk. "Artist's job," he said. "Draw the colors in the order they always come out."

Priya chewed her lip, then drew a big arc. "Red first," she said, "because Roy, your name! R-O-Y! Red, Orange, Yellow..."

"...Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet," finished Roy. "You just spelled my whole name. Roy G. Biv. That's every rainbow, every time."

Dev squinted at the chalk arc. "Why's red on the outside and purple on the inside? Not the middle?"

"Good eye," said Roy. "Red bends the least when it goes through a raindrop. Purple bends the most. So red always ends up on the outer edge, and violet tucks in close to the inside."

Dev puffed up proudly, like he'd solved the whole sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow Is a Whole Circle
chapters.text:
Roy led them up, up, into the clouds, until the backyard looked tiny below.

"Here's a secret," said Roy. "A rainbow isn't really an arc. It's a full circle."

"No way," said Dev. "I only ever see half of one."

"That's because the ground is in the way," said Roy. "It blocks the bottom half, so you only see the top."

Just then a plane zoomed past below them, no ground anywhere near it. Through its window, passengers pointed and gasped at something below the wing: a whole glowing ring of color, a complete circle with no missing half.

"Told you," said Roy. "No ground, no missing piece."

Dev pressed his nose to an imaginary airplane window. "I'm getting a window seat forever now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Your Very Own Rainbow
chapters.text:
Back in the backyard, Dev squirted his water pistol again. Two rainbows glowed in the mist this time, one bright, one faint and sitting just above it.

"Two!" gasped Priya. "Did you double the squirt?"

"That fainter one happens when light bounces twice inside some of the drops," said Roy. "It flips the colors around too. Look close — its red is on the inside."

Priya squinted at her spot. Dev stood two steps to the left, squinting at his.

"Hey," said Dev, "I think my rainbow looks different from yours."

"It is different," said Roy. "Every single person sees their own rainbow, made from their own raindrops, because everyone stands in a slightly different spot."

"So this is MY rainbow," said Dev, puffing out his chest. "Mine. Get your own, Priya."

"I've got my own right here, thanks," Priya said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows Everywhere
chapters.text:
Roy swirled them past a roaring waterfall, where mist hung in the air and a rainbow sat glowing right inside the spray.

"Rainbows show up anywhere sun meets water droplets," said Roy. "Waterfalls, garden hoses, even puffy clouds of fog."

"What about nighttime?" asked Priya. "Could there be a moon one?"

"There can," said Roy. "It's called a moonbow. Moonlight is so much dimmer than sunlight that moonbows usually look pale and silvery to our eyes, not colorful at all. Cameras can catch the colors we miss, though."

Old stories love rainbows too, Roy told them. Long ago, some people told of a glowing bridge in the sky connecting our world to another. Other old stories told of a rainbow appearing after a big storm, as a gentle sign that good things were coming.

"Rainbows have been cheering people up forever," said Roy softly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more old story," said Roy, as they floated back toward the fence. "Some tales say there's a pot of gold waiting at the end of a rainbow."

Dev's eyes went wide. "Let's go get it!"

"You can't," laughed Roy. "A rainbow moves exactly when you move. Walk toward it, and it slides away. There's no real end to reach, ever."

"So it's like chasing your own shadow," said Priya.

"Exactly like that," said Roy.

Then the colors folded themselves smaller and smaller, like a ribbon being rolled up, until Roy was just a gentle glow sitting on the porch step beside Priya's sketchbook.

Dev set his water pistol down next to it. Priya flipped to a fresh page and drew one big arc: red on the outside, violet tucked inside.

"Bend it, blend it, see it bright," Roy whispered, fading into the evening air. "See you next time the sun comes out."

Dev yawned a giant yawn. Priya closed her sketchbook.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Bend it, blend it, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you and water (like rain or spray) has to be in front of you.
Rainbows need both sunshine and water drops at the same time, which is why they often show up right after it rains.
Sunlight bends when it goes into a raindrop, bounces off the back inside, and bends again coming out.
That bending has a name: refraction. It happens because light slows down when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of every color mixed together, hiding inside it.
Long ago, in the 1660s, a scientist named Isaac Newton shined sunlight through a glass prism and split it into rainbow colors.
The colors of a rainbow always go in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet — Roy G. Biv.
Red always sits on the outside edge of a rainbow because it bends the least, and violet sits on the inside because it bends the most.
A rainbow is actually a whole circle, but the ground usually blocks the bottom half so we only see an arc.
People flying in airplanes sometimes see a full circle rainbow, because there's no ground in the way to block it.
Sometimes a second, fainter rainbow appears above the first one with its colors flipped around.
You can never actually reach the end of a rainbow, because it moves exactly as you move.

story.title: Jack and Ellie and the Whispering Shell
story.subtitle: A swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Whispering Shell
chapters.text:
It was long past bedtime in Jack's room.

Jack had a flashlight under his blanket, reading his shark book for the fifth time.

Ellie tiptoed in wearing her mermaid tail blanket. "Scoot over," she whispered.

On the windowsill sat their favorite shell from the beach, big and spiral and striped like a candy cane.

Jack kept a shark tooth tucked inside it. Ellie kept a tiny green bead she called her mermaid's treasure.

Tonight the shell was humming. Not loud. Just a low hummmmm, like the sound inside a seashell, but bigger.

"Did you hear that?" Jack whispered.

"The shell is awake," Ellie said, like it was the most normal thing in the world.

Jack touched it. The shell flashed blue-green, bright as a swimming pool at night.

WHOOOOSH.

The windowsill melted into water. The ceiling turned into waves. Jack grabbed Ellie's hand, and down they swam, bubbles trailing behind them.

"We can breathe!" Ellie squealed, not even scared, just delighted.

A shape slid past them in the blue — smooth, gray, and curved like a smile.

"That's a shark," Jack said, "but look at it bend!"

The shark flexed its whole body sideways, easy as a rubber band.

The shell, now humming on a cord around Jack's neck, whispered an answer. "Sharks don't have hard bones like you do. Their skeletons are made of cartilage — bendy stuff, like the bendy part of your ear."

Jack squeezed his own ear. "Whoa. That's why it bends like that."

"And there are more than 500 kinds of sharks swimming around today," the shell added. "Big ones, tiny ones, every kind in between."

Ellie counted sharks on her fingers until she ran out of fingers. "That's a lot of sharks!"

"Told you," Jack said, grinning. "Now come on. Let's go meet some."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Hundred Million Years Ago
chapters.text:
The water around them changed. It got quieter, and strange.

No crabs, no coral, no fish that looked familiar at all.

"Where are we?" Ellie asked, pulling her blanket tight even though it was dry now.

A long, strange shape glided by, shaped a little like a shark but with a weird flat snout.

Jack pointed. "That doesn't look like any shark in my book!"

The shell whispered, "That's because this ocean is old. Really old. Sharks swam here more than 400 million years ago — before dinosaurs, before even trees grew on land."

Ellie's eyes went wide. "Before trees?"

"Before trees," the shell said again.

Jack tried to imagine a world with no trees, no dinosaurs, nothing but ocean and these strange gliding shapes. "So sharks were here first."

"Sharks were here first," the shell agreed.

Ellie reached toward the old shark shape, curious, then pulled her hand back on her own. "I'll just wave," she said. "I don't need to touch it to be its friend."

Jack high-fived her. "Good thinking. We watch, we don't touch."

The old shark swam off into the gloom, flicking its tail like it was waving back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
Something glinted on the sandy floor below them.

Jack swam down and brushed away the sand with both hands.

A tooth. A huge, triangle tooth, long as Ellie's whole hand.

"Ellie, look at this!" Jack called, holding it up.

Ellie swam over and gasped. "Is that a dragon tooth?"

"Better," the shell whispered. "That's a tooth from megalodon — a giant shark that lived millions of years ago. It isn't around anymore. We call that extinct, which just means none are left alive today."

"So it's not going to bite us," Ellie said, relieved but also a little disappointed.

"Not today," said the shell. "But this tooth is how we even know megalodon existed. Shark skeletons are bendy and soft, so they don't usually last. Teeth are hard, though. They turn into fossils — old teeth and bones turned hard as stone — and that's almost everything we know about sharks like this one."

Jack turned the tooth over in his hands. "It's as big as my shoe!"

"Bigger," Ellie said, holding her own hand against it.

"Can we keep it?" Jack asked.

The shell hummed a laugh. "Let's see what happens when we get home."
chapters.shout_line: IT'S AS BIG AS MY SHOE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tooth Factory
chapters.text:
A live shark swam close, mouth opening lazily as it turned.

Jack counted rows of teeth, lined up like a zipper. "Why does it have so many rows?"

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," the shell whispered. "Teeth fall out while they're eating, or just wear down. New teeth are always moving forward to take their place."

"Like a conveyor belt of teeth!" Jack said.

"A shark can grow and lose thousands of teeth over its whole life," the shell added.

Ellie made a face. "Thousands? I only lost like four teeth, and that was a big deal!"

"Sharks don't even notice," the shell said. "A new one is already on its way."

Jack grinned at his sister. "Guess you're not as tough as a shark, Ellie."

"Guess you're not as tough as a mermaid," Ellie shot back, and they both laughed so hard they forgot to swim for a second and just bobbed there, giggling, while the shark swam calmly on, its conveyor belt of teeth moving forward the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow the size of a school bus slid over them, blocking the sun.

Ellie froze for one second, then saw its face — wide mouth, gentle eyes, covered in white spots like stars.

"It's huge," Jack breathed, "but it looks... friendly?"

"That's a whale shark," the shell whispered. "It's the biggest fish in the whole world, over 40 feet long."

"Forty feet!" Jack tried to picture it. "That's as long as our whole street!"

"But here's the surprising part," the shell went on. "Even though it's the biggest, it mostly eats tiny bits of floating food called plankton. It just opens its mouth and filters the water through, like a big gentle strainer."

Ellie relaxed completely, delighted. "A giant that eats tiny snacks. That's my favorite kind of giant."

"And whale sharks can live over 100 years," the shell said. "Some are even older than your great-grandparents."

Ellie waved at the whale shark as it drifted past. It didn't seem to mind one bit.

"Hi, old friend," she said softly.

The whale shark gave one slow swish of its tail and glided on into the blue, and Jack waved too, just in case it was watching.
chapters.shout_line: A GIANT THAT EATS TINY SNACKS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer and the Spark
chapters.text:
Something swam toward them with the strangest head Jack had ever seen — flat and wide, like a hammer stretched sideways.

"Whoa," Jack said. "Why is its head shaped like that?"

"That's a hammerhead shark," the shell whispered. "Its wide head is called a cephalofoil — just a fancy word for 'hammer-shaped head.' It spreads the shark's eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

"Like having eyes on both ends of a ruler," Jack said.

"Exactly like that," said the shell.

Ellie tilted her head, studying the hammerhead's snout. "Why's it wiggling its head over the sand like that?"

"It's feeling for things hiding under the sand," the shell said. "Sharks have tiny jelly-filled spots on their snouts that can sense the tiniest electric signals other animals make, just by moving. They're called the ampullae of Lorenzini — but you can just call them a shark's secret sense."

"A secret sense!" Ellie said. "Like how I always know when Jack's about to prank me."

Jack laughed. "That's not a secret sense, that's just you being smart."

The hammerhead swept its wide head one more time, found something tasty under the sand, and swam off satisfied.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
Near a patch of coral, something was doing the strangest thing — walking.

Jack blinked. "Sharks don't walk!"

"This one does," the shell whispered. "It's called an epaulette shark, and it uses its fins like little paddle-feet to walk across the reef and even across puddles left behind at low tide."

Ellie watched it flop-flop-flop along the rocks, fins planted one after another. "It's so wobbly! I love it."

"It can go hours with hardly any air in the water," the shell added, "which is how it survives in those little puddles until the ocean comes back."

Jack tried to copy the shark's walk with his own hands, paddling them along an imaginary reef. "Like this?"

"Close," Ellie giggled, "except you have way fewer fins."

The little walking shark reached a deeper pool, slipped in, and swam off normally, like it had just remembered it was, in fact, a fish.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
Up ahead, they spotted someone swimming calmly among the sharks, taking notes on a little slate.

"Who's that?" Ellie asked.

"That," the shell whispered, "is Eugenie Clark. People called her the Shark Lady. She spent years and years studying sharks, and she proved something important."

"What?" Jack asked.

"That sharks are curious," the shell said. "Curious enough that she even trained some to do little tricks, like pressing a target for a snack."

Jack watched Eugenie Clark write something down, unhurried, while a shark circled nearby like it was waiting its turn. "She's not scared of them at all."

"She knew something else, too," the shell said. "Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain. That means they help keep every other animal in the sea balanced — not too many of this fish, not too few of that one."

"So sharks are like... ocean managers," Jack said.

"Ocean managers," the shell agreed. "Not bad, Jack."

Eugenie Clark looked up, caught sight of the two kids, and gave them a small, knowing wave before turning back to her notes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Coming Home
chapters.text:
The shell around Jack's neck began to glow brighter, warm instead of cool.

"Wait," Ellie said, suddenly thinking of something. "Jack, are sharks dangerous? Like, for real?"

Jack looked to the shell for the answer, the way he always did now.

"Hardly ever," the shell whispered. "Shark attacks on people are extremely rare. Far more sharks get hurt by people than the other way around. Mostly, sharks just want to be left alone, to swim and hunt their own dinners."

Ellie thought about that. "So we just wave, like we did the whole time."

"Just wave," the shell agreed.

The water around them began to swirl, gently this time, pulling them up and up toward a soft green-blue light.

WHOOOOSH.

Jack's bedroom rebuilt itself around them — the carpet, the bed, the flashlight still glowing under the blanket.

The shell sat quiet on the windowsill again, humming low, like it was tired out from a big night of swimming.

Something new sat beside it, though: one giant, triangle-shaped tooth, long as Ellie's hand.

"We really did bring it home," Jack whispered, grinning so wide his face nearly cracked in half.

Ellie yawned, already half asleep, her mermaid blanket pulled up to her chin. "Best. Night. Ever."

Jack set the tooth carefully next to the shell, right where it belonged, and climbed into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

true_facts.text: Sharks don't have hard bones — their skeletons are made of bendy **cartilage**, like the bendy part of your ear.
There are more than **500 kinds** of sharks swimming in the ocean today.
Sharks were swimming in the ocean more than **400 million years** ago — before dinosaurs and before trees.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that lived millions of years ago. It's **extinct** now, which means none are left alive.
Because shark skeletons are soft, almost everything we know about megalodon comes from its hard **fossil teeth**.
A shark can grow and lose **thousands of teeth** over its whole life, with new ones always moving forward.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world, over **40 feet long**, but it mostly eats tiny floating food called plankton.
Some whale sharks can live more than **100 years**.
A hammerhead shark's wide head, called a **cephalofoil**, spreads its eyes apart so it can see all around itself.
Sharks have a secret sense called the **ampullae of Lorenzini** — tiny jelly-filled spots that feel other animals' electric signals.
The epaulette shark can actually **walk** across the reef using its fins like little paddle-feet.
Scientist **Eugenie Clark**, nicknamed the **Shark Lady**, proved that sharks are curious and can even learn tricks.
Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain, helping keep all the other animals balanced.
Shark attacks on people are **extremely rare** — sharks mostly just want to be left alone.

story.title: Nora and the Buried Town of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A night trip through ash, water pipes, and one very old loaf of bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Street of Five
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor. Little glass tiles lay spread across her mosaic board. She was building a path of tiny squares, blue, then gold, then white.

One tile would not sit still. It glittered, then glowed, warm as a lamp.

"Oh," said a small, bright voice. "You found me."

The tile lifted off the board. It grew a tiny face, round and smiling. "I'm Tess," it said. "Short for **tessera** — that's just a fancy word for one little tile, like the ones in your hands."

Tess spun, and the tiles on the floor rose and swirled into a glowing doorway. "Want to see where I come from?" Nora did not even blink. She stepped through.

The floor turned to stone under her feet. Noise rushed in — shouting, laughing, a donkey braying somewhere close. They stood on a real street, in a real town, long, long ago.

"Where are we?" Nora asked.

"**Pompeii**," said Tess. "A busy Roman town, near where the city of **Naples** stands today."

Nora noticed the street had stones poking up out of it, set in a row like stepping stones in a creek. "Why would they put rocks in the middle of a road?"

"Go on," said Tess. "Guess."

Nora hopped from stone to stone. "So your feet stay dry! Like a crossing!"

"Exactly right," said Tess. "And look — there's a gap between them, just wide enough for a cart's wheels to roll through."

"Smart," Nora said. "Why is the town called Pompeii, anyway?"

"Some people think it comes from an old word, ***pompe***, from an even older language called **Oscan**. It might mean **five** — maybe because five little villages joined together to make one town."

All around them, shops buzzed. Bakers called out prices. Nora counted temples, a theater, and a bathhouse, all before they'd even turned the corner. "It's huge!"

"About **eleven to fifteen thousand people** lived here," said Tess. "Noisy, isn't it?"

Nora grinned and hopped one more stepping stone — then wobbled, and giggled, and grabbed Tess's glowing edge to steady herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bread in the Oven
chapters.text:
A warm, yeasty smell drifted down the street. Nora's stomach rumbled right along with it.

"That smells like Grandma's kitchen," she said.

They ducked into a little shop with a round stone oven built into the wall. Nora peered inside — and stopped.

A loaf of bread sat right there on the oven floor. Round, with lines cut across the top like a pie. Nobody had touched it in a very long time.

"Is someone coming back for that?" Nora asked.

"Not anymore," said Tess gently. "That loaf has been sitting there since the town itself stopped, all at once, a long time ago. Everything froze just as it was — paintings still bright on walls, even little messages people had scratched near their doorways."

Nora leaned closer. There was a small stamped mark pressed into the top of the loaf. "What's that pattern?"

"The baker's own mark," said Tess. "So everyone in town knew whose bread was whose."

Nora pulled out the little notebook she always carried, the one for mosaic patterns, and copied the stamp onto a blank page. "I'm keeping this one," she said. "It's a good shape."

"A baker from thousands of years ago," said Tess, "and you just borrowed his design."

Nora's tummy rumbled again, loudly this time.

"That bread is definitely not for eating," said Tess.

"I figured," said Nora. "But it smells like it should be."

They stepped back out into the sunny street, Nora still clutching her notebook, already planning where the baker's stamp might fit in her very own mosaic.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water for Everyone
chapters.text:
A soft trickling sound led them to a stone fountain on a corner. Water poured steadily from a carved spout into a trough below.

"Wait," Nora said. "Is that real water, right now?"

"It's an echo," said Tess. "But back then, yes — very real."

Nora crouched and traced a line along the ground with her finger, following a thin seam in the stones. "Does this go somewhere?"

"Follow it and see."

The seam led under the fountain, down the street, and toward more fountains further along. "Pipes!" Nora said. "Water pipes, hiding under the road!"

"Right again," said Tess. "Pompeii had pipes running all through town, bringing water to fountains like this one. Anyone could come fill a jug — not just rich families."

Nora cupped her hands, pretending to splash her face. "Can I have a drink?"

"You could," said Tess, "except it's two thousand years old and made entirely of glow. Might taste a bit like static."

Nora laughed so hard she nearly tipped into the trough. "Fine. I'll wait till we get home."

She looked down the street at the next fountain, and the next, water glinting all the way to the edge of town. "Everybody got some," she said. "That's nice."

"It is," said Tess. "Come on — there's somewhere loud I want you to hear."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Big Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
A roar rolled down the street before Nora even saw where it came from. She jumped. Then she heard it again — cheering, not danger.

They turned a corner, and there it was: a huge oval building, built from pale stone, rising out of the ground like half a bowl.

"An **amphitheater**," said Tess. "A giant stone circle for watching shows."

Nora tipped her head back, counting rows of seats climbing up and up. "How many people fit in there?"

"Enough to make the whole town shake when they all cheered at once," said Tess. "This one was built around **70 BC** — one of the oldest of its kind ever found."

"What did they watch?"

"**Gladiators**," said Tess. "Fighters who performed here for crowds, kind of like today's big sports matches, only much, much older."

Nora climbed a few steps and spread her arms wide, pretending to be a cheering fan. "GO TEAM!" she shouted, and her voice bounced off the stone walls and came right back to her, twice as loud.

Tess laughed, a sound like tiny bells. "Careful. You'll wake up the whole town."

"They're already awake," Nora pointed out. "Everyone's outside, in every chapter."

"Fair point," said Tess. "Come on — there's a mountain I want you to meet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain That Grumbles
chapters.text:
Past the rooftops, a tall green mountain rose against the sky. It looked peaceful, almost sleepy.

The ground gave a tiny shiver under Nora's shoes. Just a little one.

Nora froze. "Did you feel that?"

"I did," said Tess calmly. "Don't worry — we're only visiting, remember. Nothing here can touch us."

Nora let out a breath. "Okay. What's the mountain called?"

"**Mount Vesuvius**," said Tess. "And here's something wild — it's still around today. Still a real, active volcano."

"Does anyone watch it?"

"All the time," said Tess. "Scientists called **volcanologists** study it closely, because so many people live near it now."

Nora knelt down and pressed her ear flat against the ground. "Maybe I can hear it thinking."

Tess giggled. "Scientists usually use special machines for that. But I like your way better."

"What's it thinking about?" Nora asked.

"That," said Tess, more quietly now, "we're about to find out."

The sky above the mountain had started to change color, from blue to a strange, heavy gray.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Letter Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The gray sky kept spreading, like spilled ink across a ceiling. Little flecks drifted down, soft as snow, but dark.

"On **August 24th, in the year 79**," said Tess, "Mount Vesuvius erupted. It sent ash and rock pouring out, and over time it covered the whole town — as deep as **thirteen to twenty feet**, like being tucked under a very thick blanket."

Nora watched the flecks land on her sleeve and brushed them off. "That's a lot of blanket."

"People who could leave, hurried off to safety," said Tess. "And far across the bay, a young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched it all happen. He didn't run. He got out his pen."

"He wrote about it? While it was happening?"

"Two whole letters," said Tess, "describing everything so carefully that scientists today still name this kind of eruption after him — a **Plinian eruption**."

Nora dug into her pocket and found a stub of pencil she always carried for sketching mosaic patterns. On the back of her hand she scribbled fast: *gray sky, soft ash, mountain smoking.*

"What are you doing?" asked Tess.

"The same thing he did," said Nora. "Writing down what I see."

Tess glowed a little brighter. "Pliny would have liked you."

The ash kept drifting, gentle and endless, settling over rooftops, over fountains, over the little bakery with its waiting loaf.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Town That Went to Sleep
chapters.text:
Everything went quiet. The ash, the street, the cheering — all of it faded to soft gray silence.

Then, out of nowhere, came the scrape of a shovel.

Nora blinked, and the scene had changed. Workers with tools were digging in dusty ground, far above where the street used to be.

"What's happening?" she asked.

"The town slept, hidden, for almost **1,700 years**," said Tess. "Until **1748**, when workers digging right here found old walls poking up out of the dirt."

Nora spotted a lumpy shape in the soil, just a little mound. "Is that a wall under there?"

One of the diggers knelt where she pointed and brushed the dirt away. A stone wall appeared, solid and real.

"Good eye," said Tess.

They moved through half-uncovered rooms. On one wall, bright painted pictures still showed, colors barely faded. "What are those?" Nora asked.

"**Frescoes**," said Tess. "Paintings made right onto the wet wall, so the colors sink in and stay. One famous set is called the Villa of the Mysteries — nobody's completely sure what the pictures mean."

Nora studied the shapes and shades. "They're kind of like my mosaics. Lots of little pieces making one big picture — just painted instead of pieced."

"People are still digging," said Tess. "Only about two-thirds of the town has been found so far. There are rooms down there nobody's seen yet."

"I want to be one of the people who finds them," said Nora. "Someone who digs up old things and figures out the story. Is there a word for that?"

"**Archaeologist**," said Tess. "And I think you'd be a good one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Mosaic
chapters.text:
Tess's glow dimmed, soft and sleepy. "One more thing before we go," she said.

A shimmer opened nearby, showing a smaller seaside town. "That's **Herculaneum**," said Tess. "Buried by the same eruption, but by something that kept even wooden furniture and old scrolls safe — things Pompeii's ash couldn't save."

"So each place kept different treasures," Nora said.

"Different, but both precious," said Tess. "Today, Pompeii is protected by a group called **UNESCO** — people who look after the world's most special places. Millions of visitors come every year, just to walk these streets."

Nora looked back at the quiet town, the stepping stones, the fountains, the painted walls. "It's not really asleep anymore, is it? Everyone keeps visiting. Everyone keeps finding things."

"Exactly," said Tess. "Ready for home?"

The glowing doorway opened again. Nora stepped through, and the stone street melted into carpet under her feet.

She was back in her bedroom, mosaic board in front of her, tiles scattered just as she'd left them. One tile sat glowing softly in the middle — shaped, she realized, like a tiny stepping stone.

Nora picked it up and set it gently into her design, right where it belonged.

"Goodnight, Tess," she whispered.

The little light blinked once, warm and sleepy, and went dark.

Nora climbed into bed, her notebook full of baker's stamps and painted patterns resting on the nightstand, ready for tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Keep placing your pieces well.

true_facts.text: Pompeii sat near the sea, close to where the city of **Naples** stands today.
The name Pompeii might come from an old word, ***pompe***, meaning **five** — maybe for five little villages that joined together.
Pompeii's streets had **raised stepping stones** so people could cross without wet feet, with gaps for cart wheels to pass through.
Back then, Pompeii was a busy town of about **eleven to fifteen thousand people**, full of shops, baths, theaters, and temples.
In one old oven, people found a whole **loaf of bread**, still shaped and stamped with the baker's own mark.
Pompeii had **pipes under the streets** carrying water to fountains all around town, for anyone to use.
The town's big stone **amphitheater**, built around **70 BC**, was one of the oldest ever found, used for gladiator shows.
**Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano today, and scientists called volcanologists watch it closely because so many people live near it.
On **August 24th, in the year 79**, Mount Vesuvius erupted and covered Pompeii in ash and rock.
A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched from across the bay and wrote it all down so carefully that this kind of eruption is still called a **Plinian eruption**.
The ash and rock piled up as deep as **thirteen to twenty feet** over the whole town.
Pompeii stayed hidden for almost **1,700 years** until workers found its old walls again in **1748**.
Nearby **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption, but it kept even wooden furniture and old scrolls safe.
Pompeii is now protected by a group called **UNESCO**, and millions of visitors walk its streets every year.
