story.title: Maya and the Great Space Race
story.subtitle: A beeping ball, a brave dog, and one giant leap.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beeping Ball (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya sat on her bedroom floor, drawing a little sailboat with a red stripe. It had been one whole week since the bridge that hummed had finished humming, and Barnacle had waved goodbye with one flipper.

Tonight her fish tank was bubbling faster than usual. Beep. Beep. Beep.

SPLOOSH! A whiskery nose popped out of the water. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, shaking water off his fur.

"Barnacle!" Maya grinned. "What's that beeping?"

"That," said Barnacle, "is the sound of history. Climb on, and I'll show you."

The water glowed like starlight, and the fish tank stretched open like a window to the sky. Maya climbed through, and up they floated, past clouds, past the Moon, until stars sparkled all around them.

A little silver ball zoomed past, beeping as it went.

"What is THAT?" Maya asked.

"That's Sputnik 1," said Barnacle. "On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched it into space. It's a satellite — a shiny ball that circles round and round the Earth, like your bathtub boat going round the drain, except much, much faster. We call that circling orbit."

"How big is it?"

"About 58 centimeters wide," said Barnacle. "Smaller than you! And everyone on Earth could hear that beep on their very own radios."

Maya listened. Beep. Beep. Beep. "It sounds like it's saying hello."

"Good guess," said Barnacle. "Follow the beep. It'll take us to where the race really begins."

Maya pointed toward the sound, and Barnacle paddled hard through the stars after it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Ride (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
A bark echoed through the stars.

Maya's ears perked up. "Was that a dog?"

"Good ears," said Barnacle. "Follow it."

They paddled toward a round silver capsule — a little space pod — with a window near the top. Behind the glass sat a furry face.

"Her name is Laika," said Barnacle. "On November 3, 1957, she became the first living creature ever to circle the Earth, right up here in space."

Maya pressed a hand to the glass. "Hi, Laika. You're so brave."

"She was," said Barnacle softly. "People all over the world cheered for her."

Maya opened her sketchbook and quickly drew a dog in a tiny space helmet, so she would always remember.

"The Americans were amazed too," Barnacle went on. "They were so surprised by Sputnik that they built a brand-new team just for space. It started working on October 1, 1958. They called it NASA."

"NASA," Maya repeated, trying it out. "Like a nickname?"

"Sort of," laughed Barnacle. "It stands for a much longer name, but NASA is easier to shout."

"NASA!" Maya shouted, and her voice echoed off the stars, bouncing all the way to the Moon and back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The First Flier (1961)
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! A rocket zoomed by, so fast it rattled Maya's teeth.

"Who was flying that?" she asked, eyes wide.

"A very brave pilot," said Barnacle. "On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human ever to go to space. He's what the Soviets called a cosmonaut — a space traveler. He went all the way around the Earth once, in about 108 minutes, faster than it takes to watch two movies."

Maya tried to picture zooming around the whole planet that fast. "Did he smile the whole time?"

"The whole time," said Barnacle. "That's exactly how people remember him — the cosmonaut who smiled his way into history."

A smaller capsule bobbed nearby with letters painted on the side.

"And him?" Maya pointed.

"That's Alan Shepard," said Barnacle. "On May 5, 1961, he became the first American in space. His trip was short and didn't go all the way around the Earth, but it was still a huge first for his country."

Maya studied both capsules carefully. "So Gagarin went in a big circle, and Shepard just went up and came straight back down?"

"Exactly right," said Barnacle, impressed. "You've got the whole race figured out already."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Promise and a Pilot (1961–1963)
chapters.text:
A deep voice boomed across the sky, loud enough to make the stars shiver.

"Listen," said Barnacle.

"We choose to go to the Moon," said the voice.

"Who's that?" Maya asked.

"President John F. Kennedy," said Barnacle. "On May 25, 1961, he dared his whole country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely, before ten more years had passed."

Maya looked up at the round, silvery Moon glowing above them. She grabbed her sketchbook and drew a little rocket flying straight toward it. "I want to go there too."

"Patience," chuckled Barnacle. "First, someone else makes history."

A small capsule zipped past, with a woman waving from inside.

"That's Valentina Tereshkova," said Barnacle. "On June 16, 1963, she became the first woman in space. She used to work in a factory, and then she circled the Earth again and again, up here among the stars."

Maya waved back hard. "Hi, Valentina!"

Tereshkova waved once more before zooming off into the dark.

"Which way now?" Maya asked, tracing a line in the air with her finger, from Earth all the way to the Moon.

"That way," said Barnacle, following exactly where she pointed. "Good eye."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Floating Walk (1965)
chapters.text:
Something strange floated outside a capsule window — a person, tumbling gently in the dark, tied on with a long cord.

"Is he lost?" Maya gasped, grabbing Barnacle's flipper.

"Not at all," said Barnacle. "That's Alexei Leonov. On March 18, 1965, he became the first person ever to step outside his spacecraft and float freely in space. We call that a spacewalk."

"A spacewalk," Maya repeated slowly, watching him drift. "How long did he stay out there?"

"About ten minutes," said Barnacle. "Just enough time to look around at the whole Earth beneath him."

Maya noticed the cord stretching from his suit back to the capsule door. "That rope keeps him safe, right? Like my swim float keeps me close to the dock?"

"Just like that," said Barnacle, nodding. "Good thinking."

Leonov gave a little wave before pulling himself back inside, safe and sound.

"He did it!" Maya cheered, clapping both hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Earthrise (1968)
chapters.text:
Everything went quiet and dark, as if someone had switched off all the stars.

"Where are we?" Maya whispered.

"Behind the Moon," said Barnacle. "Hang on."

Then, over the gray edge of the Moon, a bright blue-and-white ball rose slowly into view.

Maya gasped. "Is that... Earth?"

"It sure is," said Barnacle. "In December 1968, three astronauts flew all the way around the Moon, the first people ever to do it. One of them, William Anders, looked out his window and saw exactly what you're seeing now."

"It's so small," Maya said, quickly drawing the round blue ball in her sketchbook, with swirly white clouds across it.

"He took a photo of it," said Barnacle. "People called it Earthrise. It reminded everyone how small and precious our whole planet really is."

Maya held her drawing up next to the real thing. "Mine's pretty good too."

"The best Earthrise I've ever seen," said Barnacle, and he meant every word.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
The stardust beneath them shook with the loudest sound yet.

"Look!" Maya pointed at an enormous rocket, taller than anything she'd ever seen.

"That's the Saturn V," said Barnacle. "It stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya tipped her head all the way back to see the top. "Who built something that big?"

"A rocket builder named Wernher von Braun led the American team," said Barnacle. "And on the other side, a Soviet designer named Sergei Korolev built incredible rockets too, though nobody even knew his name until after he died in 1966. It was kept a secret the whole time."

"A secret genius," Maya said, eyes wide.

The rocket roared up and away. Barnacle and Maya followed it all the way to the Moon, where a little ladder unfolded from a spindly-legged lander.

A boot stepped down onto the gray dust.

"On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon," said Barnacle. "He called it a giant leap for mankind."

"Giant leap," Maya whispered, watching his footprint stay perfectly still in the dust, with no wind to blow it away.

"Buzz Aldrin joined him down there," Barnacle added. "And their friend Michael Collins orbited all alone above them, in a capsule called Columbia, waiting to bring everyone home."

Maya waved up at the lonely capsule circling overhead. "You're not alone up there, Michael. We see you too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Coming Home (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
BANG! A sound cracked through the quiet, and Maya jumped.

"What was that?" she asked, grabbing Barnacle's flipper tight.

"In 1970, an oxygen tank broke apart on a ship called Apollo 13, on its way to the Moon," said Barnacle gently. "It gave the crew a scare. But down on Earth, clever helpers worked day and night to figure out a fix, and all three astronauts made it safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "They were okay?"

"Perfectly okay," said Barnacle. "Home safe, every single one."

Between 1969 and 1972, Barnacle told her, twelve astronauts in all got to walk on the Moon, across six separate trips.

"Twelve!" Maya counted on her fingers, ran out, and giggled.

Then the stars around them softened into gold. Two spacecraft, one marked USA and one marked USSR, floated toward each other.

"On July 17, 1975, those two crews met up in space and shook hands," said Barnacle. "After years of racing each other, that handshake ended the Space Race, in friendship."

Maya watched the astronauts clasp hands through the open hatch. "That's the best ending."

"All races should end that way," said Barnacle, smiling.

Then the stars melted into her night light's soft glow, and Maya was back on her bedroom floor, sketchbook open to a brand-new page: Earth, the Moon, a handshake, and one little seal waving from the corner.

SPLOOSH went her fish tank, one last time, as Barnacle slipped back beneath the water.

"Goodnight, Barnacle," Maya whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreamland — SPLOOSH!

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** was launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**, the first satellite ever to circle the Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about **58 centimeters wide** and sent out a beep people could hear on ordinary radios.
**Laika** the dog became the first living creature to circle the Earth, on **November 3, 1957**.
The United States started a brand-new space team called **NASA** on **October 1, 1958**.
**Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space on **April 12, 1961**, circling the Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
**Alan Shepard** became the first American in space on **May 5, 1961**, though his flight did not go all the way around the Earth.
President **John F. Kennedy** challenged the country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely, on **May 25, 1961**.
**Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space on **June 16, 1963**.
**Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk on **March 18, 1965**, floating outside his capsule for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, astronauts flying around the Moon took the famous **Earthrise** photo of our whole planet.
**Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon on **July 20, 1969**, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank broke apart on **Apollo 13**, but the whole crew made it safely home.
The **Saturn V** rocket stood **363 feet tall**, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft met in orbit and the crews **shook hands**, ending the Space Race in friendship.

story.title: Zara and the Rock That Remembered Fire
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip around the world's hottest mountains

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Rock
chapters.text:
Zara sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, sorting her rock collection into jars. Rain tapped the window. She picked up a lumpy black rock from the bottom of her bucket, the one she always forgot to label. Tonight it felt warm in her hand. Warmer than it should.

She pressed her thumb to its shiny black skin, and it began to hum, soft and low, like a kettle about to whistle.

"Um," said Zara. "Rocks don't do that."

The black rock cracked open a tiny glowing line, like a yawn, and a voice came out, crackly and warm as a campfire.

"Name's Obby," it said. "Short for obsidian, that's me, cooled-down fire rock. Want to see where I came from?"

"You're a volcano rock?" Zara's mouth fell open.

"Bits of me," said Obby. "Hop on. I know a shortcut."

The glow opened wide enough for a six-year-old in pajamas, and Zara tumbled through, WHOOSH, into hot orange light. She landed on warm ground that smelled like matches. Mountains all around her puffed little clouds of smoke into the sky.

"Where ARE we?" Zara asked, spinning in a circle.

"Somewhere a volcano is always waking up," said Obby. "A volcano is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape from way underground. Down below, that melted rock is called magma, say it with me, MAG-ma. Once it pours out on top, it gets a new name: lava."

Zara pointed at a thin red line creeping down a far-off slope. "Is THAT lava?"

"Bingo," said Obby. "You're a natural."

She counted the smoking mountains on her fingers, one, two, three, all the way around in a big curved line, like a necklace.

"They're everywhere! Why are they lined up like that?"

"Because most volcanoes sit along the edges of giant puzzle pieces under the ground," said Obby. "We call them plates. Where they push, pull, or slide past each other, volcanoes pop up. This whole curvy line around the ocean has so many, people call it the Ring of Fire. About three out of every four of the world's awake volcanoes live right here."

"I found the ring!" Zara grinned.

"You did," said Obby. "Guess which country has more awake volcanoes than any other place on Earth?"

Zara squinted at the biggest cluster of smoking peaks and pointed. "That one?"

"Close enough, that's Indonesia," said Obby, "and it's time we went to say hello."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Fire Island
chapters.text:
Obby's glow melted the smoking ring into blue ocean and green hills: Hawaii.

Zara felt the ground rumble, gentle, like a cat purring. "Why's it shaking like that?" she asked, bouncing on her toes.

"That's Kilauea," said Obby. "One of the busiest volcanoes on Earth. It's been letting out lava almost nonstop for years and years."

Zara noticed the volcano wasn't a tall pointy mountain like she'd drawn in her notebook. It was wide and gently sloped, like a shield lying on the ground.

"That's shaped weird," she said. "It's all flat and wide, not pointy."

"Good eye," said Obby. "That's a shield volcano, wide with gentle slopes, because its lava is thin and runny and spreads out flat, like syrup on a pancake. Pointy ones, like Japan's Mount Fuji, are stratovolcanoes, their lava is thicker, so it piles up steep."

"But WHY is there a volcano way out here," Zara said, looking at the ocean all around them, "if it's not even on the edge of anything?"

Obby's glow flickered, impressed. "Smartest question yet. Most volcanoes sit at the edges of those puzzle-piece plates. But Hawaii sits over a hotspot, a place deep, deep down where hot rock keeps rising, melting a hole through the plate above it, no matter where that plate drifts."

Zara crouched by a cooling river of orange lava, close enough to feel its heat on her cheeks, far enough to be safe.

"It's like a candle under a birthday cake," she said, "melting through no matter which way you turn the cake."

"...Yeah," said Obby slowly. "That's actually a really good way to put it."

Zara beamed and did a little victory spin. "I'm basically a volcano scientist now."

"Careful," laughed Obby, "or I'll have to start paying you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Biggest One of All
chapters.text:
Obby lifted them both into the sky over Hawaii, not too high, just enough to see the whole island like a map.

"Whoa," said Zara, looking down at a huge mountain taking up almost the whole view. "Is that the BIGGEST volcano I've seen tonight?"

"It's the biggest active volcano on the whole planet," said Obby. "Its name is Mauna Loa. Even just counting from sea level up, it rises over four thousand meters into the sky. That's taller than ten Eiffel Towers stacked up."

Zara tipped her head back, pretending to look all the way to the top. "It doesn't even look that pointy for being so huge."

"Another shield volcano," said Obby. "Remember the pancake syrup? Mauna Loa just kept spreading, eruption after eruption, for a long, long time, until it became the biggest one there is."

Zara reached into her pajama pocket and pulled out her little rock-collecting notebook, she'd brought it without even noticing.

"I'm going to draw it," she announced, "bigger than the page."

She scribbled a huge wide mountain that ran off all four edges of the paper.

"That," said Obby, "is exactly how big it feels from down here."

Zara tucked the notebook away carefully. "Rock collectors need notebooks," she said. "For CLUES."

"Speaking of clues," said Obby, "how about we go find a volcano that left a really big clue, a long, long time ago, written down by someone who actually watched it happen?"

Zara's eyes went wide. "Someone wrote down a volcano?"

"Grab my glow," said Obby, "and let's go meet him."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Letter From Pliny
chapters.text:
The glow faded in on a hillside above a blue bay, a bright day gone strange and gray, with little flecks drifting down like snow.

Zara held out her hand and caught one. It was soft and gray, and nothing like snow at all.

"Ash," said Obby. "Floating down from a mountain called Vesuvius, across the water. It's erupting right now, way back in the year seventy-nine."

Zara looked at a man on the hillside nearby, scribbling fast with a feather pen, watching the mountain without ever looking down at his page.

"Who's that?" she whispered.

"That's Pliny the Younger," said Obby. "He's watching from clear across the bay, safe and sound, and writing down everything he sees. Because he wrote it all down so carefully, scientists today still use his name for this kind of big, explosive eruption. They call it a Plinian eruption."

"After HIM?" said Zara. "Just because he wrote a good letter?"

"Just because he wrote a good letter," said Obby.

Down below, thick ash was quietly covering two whole towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum, under a soft gray blanket, burying streets and walls until, hundreds of years later, people would dig them up again and find them perfectly kept, like a secret saved in a jar.

Zara thought about her own rock jars at home, each one labeled and safe.

"It's like the ash was... tucking them in," she said.

"Huh," said Obby. "Never thought of it that way. But yeah."

Zara glanced back at Pliny, still scribbling. "Somebody should tell him he's basically a rock collector too. Just writing instead of jars."

Obby's glow flickered like a laugh. "Let's leave him to it. There's a much louder volcano I want you to hear."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Bang Ever
chapters.text:
Before Zara could even ask where they were going, BOOM.

It was the loudest sound she had ever not quite heard, more like a thump in her chest than a noise in her ears. She slapped her hands over them anyway.

"That's Krakatoa," said Obby gently, "a volcano on an island in Indonesia. Don't worry, we're listening from somewhere nice and far away."

"How far away even IS far away?" asked Zara, peeking out from behind her hands.

"Picture this," said Obby. "In 1883, this volcano erupted so loud that people heard the bang about three thousand miles from here, on an island called Rodrigues. That's like you shouting in your backyard and someone hearing you all the way on the other side of the whole country."

Zara's jaw dropped. "That's not possible. Shouting doesn't go that far."

"Normal shouting, no," said Obby. "But this was probably the loudest sound in all of history."

Zara cupped her hands around her mouth and yelled as loud as she could, just to compare. Her voice barely rippled the warm air.

"Nowhere close," she admitted, giggling.

"Nowhere close," Obby agreed. "Not even a little bit."

Zara picked up a small dark pebble from the ground nearby, turning it in her fingers. "Can I keep this one? For the jar with no label?"

"Looks like it already found its label," said Obby. "Loudest Bang Pebble. Has a nice ring to it."

Zara tucked it into her pajama pocket with a happy little pat, like she was tucking in a tiny friend.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Summer That Didn't Come
chapters.text:
The light shifted again, and suddenly Zara was standing somewhere chilly, pulling her arms tight across her pajamas.

"Why's it so cold?" she said. "Aren't volcanoes supposed to be HOT?"

"This one made things cold," said Obby, "all the way on the other side of the world. In 1815, a volcano called Tambora, also in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption anyone's ever recorded. It threw so much ash and dust up into the sky that it blocked some of the sun's warmth, everywhere on Earth."

Zara frowned at a patch of snow on the ground, even though her notebook said it should be summer. "Snow... in summer?"

"Exactly," said Obby. "The next year, 1816, people in Europe and America called it the Year Without a Summer. Crops had trouble growing in the cold. People even saw snow in months that should have been warm."

Zara hugged herself. "One volcano did THAT? To the WHOLE WORLD?"

"One really, really big one," said Obby. "Tambora's still the biggest eruption anybody's ever written down."

Zara thought hard, chewing her lip the way she did over a tricky puzzle. "So a volcano way over here can mess with weather way over there, even somewhere totally different?"

"That's the big idea," said Obby. "Volcanoes don't just change their own backyard. The really big ones can change the whole sky."

Zara shivered, then grinned anyway. "I'm gonna tell my teacher a volcano made it snow in summer once, and she is NOT going to believe me."

"Bring the notebook," said Obby. "Proof helps."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The ground gave a long, deep groan, like somebody waking up grumpy.

"Stand back with me," said Obby, and the two of them watched from a safe hillside, far across a wide valley.

"This mountain is called Mount St. Helens," said Obby, "in the United States. On May 18th, 1980, something enormous happened right here. First, a huge chunk of the mountain's side slid away all at once, the biggest landslide anyone's ever recorded."

Zara's eyes went huge. "The whole SIDE of a mountain just... slid off?"

"The whole side," said Obby. "And the second that happened, the volcano erupted right behind it, blowing about thirteen hundred feet clean off the top of the mountain."

Zara tried to picture it and couldn't. "That's like... taller than my whole street, stacked up."

"Close to it," said Obby.

She noticed a small group of people far off, with notebooks and strange humming machines, watching the mountain from a safe distance, just like them.

"Who are THEY?" Zara asked.

"Scientists," said Obby. "People like David Johnston. He studied this volcano closely, because watching it carefully helps everyone understand when a volcano is getting ready to wake up, and that helps keep people safe."

Zara watched the scientists scribbling notes, just like she scribbled in her own notebook.

"We're basically the same," she said, delighted. "Just with rocks instead of machines."

"Rock collectors and volcano scientists," said Obby, "closer cousins than you'd think."

Zara saluted the distant scientists like fellow rock-club members. "Keep watching," she whispered. "I've got your back."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
The glow dropped them somewhere colder and windier, with gray waves crashing far below a cliff.

"Watch the water," said Obby, pointing out to sea.

Zara watched, then gasped, a plume of steam and ash burst straight up out of the OCEAN itself, like a kettle boiling from underneath the waves.

"There's a volcano IN the water?" she said.

"Under it," said Obby. "In 1963, right near Iceland, a volcano kept erupting underwater until it finally built up high enough to poke out above the waves. People watched a brand new island grow, bit by bit, right in front of them. They named it Surtsey."

"A volcano made an ISLAND? From nothing?"

"From nothing," said Obby. "And Iceland has tons of volcanoes, way more than most places this size, because of where it sits. Remember those puzzle-piece plates?"

Zara nodded hard.

"Iceland sits right on a crack where two of them are pulling apart," said Obby, "slow as your fingernails grow. And wherever they pull apart, melted rock can rise up and escape."

Zara held her two hands together, then slowly pulled them apart, picturing the crack opening underneath the whole island.

"So Iceland's basically getting a little bit bigger every single day," she said, "just really, really slowly."

"Most people don't even notice," said Obby, "but you just did."

Zara watched the new island steaming out in the waves, little and stubborn and brand new. "I want to visit it when it's all grown up," she said.

"Deal," said Obby. "I know a shortcut."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Quiet Giant
chapters.text:
Next, the glow opened onto wide golden grass, steam curling up from little pools in the ground.

"This whole place sits on top of an enormous volcano," said Obby. "People call it a supervolcano. It's called Yellowstone."

Zara froze mid-step. "Is it gonna erupt RIGHT NOW?"

"Nope," said Obby quickly. "Its last really huge eruption was about six hundred and forty thousand years ago, and right now scientists see no sign at all that it's getting ready to do that again. You can relax your shoulders."

Zara let out a breath and relaxed her shoulders, on purpose, like Obby said.

"But HOW do scientists even know?" she asked. "Can they see inside the ground?"

"Sort of," said Obby. "They use machines that feel tiny earthquakes too small for us to notice, like a doctor's stethoscope, but for listening to the Earth's grumbling. And they use satellites way up in space to check if the ground is slowly swelling, like bread rising in an oven. Both are signs a volcano might be waking up."

Zara pressed her ear to the warm ground, listening hard. "I don't hear anything," she reported.

"Me neither," said Obby. "Which is good news."

Zara noticed the grass nearby was thick and green and taller than anywhere else she'd seen all night. "Why's it so GREEN here?"

"Old volcano ash breaks down into really good dirt for growing things," said Obby, "soft and rich and full of good stuff for plants. That's why farmers all over the world choose to live near volcanoes, even knowing the risk, the ground grows the best crops around."

Zara pulled a long blade of grass and tucked it behind her ear like a tiny green ribbon. "Volcanoes build AND grow things," she said. "That's kind of amazing."

"Kind of," Obby agreed, "is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more thing before we go," said Obby, glow brightening one last time. "The biggest volcano anybody's ever found isn't even on Earth."

Zara blinked. "Where is it THEN?"

"Mars," said Obby. "It's called Olympus Mons, and it's about thirteen and a half miles high, almost three whole Mount Everests stacked on top of each other."

Zara tried to imagine three Mount Everests and gave up, laughing. "That's not even a real number anymore."

"Pretty real up there," said Obby, "but I think it's past somebody's bedtime down here."

The glowing crack opened one more time, warm and soft, and Zara tumbled gently back through, not a WHOOSH this time, more like sinking into a pillow.

She landed right back on her bedroom carpet, rock jars all around her, rain still tapping the window like nothing had happened at all.

Obby sat quiet and black and ordinary-looking in her palm, just a cooled little rock again.

Zara reached into her pajama pocket and pulled out the small dark pebble from Krakatoa, still there, still real. She popped it into an empty jar and wrote on a sticky label in her best careful letters: LOUDEST BANG PEBBLE. PROVEN TRUE.

She lined the jar up next to Obby on her shelf, two rock friends side by side.

"Goodnight, volcanoes," she whispered. "Goodnight, Ring of Fire. Goodnight, Obby."

Obby gave one last small, warm flicker, like a wink. "Sleep tight, little rockhound. Same time tomorrow?"

Zara grinned into her pillow. "Same time tomorrow."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Sleep tight, little rockhound.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape.
Underground that melted rock is called **magma**; once it flows out, it is called **lava**.
The curvy line of volcanoes around the ocean is called the **Ring of Fire**, home to about three out of every four of the world's awake volcanoes.
Hawaii's volcanoes grew over a **hotspot**, a place deep underground where hot rock keeps rising no matter which way the ground above it drifts.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been letting out lava almost nonstop for years and years.
Wide, gently-sloped volcanoes like Hawaii's are called **shield volcanoes**; tall pointy ones like Mount Fuji are called **stratovolcanoes**.
**Mauna Loa** in Hawaii is the biggest active volcano on Earth, rising over **four thousand meters** above the sea.
**Pliny the Younger** watched Vesuvius erupt from across the bay and wrote it all down, so big explosive eruptions are now called **Plinian eruptions**.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption was so loud it was heard about **three thousand miles away**.
**Mount Tambora's** 1815 eruption was the biggest ever recorded, and it helped make 1816 the **Year Without a Summer**.
**Mount St. Helens** erupted on **May 18th, 1980**, right after the biggest landslide ever recorded slid off its side.
In **1963**, a brand new island named **Surtsey** rose out of the sea near Iceland from an underwater volcano.
**Yellowstone** sits on a huge supervolcano, but its last giant eruption was about **six hundred and forty thousand years ago**, with no sign of another coming soon.

new_recurring.name: Obby
new_recurring.rule: A small chunk of black obsidian in Zara's rock collection. It warms up and hums, then opens a glowing crack to start each adventure. Speaks in a crackly, warm, campfire-like voice, is encouraging and a little wry, and always says 'Same…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returns to her bedroom carpet with a small dark pebble from Krakatoa, labels it 'LOUDEST BANG PEBBLE, PROVEN TRUE,' and sets it on her shelf beside the now-quiet rock Obby.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. A long story on a topic the children know better than the writer - accuracy and no brand worship.
scenarios.best_moment: His pixel art creeper was still there — but now, next to it, sat one new tiny pixel block, glowing faintly green.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Game on," said Byte. "Things are about to get a lot more games."
editor_notes: Fix the two factual errors. Credit Pong to engineer Allan Alcorn (at Bushnell and Dabney's new Atari), and soften the 2600 line to something true, such as "the 2600 made swapping cartridges a huge hit." Move Space Invaders to its 1978 arcade setting so it isn't anachronistic on a 1977 console.

Give the journey a shape instead of a carousel. Let Ben carry something from stop to stop, such as a pixel he collects at each era for the final block, or a question he finally answers in the Minecraft scene. Split or trim the crowded double-stops in Chapters 7 and 8. Use the spare words to bring the story up to the 2,400 target.

Raise the read-aloud polish. Vary Ben's reactions and cut the repeated "basically" lines. Rewrite "Things are about to get a lot more games" and "jumped the controller's button." Fold the stray bolded shout-lines into the scenes, and add some actual wordplay for band B, which the "funny" tone was asking for.

story.title: Ben and the Glowing Pixel Block
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through sixty years of video games, one block at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Blip That Started It All (1958–1962)
chapters.text:
Ben was supposed to be asleep.

Instead, he was finishing a pixel art creeper on his tablet, one green square at a time. The room was dark except for the screen's glow.

Then the glow changed. It flickered green and black, like static on an old TV. A single white dot bounced across the screen, back and forth, back and forth.

"Um," Ben whispered. "That's not my creeper."

The dot stretched into a glowing block, and the block popped open like a chest in Minecraft. Out stepped a tiny pixel person made of light.

"Game on!" said the pixel person. "I'm Byte. Want to see where games began?"

Ben blinked. "Games have a beginning?"

"Everything does," said Byte. "Grab my hand."

The room melted into green light, and Ben landed in a buzzing laboratory full of wires and humming machines.

A man in a white coat was staring at a round screen that drew wobbly lines — an **oscilloscope**, a machine that turns electricity into pictures.

"That's **William Higinbotham**," said Byte. "In **1958**, he used it to make a little bouncing-ball game called 'Tennis for Two.'"

Ben watched the dot bounce over a line, back and forth, like a tiny invisible net.

"Can I try?" Ben asked.

Higinbotham handed him a box with one knob. Ben twisted it hard. The ball zoomed sideways and bounced off at a crazy angle. Higinbotham laughed so hard his glasses slipped.

"Careful, champ," he said. "That's the whole game, right there in your hand."

Byte grinned. "One blip. That's where it all started."

The green light swirled again, faster this time, and the lab turned into something even bigger — a room-sized computer blinking with lights.

"In **1962**," said Byte, "a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends used a giant computer called a **PDP-1** to make 'Spacewar!' — two tiny spaceships shooting at each other."

Ben's jaw dropped. "The whole computer is the size of my living room!"

"Computers used to be huge," said Byte. "Now one fits in your pocket."

Ben reached for the controls and nudged his spaceship. It spun in a slow circle and dodged a shot. Steve Russell whooped.

"Nice flying!"

"Game on," Byte said again, tugging Ben's sleeve. "There's more. Way more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Brown Box on the TV (1972)
chapters.text:
The green light dropped Ben into a living room with a big boxy TV and a tangle of wires everywhere.

A man with glasses was crouched behind the TV, holding two wires that wouldn't quite reach each other.

"Need a hand?" Ben asked.

"Always," said the man. "I'm **Ralph Baer**. Folks later called me the father of video games — I just wanted to play something on my own TV."

Ben held the wires steady while Baer twisted them together. CLICK. The screen flickered, then showed two little white squares and a dot.

"That's my **Brown Box**," said Baer, grinning. "A game you can play at home, not just in some lab."

Byte floated closer. "In **1972**, Baer's box became a real toy you could buy — the **Magnavox Odyssey**. The first home video game console. A console is a box that plugs into your TV so you can play games right there."

Ben moved one of the little squares with a dial. It bumped the dot and sent it flying across the screen.

"That's basically Pong," Ben said.

"Actually," said Baer, "Pong came after mine. Everybody copies the home team."

Ben laughed. "You're like the first player one."

Baer tapped Ben's shoulder like they were teammates. "Keep that dial steady, home team."

The TV screen glowed brighter, and the living room folded away into noise — bells, buzzers, and the clatter of coins.

"Sounds like an arcade," Ben said.

"Good ear," said Byte. "Game on — next stop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Pong and the Quarter Jam (1972)
chapters.text:
Ben landed in a buzzing arcade, lights flashing, a crowd gathered around one machine.

"PONG!" said a sign in blocky letters.

"This one's by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**," said Byte. "They started a company called **Atari**, also in **1972**. Pong was the first big hit you could play on a machine in a store."

Ben watched two paddles bat a square ball back and forth. BLOOP. BLOOP.

A worker opened the coin box at the bottom, and quarters spilled onto the floor.

"Whoa! It's overflowing!" Ben said.

"There's a story," said Byte, "that one Pong machine got so many quarters, it actually jammed shut and stopped working. That part might be a bit stretched — but it shows how wild people went for this game."

Ben grabbed an empty popcorn bucket from a nearby table. "Use this! Dump the extra quarters in here!"

The worker blinked, then laughed and did exactly that. The crowd cheered as the machine clicked back on.

"Nice fix," said Bushnell, tipping an imaginary hat.

Ben bounced on his toes. "I saved Pong!"

"You kept the line moving," Byte said. "Close enough."

The lights of the arcade spun into a blur of colors, like a hundred screens turning on at once.

"Game on," said Byte. "Things are about to get a lot more games."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Box, Many Games (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
They landed in a living room that looked like a toy store had exploded — boxes everywhere, all shaped like thick little books.

"This is the **Atari 2600**," said Byte. "It came out in **1977**. Before this, a game machine could only play the one game built inside it."

Ben picked up a plastic case. "What's this?"

"A **cartridge**," said Byte. "Like a little data brick. You slide it into the machine, and it loads a whole new game — kind of like swapping Minecraft worlds."

Ben slid the cartridge into the slot. The TV blinked, then filled with rows of blocky aliens marching side to side.

"**Space Invaders**," said Byte. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It kicked off a giant arcade craze — everybody wanted to play it."

Ben grabbed the controller and blasted a row of aliens. PEW PEW PEW!

The aliens marched faster every time he cleared a row.

"They speed up!" Ben said. "That's actually kind of mean."

"That's the whole trick," said Byte. "The faster they get, the faster your heart beats."

Ben swapped the cartridge for another one, grinning. "One box, a hundred worlds."

"Now you're getting it," said Byte. "Game on — next cartridge, next year."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Pizza with One Slice Gone (1980)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like pizza.

Ben's stomach growled. "Are we stopping for dinner?"

"Not quite," said Byte, pointing at a table where a designer sat staring at a round pizza missing one slice.

"That's **Toru Iwatani**," said Byte. "In **1980**, he made a game called **Pac-Man** for a company named **Namco**. People say he got the idea for Pac-Man's round shape from a pizza with a slice taken out — though nobody's totally sure that's exactly how it happened."

Ben looked at the pizza, then at the yellow circle glowing on Iwatani's screen. "It's the same shape! Round, with a mouth-shaped bite!"

Iwatani smiled. "Close enough for a hungry kid."

Ben reached over and spun the joystick. The yellow circle zipped through a maze, gobbling little dots. Four colorful ghosts chased behind.

"They're catching up!" Ben said.

He yanked the stick toward a big flashing dot in the corner. Pac-Man gulped it down, and suddenly the ghosts turned blue and fled.

"WHOA! I SCARED THEM!" Ben shouted.

"Power pellet," said Byte. "Turns the tables for a few seconds."

Ben chased the ghosts around the maze, laughing the whole time.

"Nicely played," said Iwatani.

Byte tugged Ben's arm. "Game on. Next stop isn't quite so tasty."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Too Many Bad Games (1983)
chapters.text:
The green light dropped Ben in a messy store, shelves packed with game boxes nobody wanted.

"What happened here?" Ben asked, picking up a dusty cartridge.

"In **1983**," said Byte, "so many rushed, not-very-good games came out that people stopped trusting them. Sales dropped a lot. People call it the video game crash — not cars crashing, just a big business slowdown."

Ben turned the cartridge over. "This one looks kind of terrible."

"A lot of them were," said Byte. "Companies tried to make too many games too fast."

"So what happened to all the extra ones?"

Byte's eyes lit up. "Funny you ask. There's a story that a company dumped a bunch of unsold cartridges — including a game based on a movie called E.T. — into a giant trash pile called a **landfill**, out in New Mexico."

"A game... graveyard?" Ben grinned.

"People weren't totally sure it was true," said Byte, "until diggers actually found the cartridges buried there, in **2014**."

Ben pretended to dig with an invisible shovel. "Found one! It's... dusty."

Byte laughed. "That's the spirit."

The shelves of bad games shimmered and faded, replaced by a cozy desk with a single glowing screen covered in falling colorful blocks.

"After a mess," said Byte, "somebody always builds something better."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
Ben stared at the screen full of blocks drifting downward.

"These look like Minecraft blocks that forgot how to stand still," he said.

"This is **Tetris**," said Byte. "Made in **1984** by a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov**, at a computer center in **Moscow**. You spin the shapes so they lock together in neat rows."

Ben grabbed the controls. A long block drifted down. He spun it sideways and slid it into a gap.

The row filled completely and vanished with a FWOOMP.

"CLEAR!" Ben yelled.

"Nice fit," said Byte.

The screen dissolved into a cardboard box with a red mushroom on it.

"This is the **NES**," said Byte, "Nintendo's new home console. It came out in **1985** and brought the market back to life after the crash, with a new hero riding along."

Ben pulled out the cartridge inside. The TV lit up with a mustached man in overalls, running across green hills.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," said Byte, "designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto** in **1985**. Mario became the most famous character in video games."

Ben jumped the controller's button, and Mario hopped onto a floating block.

"He's basically bouncing on pixels," Ben said.

"Pretty much your whole hobby, summed up," said Byte.

Ben grinned and guided Mario over a gap, landing clean. "Got it."

"Game on," said Byte. "One more rival is waiting just ahead."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Fast Blue Rival (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
A streak of blue blurred past Ben so fast it left a trail of light.

"Whoa, who's that?!" Ben said.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," said Byte. "Sega made him in **1991** to race against Mario — Sega wanted their own hero, and they wanted him fast."

Ben grabbed the controls, and Sonic curled into a ball, rolling downhill in a blur. ZOOOOM!

"He's basically a speedrun on legs," Ben said.

"That was the whole point," said Byte.

The blur of blue faded into a sleek black box with a shiny silver disc.

"This is a **PlayStation**," said Byte. "Sony made it in **1994**. Instead of cartridges, it used CDs — round discs that could hold way more pictures and sound."

Ben turned the disc over, watching it flash rainbow colors. "It's shiny."

"Shiny meant fuller worlds," said Byte. "More colors, longer music, bigger games."

Ben slid the disc in, and the TV filled with a detailed, swooping world.

"This looks so much more real," Ben said.

"Every few years," said Byte, "somebody figures out how to fit a bigger world onto a smaller disc."

Ben spun in a little circle, mimicking Sonic's rolling spin. "Game on, right?"

Byte laughed. "Now you're saying it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Block (2006–Today)
chapters.text:
The next room had Ben waving his arms in the air, holding nothing.

"Why am I waving at the TV?" he asked.

"Try it with this," said Byte, handing him a white remote. "This is a **Wii**, from Nintendo, in **2006**. Instead of just pressing buttons, you move the controller, and the game copies your motion."

Ben swung the remote like a tennis racket, and on screen, a tiny character swung back.

"That's so cool, it's like I'm actually playing!"

"Lots of people who'd never tried games before picked up a Wii," said Byte, "because it felt like real movement, not just button-mashing."

The white remote melted into something Ben knew by heart — a single green cube, textured like grass and dirt.

"Wait," Ben said, laughing. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," said Byte, "made by a developer named **Markus 'Notch' Persson**, in **2011**. It let people build anything, one block at a time. It went on to become the best-selling video game ever made."

Ben stacked a few blocks into a wobbly tower. It held.

"I've been building worlds this whole time and didn't even know I was part of history," Ben said.

"Everybody who plays is part of it," said Byte. "Speaking of — one more stop."

They landed in a bright museum hall full of glowing screens and old game machines lined up like trophies.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," said Byte. "It opened in **2015**, at a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York. It keeps the most important games safe, so people remember where they came from."

Ben spotted a glass case holding a worn Pac-Man machine, right next to a dusty old oscilloscope.

"That's the very first one," he whispered. "From the lab."

"The whole story, in one room," said Byte.

The museum lights blurred into green static, and Ben landed back on his bedroom floor, tablet glowing softly in his hands.

His pixel art creeper was still there — but now, next to it, sat one new tiny pixel block, glowing faintly green.

Ben grinned and set it carefully on his nightstand.

"Night, Byte."

"Game on," Byte whispered, and the glow faded to sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game on.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, **William Higinbotham** made a bouncing-ball game called 'Tennis for Two' on a round screen called an **oscilloscope**.
In **1962**, **Steve Russell** and his friends built 'Spacewar!' on a giant computer called a **PDP-1**.
**Ralph Baer's** Brown Box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972** — the first game console you could play at home.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and made the arcade hit **Pong**.
The **Atari 2600**, released in **1977**, let players swap in **cartridges** to play lots of different games on one machine.
In **1978**, **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, starting a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man**, maybe inspired by a pizza with a slice missing.
In **1983**, too many rushed games caused a big slowdown called the video game **crash**.
A story about unsold game cartridges buried in a New Mexico **landfill** turned out to be true — diggers found them in **2014**.
In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov** invented **Tetris**, a falling-block puzzle game, in Moscow.
In **1985**, **Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.**, starring Mario, gaming's most famous character.
**Sonic the Hedgehog** was made by Sega in **1991** to race against Mario.
Sony's **PlayStation**, from **1994**, used CDs instead of cartridges for fuller pictures and sound.
**Minecraft**, made by **Markus 'Notch' Persson** in **2011**, became the best-selling video game ever.

story.title: Lena and the Keeper's Ball
story.subtitle: One old ball, two thousand years of soccer, and a goalkeeper who refuses to stay in bed

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: A Game Older Than Shin Guards
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep.

Instead she was in the backyard, diving at the garage door with a ball she'd found in her grandfather's attic box. It was heavier than her matchday ball. Scuffed brown leather, stitches like crooked smiles, a tag that just said OLD.

She tipped a low shot around the corner of the door, her favorite save, and the ball thumped into her gloves.

That was when it started to hum.

The seams glowed green-gold, warmer and warmer, until the yard tipped sideways and the garage door disappeared.

She landed on packed dirt under bright sun, holding the same ball. Except now it wasn't leather. It was round and bouncy, wrapped in silk strips, and a crowd in long robes was kicking it between two bamboo poles.

"That's cuju," said a voice. It came from the ball, and Lena decided to just accept that. "People in China have played a kicking game like this for **over 2,000 years**. One of soccer's oldest ancestors."

A boy nutmegged his friend and sent the ball drifting toward her. Lena got a foot under it without thinking, cushioning it the way she'd cushion a lazy back-pass.

The players cheered like she'd scored. "Not bad, keeper," said the ball. "Ready to see where this goes?"

"Obviously," said Lena, and the light came again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Banned in the Street, Found in a Roof
chapters.text:
The glow dropped her into a muddy lane, boots everywhere, a crowd chasing a ball the size of a melon with no rules at all.

"This is **mob football**," the ball said. "Whole villages, no teams, no limits." It got so wild that in **1314**, England's King Edward II banned it completely in London — too many bruised shins, too many broken windows.

Lena dodged a flying elbow and laughed. "You don't need to ban it," she shouted. "You need RULES!"

The ball seemed pleased. The glow swept her sideways in time, into a cold stone castle in Scotland. A workman up on a ladder pulled out an old roof beam — and something small and dusty tumbled free.

Lena dove and caught it before it hit the floor. A little lumpy ball, soft and light, wrapped in cracked leather.

"That," said the ball, "might be the oldest football in the world. Found hidden at **Stirling Castle**, maybe from the **1540s**. Inside is a pig's bladder — a soft pouch from an animal, blown up like a balloon to make it round."

Lena turned it over gently. "Lighter than mine," she said. "But I bet it mattered just as much."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Rulebook
chapters.text:
She landed on a university lawn in the middle of an argument. "You can't just pick it up and run!" one student shouted.

"In **1848**," the ball explained, "Cambridge students wrote down the **Cambridge Rules** — a first try at one shared rulebook everyone could agree on."

The glow moved her again, into a smoky London pub. A man with a notebook was scribbling furiously.

"Ebenezer Cobb Morley," the ball said. "On **26 October 1863**, he helped start the Football Association, and he personally wrote the first official rules — no carrying the ball with your hands."

Lena peered over his shoulder. "That line's smudged," she said, pointing. Morley squinted, then grinned and copied it out clean.

"Handy, having a keeper around," he said.

"Wait," Lena said. "What about goalkeepers? We use our hands."

Morley chuckled. "That," he said, "is a story for another night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Cup and the Draw
chapters.text:
Next she landed pitchside in roaring noise, boots thudding through mud.

"The **FA Cup**," the ball said, "started in **1871-72**. It's the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world."

The glow shifted her to Glasgow, **1872**. Two teams lined up for what the ball called the very first official international match — Scotland against England.

Scotland's goalkeeper looked pale as paper.

Lena crouched beside him. "Watch the hips, not the feet," she said. "Feet lie. Hips tell the truth."

He nodded, shaky but steadier.

The match finished **0-0**. Not one goal either way.

"Guess we make a good defense," the keeper said afterward, grinning.

"Guess we do," said Lena.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Leagues and a World Agreement
chapters.text:
The glow dropped her among club owners arguing over a messy calendar covered in crossed-out dates.

"In **1888**," the ball said, "William McGregor organized the **Football League** — the world's first proper football league, where teams played a full season instead of random matches whenever."

"That's just a fixture list," Lena said. "My club has a spreadsheet for this." She grabbed a pencil and sketched teams into neat rows. McGregor leaned in, impressed.

The light swept her to Paris, **1904**. Seven serious-looking men from seven countries signed a paper.

"**FIFA**," the ball said. "Football's world organization, founded that year, so every country could agree on one set of rules."

"So it's like finally agreeing which snacks everyone brings to the tournament," Lena said.

The ball didn't disagree.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Uruguay, 1930
chapters.text:
The next stadium was deafening, blue-and-white flags everywhere.

"The very first **FIFA World Cup**," the ball said, "was played in **Uruguay in 1930**. The host team beat Argentina in the final."

A man in a sharp suit stood near the tunnel, watching the crowd like it was a gift he'd personally wrapped.

"Jules Rimet," the ball said. "The FIFA president who pushed hardest to make this whole tournament happen. They even named the original trophy after him."

"Why bother?" Lena asked him. "Why build something this huge?"

Rimet smiled. "So countries could compete fairly, together, instead of apart," he said.

Lena watched the stands shake with noise and decided that sounded like a pretty good reason.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Dog Who Found the Cup
chapters.text:
London, and a glass trophy case stood empty. Police paced around it, frowning.

"In **1966**," the ball said, "the World Cup trophy was stolen, right here in London."

Lena scanned the ground the way she read a penalty taker's run-up — looking for the one detail that mattered. Near a hedge, something was wrapped in newspaper.

A small dog was already sniffing at it, tail going like a windshield wiper.

"That's **Pickles**," the ball said. "He's the one who finds it. A week after it goes missing."

"FOUND IT!" Lena shouted, waving over the nearest officer.

The bundle was unwrapped. The trophy gleamed, perfectly safe.

"England hosted that whole tournament," the ball added. "And won it. Their only title so far."

Lena gave Pickles a gentle scratch behind the ears while the crowd outside began to roar.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Three Cups and a Red Card
chapters.text:
Golden afternoon light, and a man juggling a ball off his knees like it weighed nothing at all.

"**Pele**," the ball said. "The only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams — **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

He flicked the ball to Lena. She got it up, down, up again, wobbling only once.

"Keeper's feet," he said, approving. "Better than you think."

The ball hummed on. "That same **1970** tournament, a referee named Ken Aston started using yellow and red cards. He got the idea from traffic lights — yellow to slow down and be careful, red to stop completely and leave the field."

"And since Brazil got to keep that first trophy for good after their third win," the ball added, "FIFA had to make a brand new one in **1974**."

"Fair's fair," Lena said. "You win it three times, it's basically yours."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Ban That Should Never Have Been
chapters.text:
A gate stood locked with a sign on it, but in the park just outside, a women's team was training anyway, sharp and fast.

"**Lily Parr**," the ball said, "helped make the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** one of the most popular teams in all of England."

"So why the locked gate?" Lena asked.

"Because in **1921**, the FA banned women's football completely."

"That's not fair," Lena said flatly. "That's not fair at all."

"No," the ball agreed. "It wasn't."

The glow carried her forward, fast, to **1971** — fifty years later — when the FA finally lifted that ban.

And further still, to a packed stadium in China in **1991**, the very first official Women's World Cup. The crowd erupted as the final whistle blew.

"**The United States** won it," the ball said.

Lena jumped up, fist in the air, cheering louder than she had all night.

"Best chapter yet," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back in the Yard
chapters.text:
The glow faded, and the grass turned back into her own backyard, porch light steady and yellow again.

Lena stood there, breathing hard, the old ball warm in her gloves. She turned it over. The stitches looked the same — scuffed, crooked, ordinary — except for one faint thread of gold, new, tucked right along the seam.

She traced it with her thumb and smiled.

Tomorrow's practice, she decided, needed a diving save worthy of 1872.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's practice, she decided, needed a diving save worthy of 1872.

Cambridge students wrote down the **Cambridge Rules** in **1848**, an early try at one shared rulebook.
The Football Association was founded on **26 October 1863**, and banned carrying the ball with your hands.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote the first official rules of football in 1863.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere today.
The first official international match, Scotland versus England, ended **0-0** in Glasgow in **1872**.
William McGregor organized the **Football League** in **1888**, the world's first proper football league.
**FIFA**, football's world organization, was founded in Paris in **1904**.
The first **FIFA World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host team won it.
In **1966**, the stolen World Cup trophy was found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Pele** is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
The first official Women's World Cup was held in China in **1991**, and **the United States** won it.

story.title: Arjun and the Umpire of the Night Shift
story.subtitle: An inning through why bodies sleep, with a wing-raised verdict from Ollie the Owl

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Not Out (But Also Not Awake)
chapters.text:
Arjun had the flashlight under the blanket and his comic open to the best page — the hero's winning six. Five more minutes, he told himself. He always told himself that.

Then the panel beside the hero's bat began to glow, soft green, like a nightlight with opinions. Arjun poked it. That poke started everything.

A small cartoon owl popped out, wearing a white umpire's coat, one wing raised like he was signaling a boundary. "Finally," the owl said. "I've been knocking for ten minutes. I'm Ollie. I call the night shift."

"An umpire. For sleep?"

"For sleep," said Ollie. "Come see the first match ever properly watched."

The panel swallowed them with a **WHOOSH**, landing in a quiet room in **Chicago**, **1953**. A boy slept on a cot, wires taped gently near his eyes. A young scientist, **Eugene Aserinsky**, leaned close, watching something nobody had properly watched before.

Arjun leaned in too. "His eyes. They're moving under his eyelids. Like he's watching something."

"Good eyes," said Ollie. "Aserinsky and his teacher, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, found the same thing in **1953**. They named it **REM sleep** — rapid eye movement. Kleitman spent so much of his life watching people sleep, people still call him the father of sleep science."

"So the kid's dreaming. Right now. Behind closed eyes."

"First proof in history," Ollie said. "Not bad for a Tuesday."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Ninety-Minute Overs
chapters.text:
Ollie whisked Arjun to a dream-version of a cricket stadium, floodlights humming, scoreboard ticking.

"Why a stadium?" Arjun asked.

"Because sleep plays in innings too," said Ollie. "Watch the clock."

The scoreboard climbed: twenty minutes, forty-five, seventy — at ninety it chimed and flipped back to zero.

Arjun did the math out loud. "Ninety minutes. That's like one proper session before a break."

"Exactly like that," Ollie said. "A full night is built from cycles about **ninety minutes long**. Quiet, slow sleep for a while — that's called **non-REM** — then an active, dreaming stretch, **REM**, before it starts again."

On the practice pitch below, a sleeping cartoon batter's legs twitched during the dreaming stretch, then went completely limp.

"Why'd he go floppy?" Arjun asked.

"During REM, the brain's almost as busy as when you're awake," Ollie said. "But the body switches the muscles off, so you don't actually swing the bat in your sleep."

Arjun grinned. "Useful rule."

"Most useful rule in the ground," said Ollie, signaling four cycles complete with one wing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Growth Innings
chapters.text:
Next stop was a dressing room with a glowing diagram of a brain, propped up like a trophy.

"Why do I need so much sleep?" Arjun asked. "I'm not even tired most nights." Five more minutes, right.

"Grown-ups sleep less because they're done growing," Ollie said. "You're not. Watch the deepest part of non-REM — the slow, heavy part."

A dial on the diagram lit brightest during that deep stage.

"That's when the body releases the most **growth hormone**," Ollie said, "the stuff that helps you grow taller, heal up, and get stronger. Big reason kids need extra sleep."

Arjun checked himself, half expecting a comic-book growth spurt. Nothing happened immediately.

"Not instant," Ollie said, reading his face. "A nightly top-up. Not a cheat code."

"Still," Arjun said, "I'm telling my coach sleep is basically training."

"Tell him every single night," said Ollie, "and that's the whole point of tonight's match."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Clock Behind His Eyes
chapters.text:
They flew into a small, ticking room shaped like the inside of a wristwatch.

"What is this place?" Arjun said.

"The control room," said Ollie. "A tiny bit of brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — just say 'the master clock,' easier — sits right above where your two eye nerves cross. It tells the body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up."

Arjun spotted a label on the gears: CIRCADIAN. "What's that mean?"

"**Circadian**," Ollie said, "comes from old words meaning 'about a day.' This clock runs close to twenty-four hours, resetting every morning with sunlight."

Arjun noticed three nameplates bolted beside the gears: **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, **Michael Young**.

"Who are they?"

"The scientists who found the actual genes — tiny instruction codes inside your cells — that keep this clock ticking," Ollie said. "They won the **Nobel Prize** for it, in **2017**. Everybody's got gears like these, right behind the eyes."

Arjun tapped the glass politely instead of the gears themselves. "Don't want to mess up anyone's clock."

"Wise umpire," said Ollie.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Sleepy Juice
chapters.text:
In a little glass lab, bottles lined a shelf, each glowing faint silver.

Arjun picked one up and sniffed. "Smells like nothing."

"That's **melatonin**," Ollie said, "the hormone that tells your body it's bedtime. Scientist **Aaron Lerner** and his team first pulled it out and bottled it, back in **1958**."

"So this is what makes me yawn?"

"Partly. Your own body makes it every evening, right on schedule with that master clock we just saw." Ollie wobbled the bottle. "No need to borrow one. You've got a built-in factory."

Arjun set it down carefully, like a man handling a sponsor's trophy. "Good. Wasn't going to drink mystery lab juice anyway."

"Smart," Ollie said. "Also it wouldn't do much outside a body. It's a signal, not a magic potion."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Brain's Wash Cycle
chapters.text:
The panel opened onto Arjun's own bedroom — except every comic on the shelf was floating, pages sorting themselves mid-air.

"Hang on, that's MY room," Arjun said.

"Sleep does this every night," Ollie said. "While you're out, your brain takes the day's mess — what you learned, what you practiced in the nets — and files it into long-term memory. Good sleep is basically good filing."

Arjun watched a floating page of batting tips slot neatly behind today's net practice. "So if I sleep well, I actually remember the tips better?"

"Correctly filed," Ollie said.

Then the lights dimmed and a soft blue wave rinsed through the floating shelves.

"And that?"

"A nightly rinse," said Ollie. "Scientists call it the **glymphatic system** — think of it as a cleaning crew flushing waste out of a sleeping brain. Power-wash, but gentle, and only while you're asleep."

Arjun watched his comics come out looking cleaner, somehow brighter. "Handy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Eleven Days Awake
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a sunny driveway in **San Diego**, **1964**. A teenager sat surrounded by notepads, eyes rimmed red, grinning gamely for a photographer.

"Who's that?" Arjun asked.

"**Randy Gardner**," Ollie said. "Seventeen years old. Science-fair project. He stayed awake about **eleven days** — one of the longest stretches anybody's ever properly recorded."

Arjun, world champion of wanting five more minutes, looked intrigued despite himself. "Eleven days. That's basically a cheat code for more comic time."

"It is not," Ollie said flatly. "By the end he couldn't focus, couldn't remember things, wasn't quite himself. Doctors watched the whole thing and still say: don't try to beat this. Not a record worth chasing."

Arjun watched cartoon Randy nearly fall asleep standing up mid-interview, and decided eleven days sounded less like a cheat code and more like a very long, very bad homework assignment.

"Right," Arjun said. "Five more minutes awake, sure. Eleven more days, hard no."

"Progress," said Ollie.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sleepiest Team in the League
chapters.text:
The last stop before home was a wide, night-blue savanna panel.

"Last over," Ollie said. "Even the animal kingdom keeps odd hours."

A dolphin swam past with one eye open. "Only half its brain sleeps at a time," Ollie said. "Same with some seals. One half naps, the other half keeps watch — or keeps swimming."

A giraffe nearby dozed standing up. "Giraffes get by on under two hours a day, in short standing naps. Shortest sleepers of any big animal its size."

Arjun pointed at a tiny fly dozing on a leaf. "Even bugs sleep?"

"Even fruit flies rest like this," Ollie said. "Which tells scientists sleep is an old, old habit — almost as old as animals themselves."

Arjun looked proud of the fly, somehow. "So basically the whole team sleeps. Just different shifts."

"Whole team," Ollie agreed. "People spend something like a third of their life doing it. Might as well get good at it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Stumps
chapters.text:
The panel folded shut like a book closing itself, and Arjun was back under his blanket, flashlight dimmer than before, comic open to the very same page.

Ollie's wing poked briefly out of the panel's corner. "Last call," he said. "Umpire's decision."

"I know, I know," Arjun said, already yawning. "Five more minutes."

"Not tonight," said Ollie. "Even champions need the full match, not just the highlights."

Arjun clicked off the flashlight. In the dark, the comic's last panel glowed one more second — a tiny cartoon umpire lifting a wing, calling stumps — before fading to ordinary paper.

He pulled the blanket up, already halfway into his own ninety minutes, already filing away a whole night's worth of facts for his cricket coach.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole team to convince that sleep was basically training.

true_facts.text: Scientists **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** discovered **REM sleep** in **1953** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes move under his eyelids.
A night's sleep is built from repeating cycles about **ninety minutes** long, switching between quiet **non-REM** sleep and active, dreaming **REM** sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when you're awake, but the muscles go limp so you can't act out your dreams.
The deepest stage of sleep triggers the most **growth hormone**, which is one reason growing kids need extra sleep.
A tiny part of the brain called the **master clock**, sitting right above where the eye nerves cross, tells the body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up.
The word **circadian** comes from old words meaning 'about a day,' because the body's clock runs close to twenty-four hours.
In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep that clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone **melatonin** was first pulled out and bottled in **1958** by scientist **Aaron Lerner** and his team.
Sleep helps the brain file the day's experiences into long-term memory, so good sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the **glymphatic system** flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** of **San Diego** stayed awake about **eleven days** for a science-fair project.
Doctors say nobody should try to beat a no-sleep record — going without sleep quickly hurts mood, focus, and memory.
Dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming.
Giraffes are some of the shortest sleepers of any big animal, sometimes getting by on under two hours a day in short standing naps.
