story.title: Tom and the Gear That Remembers
story.subtitle: One rusty gear, nine stops, two hundred years of wheels.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gear in the Toolbox (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom was supposed to be asleep two hours ago. Instead he knelt on the garage floor, headlamp cutting through grease-smell, his mountain bike's derailleur in pieces around his knees.

The back wheel had wobbled on today's trail run, and problems like that made Tom's brain itch until he fixed them.

Reaching for a wrench, his fingers found something else at the bottom of the toolbox: a gear, caked in rust, too old for any bike he owned.

He rubbed it clean with his thumb. The teeth caught the light and — **CLICK** — the gear spun on its own, glowing green like a firefly trapped in metal.

"Okay," Tom said to the empty garage. "That's new."

The hum rose into a whoosh, and the garage walls folded away like a tent coming down. Tom was standing on a muddy road in the rain, facing a man balanced on two wooden wheels with no pedals at all.

"Karl von Drais," the man said, tipping his hat without falling off. "**1817**. I call her the Laufmaschine — the running machine."

No pedals, no chain. Just two wheels, a seat, and handlebars. "So how do you go?" Tom asked.

Von Drais pushed off the ground with both feet, scooting forward like a giant two-wheeled skateboard.

"People call it the hobby horse," Tom said. "Or the **draisine**."

Von Drais blinked, surprised. "Word travels fast where you're from."

Tom watched the handlebars turn the front wheel exactly like his own bike's did. "The steering's basically right already," he said. "You got the important part first try."

The gear buzzed in his pocket, impatient. Tom grinned. "I think it wants to keep going."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
The next whoosh dropped Tom onto cobblestones, and his teeth rattled before his feet even landed.

A man wheeled past on a machine that looked almost like a real bike — except the pedals were bolted straight onto the front wheel.

"Pierre Michaux," the man called over his shoulder, "with my partner Pierre Lallement. We call it the **velocipede**."

Tom winced as the front wheel juddered over every stone. "People nicknamed this the boneshaker, didn't they?"

"With good reason," Lallement said, climbing off to rub his back.

Tom crouched by the front wheel, tracing the crank with one finger. "Pedals right on the wheel means every turn of your legs is one turn of the wheel. No gears to help you."

"Exactly so," said Lallement. "I even filed papers in America, in **1866**, so nobody could copy the idea without asking me first."

"A patent," Tom said. "Officially claiming you thought of it first."

Lallement looked pleased. "Precisely."

Tom tried a lap himself, bones rattling, and nearly laughed out loud. "This explains so much," he said. "Somebody needed to get those pedals off the front wheel."

The gear in his pocket hummed again, like it agreed completely.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header (1870s)
chapters.text:
Tom landed in front of a wheel taller than he was.

A rider sat perched way up top, a tiny wheel trailing behind like an afterthought.

"They're called penny-farthings," the rider said, "after two old coins — one huge, one tiny, just like these wheels."

"How do you even get up there?" Tom asked, craning his neck.

"Carefully," the rider said, swinging a leg up. "One turn of the pedals on this big wheel sends you much farther than on a small one. Faster, with less pedaling."

Tom's engineer brain clicked the gear ratio into place instantly. "Bigger wheel, more distance per turn. That tracks."

Then the rider hit a stone, and the whole bike pitched forward.

Tom's stomach dropped — but the rider only tumbled onto a soft patch of grass, rolling once, laughing as he stood.

"We call that taking a header," he said, brushing off his knees. "Happens to everyone eventually. Perfectly survivable, mostly to your pride."

Tom let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "Sitting that high above the front wheel seems like a design flaw."

"You're not wrong," the rider admitted. "Someone really ought to fix that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Equal Wheels (1885)
chapters.text:
A workshop this time, full of metal tubing and the smell of oil.

A man was welding two wheels — same size, low to the ground — onto a frame shaped almost exactly like Tom's own bike.

"John Kemp Starley," he said, not looking up. "The **Rover Safety Bicycle**. **1885**."

Tom crouched beside the back wheel and spotted it immediately: a chain, looping from pedals at the center of the frame back to the rear wheel.

"You moved the pedals off the wheel entirely," Tom said. "And the chain lets you gear it however you want."

Starley nodded. "No more giant front wheel. No more headers."

Tom swung a leg over the finished frame. Low seat, both feet near the ground, steady as anything. "This is basically a modern bike," he said, genuinely startled.

"That was rather the point," Starley said. "Safer, easier — for anyone to ride, not just the daring ones."

Tom pedaled a slow circle around the workshop, grinning. "Everyone after you is basically just improving this."

The gear buzzed warm in his pocket, like applause.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Air Under the Wheel (1888)
chapters.text:
The road outside the next stop was rough gravel, and a boy wobbled along it on a tricycle with solid rubber tires, teeth chattering.

A man knelt beside him, holding a rubber tube he'd wrapped in canvas and pumped full of air.

"John Boyd Dunlop," he said. "I'm a vet by trade, but I couldn't watch my son get shaken to pieces on this road."

Tom crouched to press a thumb into the tube. It gave, springy, like a tiny cushion. "Air inside rubber. A **pneumatic** tire."

"My own word for it," Dunlop said, fitting it onto the wheel. "**1888**."

They rolled the tricycle over the same gravel. The boy's face changed instantly — no more rattling, just a smooth hum.

"That's the same trick my mountain bike tires use," Tom said, thinking of every rock garden he'd rolled over without a single bruised wrist. "You just didn't have rubber compounds yet."

Dunlop laughed. "One invention at a time, please."

Tom patted the tire like an old friend. "This one's going to matter more than you think."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
Suddenly the street was packed — bikes everywhere, bells ringing, riders in long coats weaving between carriages.

"The **Golden Age of Bicycles**," said a woman riding past, slowing to match Tom's walk. "Millions of these sold across Europe and America, right about now."

Tom whistled low. "Millions. That's a lot of workshops suddenly very busy."

"And a lot of freedom," the woman said. "Susan B. Anthony said riding a bicycle has done more to **emancipate** women than anything else in the world — set them loose to go wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted, without waiting on anyone else."

Tom noticed several women riding in looser, shorter trousers instead of long skirts. "Those aren't normal clothes for now, are they?"

"Long skirts catch in gears and wheels," the woman said. "So we invented something safer to wear. People called them bloomers."

Tom watched the crowd roll past, dozens of ordinary people suddenly going faster and farther than their parents ever had. "The bike didn't just change how people moved," he said slowly. "It changed what people were allowed to do."

The woman smiled. "Now you're getting it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bicycle Shop in Dayton (1890s)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like metal shavings and bicycle grease, shelves lined with wheels and spokes.

Two brothers were bent over a workbench, adjusting a chain with the kind of focus Tom recognized from his own garage.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," one of them said, not looking up. "We run a bike shop here, in **Dayton, Ohio**."

Tom picked up a length of thin metal tubing from the bench. Light, but barely bent under pressure. "This is strong for how little it weighs."

"Exactly why we use it," Orville said. "Same with spoked wheels — strong, but not heavy."

Tom's eyes went wide. "Wait. You two are the ones who—"

"Build a flying machine?" Wilbur finished, smiling. "Not yet. But those tricks we're learning right now, on bicycles, will matter later. **1903**, if you want the year."

Tom looked around the shop — spokes, light tubing, careful balance — and understood. "You're basically engineering a plane and you don't even know it yet."

"Everything's connected," Orville said, "if you're paying attention."

Tom decided, right there, that he was going to pay a lot more attention from now on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Gears for Hills (1903–1930s)
chapters.text:
A crowd lined a French road, cheering as riders streamed past in a blur of spinning legs.

"The **Tour de France**," shouted a man beside Tom. "Started in **1903**. These days it covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France, over three weeks."

Tom's jaw actually dropped. "Three weeks. On a bike."

He watched one rider hit a steep hill and simply flick a small lever, the chain jumping smoothly to a different-sized gear.

"That's a **derailleur**," the man explained. "A system that shifts your chain between gears. Became common on bikes in the **1930s**. Makes climbing hills a whole lot kinder on your legs."

Tom thought of every brutal climb on his own mountain bike trail, the one where he always wished for one more easy gear. "I would've loved this before Starley's chain even existed."

"Every piece builds on the last," the man said. "That's engineering for you."

Tom grinned, already itching to get back to his own garage and tune that derailleur properly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back Down the Mountain (1970s–Now)
chapters.text:
The last whoosh dropped Tom onto a dusty California hillside, wide tires crunching under two riders bombing down a dirt trail.

"**Marin County**, **1970s**," one rider called, skidding to a stop in a cloud of dust. "We wanted to ride downhill, fast, without wrecking a road bike. So we built these instead."

Tom crouched by the knobby tread. "Mountain bikes. These tires are basically what I ride every weekend."

"Same decade, kids in the city were building small, tough bikes for tricks and dirt racing," the rider added. "Copying motorcycle racing. They called it **BMX**."

Tom laughed. "Two totally different bikes, same decade, same idea — make it tougher."

The gear in his pocket hummed one last time, warm and steady, and the hillside folded gently back into his garage.

He stood there a second, headlamp still on, derailleur still in pieces on the floor — except now the old gear sat glowing faintly on his workbench, teeth catching the light.

Tom thought about wooden wheels with no pedals, about giant front wheels and headers, about a bike shop in Ohio that led to the sky. Somewhere out there right now, he knew, over a billion bicycles were rolling along, more than any other vehicle on Earth, some of them in cities where bikes outnumbered cars entirely.

He picked up his wrench and got back to work on the derailleur, smiling at how much history was riding on two wheels under him every single weekend.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, that derailleur was finally going to shift exactly right.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all, pushed along with the feet.
People nicknamed von Drais's invention the **hobby horse**, or the **draisine**.
In the **1860s**, Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement built the **velocipede**, with pedals bolted straight onto the front wheel, nicknamed the **boneshaker** for its rough ride.
Pierre Lallement officially claimed his pedal bicycle design in the United States in **1866**, so nobody could copy it without asking first.
In the **1870s**, the **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, letting one pedal turn send the rider much farther.
The penny-farthing was named after two very differently sized old coins, a big penny and a tiny farthing.
Falling off a penny-farthing head-first was common enough to get its own name: **taking a header**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two equal-sized wheels and a chain connecting the pedals to the back wheel.
The safety bicycle's low, even wheels made it far easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design everywhere.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented a practical air-filled rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother.
The **1890s** bicycle craze, called the **Golden Age of Bicycles**, saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Susan B. Anthony said riding a bicycle gave women more freedom to go places on their own than almost anything else at the time.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bicycle shop in **Dayton, Ohio**, before building the first successful airplane.
The **Tour de France**, the world's most famous long-distance bike race, began in **1903** and today covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France.

story.title: Hana and the Unsinkable Chart
story.subtitle: A girl, a glowing compass, and the biggest ship the world had ever seen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Needle That Wouldn't Sit Still
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep. Instead she lay on her bedroom floor, flashlight under the quilt, a cracked old map of the North Atlantic spread across the carpet. She'd found it at a flea market — one folded, salt-stained chart, and a dented brass compass rattling around in the same wooden box. Two dollars. Hana thought that was a steal for something this old.

She traced her finger along a thin black line on the map, a shipping route running from a port called Southampton all the way to New York City. The compass beside her, for no reason at all, began to turn. Its needle spun once, twice, then settled, glowing a cold blue-white that had no business coming out of hundred-year-old brass.

"That's new," Hana whispered.

The glow spread across the carpet like spilled moonlight. The map seemed to breathe under her hand. Then the bedroom floor wasn't carpet anymore — it was wet, splintery wood, ringing with hammers, smelling of coal smoke and salt.

She was standing on a platform above a half-built ship's hull, its steel ribs rising around her like the inside of a whale. A man in overalls was chalking numbers onto a long steel beam running along the very bottom.

"That there's the keel," he said, catching her stare. "The backbone of her. Lay it first, build the whole ship around it." He tapped the chalked date. "Thirty-first of March, **1909**. Today's the day we started her."

Hana's eyes went wide. She was standing in **Belfast, Ireland**, at the Harland & Wolff shipyard — and she already knew the ship's name, stitched into her compass box in faded gold thread: **Titanic**.

"Only one you're building?" she asked.

"Her and two sisters," the man said. "**Olympic's** already sailing. **Britannic's** keel goes down right after this one."

Three ships, one family. Hana's map had just gotten a lot more interesting. In her pocket, the compass buzzed, impatient, like it wanted to show her more already.

"Slow down," she told it. "I just got here."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Deck the Length of Four City Blocks
chapters.text:
The blue light spun again, hauling Hana forward through time like a page turning. When it let go, she stood on a crowded dock, and the ship above her didn't look half-built anymore. It looked impossible.

She tipped her head back and still couldn't see the top of it. A sailor beside her noticed her craning her neck. "Bigger than you'd think, miss. Near enough **882 feet**, bow to stern. Biggest ship afloat."

Hana pulled out her own folded map and held it against the hull, comparing paper to steel. Even her best guess had been too small.

She counted the four huge smokestacks rising overhead, but only three had smoke curling out of them. "Why's that one empty?"

"Keeps her looking balanced," the sailor said. "Makes her look even more powerful. Only three are hooked up to boilers — the fourth's mostly for show."

A ship with a fake chimney. Hana had never put that detail on a map before.

An officer passing overhead heard her asking about safety and leaned on the rail. "Sixteen separate compartments down in the hull," he said, "each one sealed off by steel doors. Flood one, even two, and she'll still float. Folks are already calling her the ship that can't sink."

Hana felt a small chill despite the sunshine. Ships that "can't sink" were exactly the kind of thing maps never warned you about.

A sign on the dock read **10 April 1912**, bound for New York. The gangway lifted. A horn sounded, long and low — **WHOOOOSH** — and the crowd roared as the biggest ship in the world eased away from England for the very first time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Something in the Dark
chapters.text:
Days blurred past in the compass's blue light, nights at sea sliding by like turning pages. Then, one night, the air itself changed — bitterly cold, dead calm, no moon at all.

Hana stood near the bow beside two lookouts, watching the black water for any shimmer of ice. The ship hummed along smoothly, confident, enormous.

A bell rang out, three sharp strikes. "Iceberg, right ahead!" someone shouted.

The deck tilted faintly under Hana's shoes as the ship turned, hard and too slow. A long, dark shape, taller than the deck rails, slid past just off the side — close enough that Hana could feel cold air pouring off the ice.

"What time is it?" she asked, gripping the rail.

"**Eleven-forty**," a sailor said grimly, checking his pocket watch. "Night of **April 14th, 1912**."

Footsteps on the stairs. Captain **Edward Smith** appeared, calm as still water, listening to a quick report from below. "Shut the watertight doors," he said. "She was built to take a hit. Let's see her prove it."

Somewhere deep in the ship, steel groaned. The deck did not tip over. The lights did not go out. For a long moment nothing happened at all, and Hana let out a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. The night was far from over — but for now, the ship still floated beneath her feet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Dots, Dashes, and Not Enough Boats
chapters.text:
Belowdecks, a tiny room clattered with a strange rhythm — dots and dashes tapped on a brass key into a crackling machine. A wireless, Hana realized: a kind of radio, sending messages through thin air without a single wire strung between ships.

Two operators, **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, bent over it like statues. "What are you sending?" Hana asked.

"**CQD**," Phillips said, not looking up. "Old distress call. Means come quick, danger." He paused, then tapped a newer pattern. "And just in case — **SOS**. Easier to pick out of the static."

Hana listened to the rhythm — three short, three long, three short — and grinned despite everything. "Dot dot dot, dash dash dash, dot dot dot. I know that one."

Up on deck, crew were lowering lifeboats on creaking ropes, far too few of them for everyone aboard. Hana counted the boats and did the math on her fingers. "There's not enough," she said.

The officer loading one didn't argue. "Room for about **1,178** folks," he said grimly. "Nowhere near everyone. Women and children, this way, please — move along now."

A little girl climbed toward a boat clutching a small fluffy dog to her chest, refusing to let go even as hands reached for her. The sailor helping her simply nodded and let the dog come too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Band Played On
chapters.text:
Over the groan of metal and the shouts of crew, Hana heard something strange: music. Bright violin music, drifting up from the deck like nothing at all was wrong.

A small band stood near the grand staircase, led by a violinist named **Wallace Hartley**, playing steadily while families moved past toward the boats. "They say the band kept playing almost to the very end, to keep everyone calm," murmured a woman wrapping a coat around her shoulders. "Nobody's completely sure which songs — but everyone remembers the music." Hana decided she liked a story that admitted what it didn't know.

Nearby, a woman in a fur-trimmed coat was arguing with a crewman, insisting her lifeboat row back to help, grabbing an oar herself when nobody else would. "Name's Margaret Brown," she told Hana with a wink, hauling like she'd done it her whole life. "Folks'll call me plenty of things after tonight. Let 'em." Hana would later learn people nicknamed her the **Unsinkable Molly Brown** for exactly this.

Someone pressed a shivering Pomeranian into Hana's arms while its owner climbed down a rope ladder. The little dog licked her chin the entire way down, utterly unbothered by the whole business, and Hana decided dogs had the right idea about most things.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Three Hours in the Dark
chapters.text:
By **2:20 in the morning** — not even three full hours after the iceberg — the great ship that had once seemed too big to sink slipped beneath the water's surface. Hana watched from a lifeboat at a safe distance, the compass clutched tight and warm in her hand.

It was a hard night, and not everyone made it through it. But far off across the black water, lights were coming.

A steamship called the **Carpathia** had turned around the moment it caught the wireless call, steaming through ice-strewn dark for hours to reach them. By sunrise its crew was hauling cold, tired survivors up rope ladders onto its deck, wrapping them in blankets, pouring hot drinks into shaking hands.

Wedged between two life jackets, small and shivering, Hana spotted something familiar — the same Pomeranian from before — and bundled it inside her coat until its owner could be found a few feet away, overjoyed.

As dawn came up pink over calm water, Hana counted heads lifted onto the Carpathia's deck, one after another, safe. The compass in her pocket had gone quiet and cool, as if it, too, needed to catch its breath.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rules Written in Ice
chapters.text:
Weeks later — the compass skipped ahead again, impatient as always — Hana found herself in a wood-paneled room full of serious officials arguing over charts and ship diagrams.

"You're going to make them carry enough lifeboats this time, right?" Hana asked, before anyone had even said it out loud.

One official glanced up, startled, then nodded slowly. "That's exactly the idea, young lady. Every ship, enough boats for every person aboard. No exceptions."

Another explained a new patrol that would watch the ocean every spring for dangerous ice and warn ships before they got too close. Hana grinned. "An ice patrol. Like a map that updates itself."

"Young lady," the official said dryly, "you have a future in shipping regulations." Hana decided that was the strangest compliment she'd ever gotten.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Chart at the Bottom of the Sea
chapters.text:
The compass spun one more time, faster than ever, and the light turned deep green instead of blue — ocean-deep, pressing, cold.

Hana found herself aboard a small research ship, decades later, leaning over the shoulder of an oceanographer — a scientist who studies the sea — named **Robert Ballard**, watching a screen crawl along a dark, grainy seafloor.

"There," Ballard said quietly, on **1 September 1985**, pointing at a shape rising out of the mud nearly **12,500 feet** down. One of Titanic's huge boilers, then a railing, then, impossibly, the ship itself, broken into two pieces resting about **370 miles** off the coast of **Newfoundland, Canada**.

Hana spotted something small glinting on the screen — a single dinner plate, sitting undisturbed exactly where it had settled, decades before. "People keep finding plates, shoes, all sorts of things," Ballard said. "Museums everywhere display them now."

Later still, the compass flickering through decades like skimming stones, Hana glimpsed a building shaped like a ship's bow opening in Belfast in **2012**, exactly a hundred years after the sinking.

Then the green light folded in on itself, and Hana was lying on her own bedroom carpet again, map spread in front of her, compass warm and still in her hand. The glow was gone. But the shipping route she'd traced earlier now had a tiny new mark beside Southampton — a small dot that hadn't been there before.

Hana traced the dot with her finger, smiling at the ceiling. Somewhere out there, a real wreck sat quiet on the seafloor, and a whole family of maps was waiting for her to find the next one.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a hundred more routes to trace.

true_facts.text: At about **882 feet** long, Titanic was the biggest ship in the world at the time.
Her hull had **16 watertight compartments**, which is why people called her nearly unsinkable.
Titanic left **Southampton, England**, on **10 April 1912**, heading for New York City.
**Captain Edward Smith** stayed with his ship, trying to keep her steady to the end.
The wireless operators sent out both the old **CQD** distress call and the newer **SOS**.
Titanic only carried lifeboats for about **1,178 people**, far fewer than everyone aboard.
Passenger **Margaret 'Molly' Brown** helped row her lifeboat and earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
Survivors said the ship's band kept playing music as she sank, though which songs is still debated.
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and pulled survivors from their lifeboats the next morning.
Titanic sank at around **2:20 a.m.** on **15 April 1912**, under three hours after hitting the iceberg.
After the disaster, a new **Ice Patrol** was formed, and new rules required enough lifeboats for everyone aboard any ship.
The wreck was found on **1 September 1985** by **Robert Ballard's** expedition, about **12,500 feet** down.

new_recurring.name: Fathom the Compass
new_recurring.rule: A dented brass compass that glows blue-white when Hana traces a route on an old map, pulling her into the real history behind that place; it always spins again, cool and quiet, to bring her safely home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Hana returned to her bedroom carpet to find a tiny new mark drawn beside Southampton on her map, right where Titanic's real voyage had begun, with the compass warm and quiet in her hand.

request.care_notes: Focus on the engineering marvel of the ship, how it was built, the technology of the time, and the rescue efforts that followed. Avoid graphic descriptions of the sinking, drowning, or the suffering of passengers. Emphasize the historical lessons learned about safety at sea.

story.title: Max, Sami, and the Brick That Started It All
story.subtitle: A journey through ninety years of clicks, in one very old brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Workshop in Billund (1932)
chapters.text:
It was past ten o'clock, and the basement floor was a disaster of gray and black Technic beams.

"My robot arm is going to crush yours," Max said, snapping a gear onto an axle. He was building a claw. Sami was drawing one — same idea, way less plastic, way more pencil.

"Drawings don't break," Sami said. "Yours will. You always build too fast."

They were still digging through the bottom of the parts bin, hunting for one more connector pin, when Max's fingers closed on something heavier than plastic should be. It was a single old brick, red going brown, dust packed into its studs. It was warm. It should not have been warm.

It hummed. Then it pulsed a soft green, like a firefly deciding something.

"Don't touch it," Sami said, and touched it.

**CLICK.**

The basement smelled like sawdust. The Technic beams were gone. They were standing in a wooden workshop with curled shavings on the floor and a sign over the door that read BILLUND.

A man in an apron was sanding a toy duck. He looked up, not even surprised, like kids falling out of nowhere happened to him all the time.

"You're early for the bricks," he said. "I only work in wood. For now."

"Who are you?" Sami asked.

"Ole Kirk Christiansen," he said. "I started this workshop right here in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**. Toys, ladders, ironing boards — whatever sells, I build it."

Max turned the duck over in his hands. No wheels, no gears, nothing that moved. "This is going to turn into LEGO?" he said, half a question, half a dare.

"Everything turns into something," Ole Kirk said, and smiled like he knew a secret.

The old brick in Sami's pocket buzzed, warmer now, like it liked hearing its own beginning. Sami pulled it out and said the year out loud — "**1932**" — and the workshop folded away like a page turning.

"Okay," Max said, as the light went green again. "That brick listens."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
The green faded and left them standing in the same workshop, but the sign outside had changed.

"LEGO," Max read off the new sign. "Wait — is that the actual name?"

Ole Kirk was there again, a little grayer, nailing a sign to the wall. "I named it in **1934**," he said. "Short for *leg godt* — that's Danish for **'play well.'**"

Sami grinned. "That's it? That's the whole secret?"

"There's a story some people like even more," Ole Kirk said, leaning on his hammer. "They say *lego* also means **'I put together'** in Latin. Nice coincidence, if it's even true — but I didn't know a word of Latin when I picked the name. I just wanted something that meant *play well*."

"So it's a legend," Sami said, delighted, writing it straight into the sketchbook under his arm. "A cool one, but a legend."

"Exactly," said Ole Kirk.

Max, who liked facts to stay facts, looked almost disappointed, then not. "Still a good name," he admitted.

The brick in Sami's hand gave a small, impatient buzz, like it was waiting for someone to say the magic words.

"Play well," Max said, testing it.

Nothing.

"**LEGO**," Sami tried.

Still nothing.

Max rolled his eyes and said it properly: "*Leg godt.*"

**CLICK.** Green light, and the workshop walls blurred.

"Called it," Max said, even though Sami had actually said it first, which Sami was absolutely going to bring up for the rest of the night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Machine (1947–1949)
chapters.text:
The smell of sawdust was gone. In its place: oil, metal, and a machine the size of a small car, clanking and hissing in the corner of a bigger workshop.

"What is THAT?" Max said, already circling it like it might start walking.

"That," said a voice, "is the future." A younger man wiped his hands on a rag — not Ole Kirk this time, but someone with the same sharp eyes. "Godtfred. Ole Kirk's son. In **1947** we got one of the first machines in Denmark that could squeeze melted plastic into a mold and spit out a toy in seconds. We call it injection molding — melt it, squirt it into a shape, let it cool, done."

Sami peered through a little window in the machine, watching orange goo get pressed into something. "What's it making?"

"Watch," Godtfred said.

The machine clunked, and out dropped a small hollow brick with four studs on top, like a tiny plastic step. "We call these **Automatic Binding Bricks**," Godtfred said. "Made in **1949**. Stack them, and they sort of hold on. Sort of."

Max picked one up and set another on top. He pressed. It stayed — barely — then slid sideways and fell apart.

"Sort of," Max repeated, unimpressed. "My Technic pieces don't do *sort of*."

"Give it time," Godtfred said, grinning.

Sami, sketchbook already open, drew the hollow underside of the brick, empty as a little room with no furniture. "It needs something *inside* here," he said, tapping the blank space. "Something to grab the bumps on the brick below."

Godtfred went very still, then grabbed a pencil of his own. "Say that again."

The brick in Max's pocket thrummed like it agreed completely, and the whole workshop buzzed green.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Brick That Clicks (1958)
chapters.text:
They landed in the same workshop, but older now — more machines, more shelves, and Godtfred hunched over a drawing table with a pencil behind his ear.

"You again," he said, not looking up. "Your friend's idea. Tubes. I've been drawing tubes for weeks."

He held up a brick, and this time the underside wasn't empty — little round tubes hung down inside it like tiny chimneys.

"Drop the stud from the brick above into one of these," Godtfred said, "and it doesn't just sit there. It grips."

Max took two bricks, lined up the studs with the tubes, and pressed.

**CLICK.**

He pulled. It held. He pulled harder, swinging the two bricks like a tiny dumbbell. Still held.

"IT LOCKS!" Max shouted, and for once in his life he didn't care that Sami heard him sound that excited about something that wasn't a robot.

"We patented this exact design on **January 28th, 1958**," Godtfred said. "A patent means nobody else is allowed to copy it without asking us first."

Sami, always the one to ask the next question, pointed at Max's own pocket. "Does that old brick — the one that brought us here — does it fit *this* new design?"

Max pulled out the warm, dusty brick, pressed its studs into one of Godtfred's brand-new bricks, and —

**CLICK.**

Perfect fit. Ninety-whatever years apart, and it still worked.

"A brick from today," Godtfred said, watching, "will still fit a brick made long after I'm gone. We basically never changed the design again."

"So I could build with my grandpa's old bricks," Sami said slowly, like he was doing math in his head.

"If he has any," said Godtfred, "you absolutely could."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Fire (1960)
chapters.text:
The next jump landed them outside, in cool night air, looking at a warehouse glowing orange at the edges.

"Is that—" Sami started.

"It's already out," said a voice behind them. An older Godtfred, arms crossed, watching calmly instead of panicking. "Everyone's safe. It's just wood — the wooden toy warehouse. **1960**. Firefighters already came and went."

Max looked at the dark, empty window frames where toys used to be stacked. "So... you lost all your wooden toys?"

"We did," Godtfred said. "And here's the strange part — it didn't feel like only bad news. We'd already started wondering if plastic bricks were where the real future was. The fire just made the decision for us. We stopped making wooden toys for good, and put everything into the bricks."

Sami studied the warehouse a moment longer, then turned his back on it, sketchbook open, and started drawing instead the thing that wasn't burned: a tidy row of plastic bricks on a shelf nearby, untouched.

"That's the move," Max said, nodding at the drawing. "Draw the thing that's still standing."

"That's always the move," Sami said.

The old brick warmed in Max's hand, gentle this time, almost like it was saying *good call, moving on* — and the orange light faded to green.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bigger, Smaller, Stronger (1963–1969)
chapters.text:
They landed in a factory that smelled completely different — sharper, cleaner, less like melted candle wax.

"New plastic," said a worker nearby, holding up a brick that looked exactly the same but somehow felt tougher in Max's hand. "**1963**. We switched to something called ABS — plastic that doesn't crack easy and keeps its color, even if a kid leaves it in the sun or steps on it for the hundredth time."

Max bent the brick's corner against his thumb, hard. It didn't even flex. "My Technic pieces are made of this," he said, impressed despite himself.

The scene shifted again — same ground, different year — and suddenly they were standing at the gates of an actual amusement park, built entirely out of giant brick models: towers, dragons, whole miniature towns.

"**LEGOLAND**," Sami read off the gate. "**1968**. Right next to the factory."

And one more shift: a toddler-sized version of the brick sat on a table nearby, fat and easy to grab.

"That's **DUPLO**," said the worker, tagging along now like a tour guide who refused to leave. "**1969**. Made for littler hands — but line up the studs right, and it still fits a regular brick on top."

Sami grabbed one of each size and stacked them. They locked together, big stud into small tube, perfectly.

"Everything still fits everything," Sami said. "That's actually kind of amazing."

"That's the whole point," said the worker, and the brick in Max's pocket buzzed its agreement, green and steady.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Gears and Faces (1977–1979)
chapters.text:
The next workshop was full of gray beams, gears, and little plastic axles — and Max actually gasped out loud.

"That's — that's Technic stuff," he said, picking up a gear and spinning it on a pin. "**1977**. This is literally what I build with every single day."

"Beams, gears, real moving parts," said a designer nearby, grinning at Max's face. "We figured kids wanted things that actually *worked*, not just sat there looking nice."

On the next table over, Sami found something small and yellow with a round head and stick-figure arms. "What's this guy?"

"Our first minifigure," the designer said. "**1978**. Arms that actually move. Heads and hats you can swap around."

Sami swapped the little figure's hat for a different one in about two seconds. "He looks completely different now. Same guy though."

"That's the trick," the designer said. "Same parts, new story, every time."

A calm, confident-looking man walked past, maybe thirty, clearly in charge of something. "That's Kjeld," the designer said quietly. "Ole Kirk's grandson. Grew up playing with these exact bricks. Took over running the whole company in **1979**."

Max watched Kjeld go, then looked down at the Technic gear still spinning on his finger. "So the guy in charge used to be a kid with a bucket of bricks. Just like us."

"Just like you," the designer agreed, "except he actually inherited the company. You just get the basement."

Sami laughed so hard he nearly dropped the minifigure's second hat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Hard Times and a Movie (1999–2014)
chapters.text:
The workshop was gone. In its place: a store wall covered floor to ceiling in spaceships, helmets, and small plastic figures holding glowing swords.

"**Star Wars** LEGO sets," Max said, stunned. "Since when does LEGO do movies?"

"**1999**," said Kjeld, older now, standing nearby with his hands in his pockets. "First licensed theme. Not the last."

"Around the year **2000**," he went on, "people were calling the plain brick one of the greatest toys of the whole century. Which should've felt great."

"Should've?" Sami asked, catching the tone.

"We got distracted," Kjeld admitted. "Too many wild ideas, not enough bricks. In the early 2000s we got so close to running out of money completely that the company almost had to shut its doors."

Max frowned. "So what happened?"

"A new leader, **Jorgen Vig Knudstorp**, took over in **2004**," Kjeld said. "He made one simple call: stop chasing everything, go back to making the best brick sets we possibly can. It worked. We turned the whole thing around."

The scene shifted one last time, to a dark room with a glowing screen — and on it, tiny LEGO characters ran across a bright, blocky world.

"**The LEGO Movie**," Sami said. "**2014**. I've seen this."

"Everyone had," Kjeld said, smiling now. "Turns out people never really stopped loving the bricks. They just needed reminding."

The old brick in Max's hand pulsed one long, warm green — the longest pulse yet — like it was proud of how the story turned out.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Basement Floor
chapters.text:
**CLICK.**

The basement floor was cold concrete again, Technic beams scattered everywhere exactly where they'd left them.

Sami blinked. "Did that actually just happen?"

Max held up the old brick. Still warm. Still real. "I don't think I imagined a plastic machine the size of a minivan."

They sat there a minute, listening to the house creak upstairs, the way it always did.

"You know what's wild," Sami said finally, "the company's still in **Billund** — same town, same ground where that first workshop stood."

"And it's still the same family running it," Max added. "The **Kirkbi family** — Ole Kirk's descendants — they still own most of it today."

Sami reached for his sketchbook and drew one thing: a single brick, with tubes underneath and studs on top, the exact same shape from 1932 all the way to right now.

Max pressed his robot claw's last pin into place, finally finished, and set it down next to Sami's drawing.

"Truce," Max said. "Yours is better at telling the story. Mine's better at crushing things."

"I'll allow it," Sami said.

The old brick sat between them on the carpet, glowing one last soft green before going quiet — ordinary, patient, waiting for whatever year came looking for it next.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a whole bin of bricks still waiting to be built into something new.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started the company in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**, making wooden toys and ladders.
In **1934** he named the company **LEGO**, short for the Danish words *leg godt*, meaning **'play well.'**
Some people say *lego* also means **'I put together'** in Latin, but that's probably just a fun coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
In **1947** the company got one of the first machines in Denmark that could melt plastic and squirt it into molds to make toys.
In **1949** they made hollow plastic bricks called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — the very first ancestor of today's LEGO brick.
**Godtfred Kirk Christiansen** redesigned the brick with little tubes underneath, and the new locking design was officially patented on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick made in **1958** still fits perfectly with a brick made today, because the design has barely changed.
A **1960** fire destroyed the wooden toy warehouse, and afterward the company decided to focus only on plastic bricks.
In **1963** LEGO switched to a tougher plastic called ABS, which doesn't crack easily and keeps its color.
The first **LEGOLAND** theme park opened in **Billund in 1968**, right next to the original factory.
**DUPLO** bricks, sized for little kids, came out in **1969** — and they still click together with regular LEGO bricks.
The **LEGO Technic** line, with gears and moving parts, launched in **1977**.
The first **minifigures**, with movable arms and swappable heads and hats, showed up in **1978**.
**Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen**, the founder's grandson, took over running the company in **1979**.

new_recurring.name: The Old Brick
new_recurring.rule: A single warm, dusty brick that glows soft green and hums. It only clicks forward to the next moment in history when a child correctly says or discovers the key fact of the current stop. At story's end it glows once, long and warm, then…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Max and Sami land back on the basement floor with the glowing brick cooling between them, Max's finished Technic claw sitting next to Sami's finished drawing of the very first brick.

scenarios.why: #48: C15 cell, a care topic at length. Honest about what happened, never graphic.

editor_notes: Fix the Pliny history, which is the emotional and factual heart of the story. Have him promise to remember everything, and let Isla learn that years later he wrote two letters to the historian Tacitus about that day. Place him at Misenum, and make him older or hedge his age.
Cut the duplicate 'Tomorrow…' paragraph so the story ends on one clean line. Remove the stray standalone '**PLINY!**' and let the shout live inside the scene.

Repair the internal and historical slips. Remove 'from yesterday', 'days ago' and the unmentioned Herculaneum recall. Correct the earthquake timing relative to Pliny's birth. Describe Herculaneum's burial as superheated surges of volcanic material rather than wet mud. Move the Villa of the Mysteries to a later 'centuries later, diggers found…' beat. Hedge the eruption date ('traditionally August 24th, though some evidence points to autumn').

story.title: Isla and the Buried City
story.subtitle: A night with the tile that remembers Pompeii

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Hummed
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was cross-legged on her bedroom floor at eleven at night, sorting a shoebox of flea-market junk by headlamp. Case files, she called these nights. Mysteries nobody else wanted to solve.

Most of the box was nothing: buttons, a rusty key, half a teacup. But near the bottom, wrapped in a sock, was a small flat tile. It was chipped and worn almost smooth, with flecks of red and black glass still stuck in one corner.

She turned it under her magnifying glass. Some kind of mosaic piece, she guessed — a little chip of colored stone or glass that Roman builders fit together, thousands at a time, to make a picture. Archaeologists call a single piece a **tessera**.

The tile felt warm. Then it felt hot. Then the whole room filled with a low hum, like a seashell held to her ear, and the light around the edges of her vision turned gold.

When it faded, Isla was standing on a stone street in blazing sun, holding the exact same tile.

The street was crowded and loud: cart wheels, a man shouting about olives, a dog arguing with a chicken. Isla noticed something strange about the road itself. Big flat stones stuck up out of it in a row, like stepping-stones across a river, with gaps on either side just wide enough for a cart wheel.

"Those keep your feet dry when the street floods," said a voice next to her. "Carts still fit through the gaps. Clever, don't you think?"

A boy about her own age stood there, a thin wooden tablet coated in wax tucked under one arm, a metal stylus already smudged with notes. He was looking at her like she was the strange one, which, fair enough, she had just fallen out of thin air.

"Where am I?" Isla asked.

"Where are you? You're in **Pompeii**," the boy said, like that explained everything. "And who, may I ask, are you?"

"Isla. Who are you?"

The boy smiled in a way that told Isla he was absolutely not going to answer that properly. "People call me a lot of things," he said. "Mostly, I write things down." He held up the wax tablet. It was already half full of cramped little letters.

Isla decided right then that figuring out his name was going to be her first case. She tucked the tile into her pocket — it was still faintly warm — and fell into step beside him.

"So," she said, "show me everything."

"Everything," the boy said, "might take a while. But I can start with the forum."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Forum and the Five Villages
chapters.text:
The forum turned out to be the town square, except nothing about it was square-shaped or quiet. Isla counted columns until she lost track, past a temple, past stalls selling bread and fish sauce, past a crowd arguing about politics in front of a wall covered in painted slogans.

"People vote for mayor here?" Isla asked, squinting at the paint.

"Every election," the boy said. "Someone paints 'Vote for him, he's honest' on the wall outside his bakery. Then somebody else paints theirs on top." It was, Isla realized, basically an ancient campaign poster — just permanent, and on somebody's actual house.

She tried to guess how many people lived here, watching the crush of elbows and baskets. "A few hundred?" she tried.

The boy laughed. "More like eleven to fifteen thousand. Shops, bathhouses, theaters, temples — it's a real town, not a village." Pompeii, he explained, sat on the Bay of Naples, in what people someday would call southern Italy.

"Okay, mystery two," Isla said. "Why is it called Pompeii?"

The boy tapped his stylus against his chin. "Nobody's completely sure. But the old local word for 'five' was *pompe*. Some people think five villages joined together, long before my time, and the name stuck."

Isla liked that answer precisely because it wasn't a clean one. A name with a maybe in it was more interesting than a name with a period at the end.

They passed a bathhouse with steam curling out the door, and a theater cut into a hillside, benches stacked like a stone staircase. Isla wanted to stop at every single building, which was a problem, because the boy kept walking, scribbling as he went.

"You write an awful lot," she said.

"I write to my uncle," he said. "He likes details. Everything, exactly as it happened — no exaggerating."

"What's he do?"

"Commands ships," the boy said, already turning a corner. "Come on. You wanted to see the water."

Isla filed that away. A boy who wrote careful letters to an uncle who commanded ships. Case notes, page two.

She followed him past a wall where somebody had scratched a joke into the plaster at ankle height, half-rubbed away by a thousand years of nobody reading it yet. She grinned. Even two thousand years ago, somebody couldn't resist doodling on a wall where they weren't supposed to.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water for Eleven Thousand People
chapters.text:
A fountain gurgled at the corner of the next street, water spilling from a stone spout shaped like a lion's mouth. Isla crouched to look closer. A thin, dark pipe ran into the base of it.

"Lead," the boy said, before she asked. "Pipes like that one run under most of the streets. They bring water all over town — fountains, bathhouses, even some houses."

Isla thought about her own house, where water just appeared out of a tap and nobody thought twice about it. "How does the water even get here? There's no pump."

"No pump needed," the boy said. "Just height. Water runs downhill from higher ground outside town, through channels, into pipes, into fountains like this one. Gravity does the pushing."

Isla tested it: she dropped a leaf into the spout and watched it spiral down and vanish into the lion's mouth, then bob back up in the trough below. Simple. Obvious, once you saw it. She loved those kinds of answers — the ones that made you feel briefly brilliant for noticing.

"So every corner has one of these?" she asked.

"Most blocks, yes. Nobody should have to carry water very far."

A woman filled two clay jugs at the fountain, balanced one on each hip, and walked off without spilling a drop, like she'd done it ten thousand times. Probably she had.

Isla noticed something else: the street sloped very slightly downhill, and a thin trickle of water ran along the gutter beside the stepping-stones from yesterday. "Is that from the fountains too?"

"Runoff," the boy said. "Overflow has to go somewhere. It rinses the street. Mostly."

"Mostly," Isla repeated, eyeing the ground with new suspicion. Some mysteries, she decided, you were better off not solving with your nose.

The boy, for his part, seemed delighted that she cared about pipes at all. Most visitors wanted gladiators and temples. Isla wanted to know how the whole machine of the town actually worked, underneath the parts everyone noticed.

"You ask good questions," he said, almost grudgingly, and wrote something down.

"What was that?"

"Case notes," he said, and wouldn't say another word about it, which only made Isla more determined to get a look at that tablet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Oldest Arena
chapters.text:
A roar rolled across the rooftops, so loud Isla felt it in her chest before she heard it properly.

"That," the boy said, "is the amphitheater."

They rounded a corner and there it was: a huge oval bowl of stone, packed with people, built right into a bank of earth like a cup pressed into sand. Isla had seen plenty of sports stadiums. This one still made her stop walking.

"How old is this place?" she asked.

"Built around 70 BC," the boy said. "One of the oldest buildings of its kind the Romans ever put up. People come from towns all around to watch the games here."

Isla did the math in her head, which took a second, because the number was bigger than she expected. "That's over a hundred years before you were even born."

"Thank you for that," the boy said dryly. "I hadn't noticed how old the building was until a stranger from nowhere pointed it out."

Isla laughed. She was starting to like him, mystery name or not.

Inside, rows of stone benches rose in a steep curve, and the noise from the crowd came in waves — a cheer, then a groan, then a cheer again. She didn't need to see what was happening down in the sand to know a crowd when she heard one.

She noticed a number carved crudely into a stone step near the entrance, half worn away. "Somebody carved that," she said. "On purpose, right? Like a seat number, or a score?"

"Could be either," the boy admitted. "People scratch all sorts of things into these walls. Numbers. Names. Jokes about the gladiators, mostly unkind ones."

"So basically texting," Isla said.

The boy frowned, pen hovering. "I don't know that word."

"Never mind. Future thing."

He wrote it down anyway, which Isla found both hilarious and slightly alarming, since whatever he was writing to his uncle was clearly turning into a very strange letter.

They didn't stay for the games. Isla decided she'd rather keep walking the town than watch whatever was making the crowd that loud, and the boy didn't argue. He just nodded, like that was exactly the answer he'd hoped she'd give, and led her back out into the sunlight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Crack in the Wall
chapters.text:
Two streets over, Isla stopped in front of a painted wall. Most of it was a bright picture — a feast, a garden, a woman holding something she couldn't quite make out — but one corner looked different. The paint there was a slightly different shade, and underneath it, if she tilted her head, she could see a thin crack patched over with fresh plaster.

"Somebody fixed this," she said. "Recently."

The boy looked impressed, which Isla noted and filed away as a small personal victory. "You've got a good eye. There was an earthquake, years back, before I was born. It knocked down parts of the town — temples, walls, this fresco included." He tapped the painting. Fresco, he explained, was just the word for a picture painted straight onto wet plaster, so the color sank right into the wall instead of sitting on top of it.

"How bad was it?" Isla asked.

"Bad enough that some buildings still aren't finished being repaired," the boy said. "Scaffolding over there. New paint over here. The whole town's still patching itself up."

Isla ran a finger near the patched crack, careful not to actually touch the paint. An earthquake strong enough to crack a wall that thick, strong enough that years later people were still fixing the damage. It made the ground under her feel slightly less solid than it had a minute ago.

"Does it happen a lot? Earthquakes?"

"Often enough that nobody panics anymore," the boy said. "We live right next to a mountain. The ground grumbles sometimes. You learn to live with a grumbling neighbor."

He said it lightly, like it was nothing, and pointed up past the rooftops at a long green slope rising in the distance, wide and calm, with little farms climbing partway up its sides.

"That's the mountain?" Isla asked. It didn't look dangerous. It looked like a very large, very pleasant hill, the kind you'd want to have a picnic on.

"That's Vesuvius," the boy said. "Quiet as anything. Grapes grow well on its slopes. Some of the best wine in the region comes from up there."

Isla looked at the mountain a moment longer than she meant to. Something about the word *quiet* sat strangely next to the word *grumbling*, like two puzzle pieces that almost fit but not quite.

"Come on," the boy said, snapping his tablet shut. "I want to show you one more place before the light changes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Letters Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The light didn't just change. It jumped.

One moment Isla was in the crowded street. The next, she was standing on a breezy hillside across the water, the whole bay spread out below her like a map, with Pompeii a smudge of rooftops on the far shore. The boy was beside her, tablet in hand, except he looked older now — not by much, but enough that Isla noticed.

"Where did the time go?" she asked.

"Forward," the boy said quietly. "To the day I actually wrote the letters my uncle wanted."

Across the bay, a strange cloud was rising from the top of Vesuvius — the same quiet, grape-growing mountain from before, except now it wasn't quiet at all. The cloud climbed and climbed, then spread out wide at the top, like nothing Isla had ever seen a cloud do.

"What is that," she said, not really a question.

"That," the boy said, writing fast now, "is what I'm about to describe to my uncle. He's already sailing toward it — he commands the fleet docked right below us, and when he saw that cloud, he didn't sail away from it. He sailed closer, to see if he could help anyone trapped along the shore."

Isla stared at him. "Your uncle is sailing *toward* the volcano?"

"He's always been like that," the boy said, and for the first time, his voice wasn't quite steady. "Brave, or nosy, depending who you ask."

The date, Isla would learn later, was **August 24th, 79 AD**. Ash and pumice — light, bubbly, pale rock, blasted straight out of the mountain — were already falling on Pompeii, and would keep falling until the town lay buried under as much as **twenty feet** of it, deeper than Isla's whole house was tall.

"Is everyone going to be okay?" Isla asked, and she meant it as a real question, not a comfort.

The boy kept writing, jaw tight. "Many people got out in time, by road or by boat, in the hours before it got worst. Not everyone made it. My uncle reached the shore to help with the rescue boats — that part, at least, I know for certain, because people who were there told me so afterward."

Isla didn't say anything. She just watched him write, steady and careful, exactly as he'd promised his uncle he would: no exaggerating, every detail true.

"You should write it exactly like you're seeing it," she said finally. "Because someday, that's the only way anyone's going to know what this looked like."

The boy looked at her properly for the first time in a while. "That's exactly what I intend to do."

He signed the bottom of the tablet with a flourish, and Isla, leaning in without really meaning to pry, finally read the name.

*Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus.*

"PLINY!" Isla shouted, loud enough that a gull startled off a nearby rock. "You're *Pliny the Younger*! And your uncle is Pliny the Elder — the one who—"

"The one who went to rescue people, and whose letters about that day gave a name to every violent eruption like this one, ever since," Pliny said, almost smiling despite everything. "Scientists still call them **Plinian eruptions**. After me. I rather like that, honestly."

Isla sat down on the hillside grass next to him, and for a while neither of them said anything else. Across the water, the cloud kept climbing, and somewhere below it, a whole town was being wrapped up in ash like a gift nobody had asked for — one that wouldn't be opened again for a very, very long time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Men Who Dug in 1748
chapters.text:
The hillside dissolved into gold light again, and when it cleared, Isla was standing in a dusty pit, surrounded by men in old-fashioned coats, shovels in hand. Pliny was gone. The tile in her pocket had gone warm again, and this time it had clearly skipped nearly seventeen hundred years in one go.

"What year is it?" she asked a passing worker, who didn't even glance at her — which Isla decided meant something about this particular kind of time travel, and filed away as mystery number four.

**1748.** Pompeii had been buried so completely that for centuries almost nobody remembered exactly where it was. Workers digging in the area that year had struck ancient walls, then pottery, then whole rooms, and realized they'd found something nobody alive had seen in nearly two thousand years.

Isla crouched near a half-cleared doorway where a man was carefully brushing ash away from a low stone oven. Inside it, blackened but still perfectly shaped, sat a round loaf of bread — you could still see the baker's mark pressed into the crust, like a stamp.

"It just... stayed like that?" Isla asked.

"The ash fell so fast, and sealed everything so completely, that it froze the whole town in place," the worker said, not even looking up. "Paintings on walls. Writing scratched into plaster. Even that bread, still shaped exactly the way the baker left it."

Isla thought of the graffiti joke she'd grinned at days ago, and the campaign slogans painted on the bakery wall, and felt a strange little shiver — not of fear, but of something closer to awe. All of that had been waiting here the entire time, under the ash, for someone to finally dig down and find it.

She wandered further and found a room with walls still blazing in red and gold, figures mid-ritual, caught forever in paint. Later, she'd learn these were part of something called the Villa of the Mysteries — a name practically built for a girl like her.

"And a town nearby got buried too, didn't it?" she asked, remembering something Pliny had mentioned once, in passing. "Smaller one. By the sea?"

"**Herculaneum**," the worker said. "Buried by different material — something hotter and wetter that set almost like concrete. Preserved things Pompeii couldn't. Wooden furniture. Scrolls, even, rolled up tight, waiting to be read."

Isla stood very still for a second, picturing two thousand years of handwriting sitting in the dark, still legible, still waiting. That, she decided, was the best kind of mystery there was: one where the clues had been sitting right there the whole time, patient as anything, until somebody finally thought to look.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Picture in the Tile
chapters.text:
The light shifted one final time, gentler now, and Isla found herself standing above the ruins — not in them, but looking down, the way you might look at a map. Below her stretched streets, stepping-stones, the amphitheater, the forum, all laid bare under open sky, swarmed with visitors taking photographs.

"So people dig here, even now?" she asked, to nobody in particular, and a voice answered anyway — Pliny's, she realized, or something very like him, carried faint on the breeze.

"Even now. Pompeii is one of the most visited ancient sites on Earth these days — a protected place, kept and studied for everyone, forever. And they still haven't finished. Only about two-thirds of the town has ever been dug out. The rest is still down there, waiting."

Isla grinned at that. An entire third of a Roman town, still sealed under the ground, still unsolved. It was, she thought, the single best fact anyone had told her all night.

"And the mountain?" she asked, looking toward where Vesuvius would be.

"Still there. Still active. People live close by it even today, and scientists keep a very careful watch, because so many of them do."

Isla nodded slowly. A quiet, grape-growing mountain that could change everything in a single afternoon — that was worth keeping an eye on.

The gold light folded in around her one last time, and she landed back on her own bedroom floor with a soft thump, the shoebox still open beside her, the headlamp still shining its little circle on the carpet.

The tile sat warm in her palm. She turned it over, and this time, where before there had been only a chip of red and black glass, there was now a tiny, perfect picture: a street, a fountain shaped like a lion, a mountain rising quiet in the distance.

Isla set it carefully on her desk, next to her case notebook, and wrote at the top of a fresh page: *Case solved. Mostly.*

Because the truth was, two-thirds of a city wasn't the only thing still waiting underground. She had a feeling this tile had plenty more it hadn't shown her yet.

Tomorrow, there would be homework, and breakfast, and the ordinary business of being eleven. But the tile would still be warm on her desk when she got home, and somewhere in it, she was fairly sure, another street was waiting to be found.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there would be another street waiting inside the tile — and Isla already couldn't wait to find it.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real Roman town near the modern city of **Naples**, in what is now southern Italy.
The name **Pompeii** might come from an old word for **"five,"** maybe because five villages once joined together to form the town.
Pompeii's streets had raised **stepping-stones** so people could cross without stepping in mud, with gaps wide enough for cart wheels.
Dark **lead pipes** carried water from higher ground into fountains and bathhouses all across town, pushed along by gravity alone.
Pompeii's **amphitheater**, a huge stone arena for watching games, was built around **70 BC**, making it one of the oldest of its kind.
On **August 24th, 79 AD**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried the town in ash and rock.
The eruption buried Pompeii under as much as **twenty feet** of ash and pumice, a light, bubbly volcanic rock.

A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two detailed letters about it — which is why scientists still call this kind of violent eruption a **Plinian eruption**.
The ash fell so fast that it froze the whole town in place, preserving things like **bread still shaped inside an oven**.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten until workers digging in **1748** found ancient walls and uncovered the buried town.
Colorful wall paintings called **frescoes** were found in Pompeii, including the famous ones in the **Villa of the Mysteries**.
A nearby town called **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption, but under material that preserved even **wooden furniture and scrolls**.
Even today, only about **two-thirds of Pompeii** has been dug out, and **Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano that scientists carefully watch.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Isla returned to her bedroom floor with the mosaic tile now showing a tiny picture of a Roman street and fountain, and wrote in her notebook that the case was 'solved, mostly,' certain the tile still had more buried stories left to show her.
